title: Improve performance of spline prefiltering
body:
## Context

Higher-order interpolation (order >= 2) prepares spline coefficients with
causal and anti-causal IIR recurrences. This spline prefiltering step can
take substantially more time than the subsequent interpolation kernel. This MR
parallelizes eligible prefilter passes and removes redundant memory passes,
copies, and per-call metadata transfers. It also reduces repeated coordinate
arithmetic in batched interpolation. Public signatures are unchanged.

These changes complement other interpolation performance MRs from earlier this
year (#1055, #1060). With those improvements, the spline prefilter became the
dominant cost.

On `main`, preparing spline coefficients consumed **88–95% of GPU kernel
time** in representative order-3 rotations, motivating the focus of this
MR. 

Two new cooperative kernels accelerate real float32/float64 workspaces, while
the pre-existing general per-line kernel handles complex-valued and remaining cases not
eligable for these faster cooperative kernels. All three kernels support spline
orders 2–5 and reuse the existing boundary formulas. Public signatures are
unchanged; regrouping recurrences can change floating-point rounding. The output
matches the prior implementation to within a small floating point tolerance.

Here a **line** varies along the filtered axis with all other indices fixed;
a **sample** is one value along that line. Consecutive samples follow axis
order and need not occupy adjacent memory addresses. For C-contiguous arrays,
their stride is 1 element along the last axis, 3 along the width of an RGB
image, and the image width along axis 0 of a 2D image.

## Optimization 1: Shared-memory warp prefilter for contiguous and interleaved lines

Commits: 09927f8f (kernel), c1f6f0e7 (device-aware float64 dispatch),
and 5aca9205 (bank-access explanation). Shared kernel documentation:
81db51e2 (also covers Optimization 2).

This kernel increases within-line parallelism from **one thread per line to
one warp (32 threads) per contiguous line**. For interleaved data
(e.g. RGB or RGBA images), one warp handles a group of 2–4 channel lines
together. Each warp stages a contiguous line, or a contiguous
`(samples, channels)` block with 2-4 interleaved lines, using coalesced global
loads. A "lane" is a thread's position within a warp. Each lane handles a
**run**: a consecutive chunk of samples along the filtered line. Lanes
summarize their chunks, combine the summaries through warp shuffle scans, then
filter their chunks in shared memory and store results coalesced. The same
kernel handles scalar, RGB/RGBA, and other small trailing dimensions, and
accepts element-aligned output views.

For one sample, the forward recurrence is `y[i] = z*y[i-1] + g*x[i]`, where
`x[i]` is the current line's input value (an image sample or an intermediate
result from earlier filtering), and `y[i]` is the intermediate coefficient
after this causal update. The reverse sweep and any remaining poles complete
the spline coefficients for this axis. `z` is the spline pole, and `g` is the
normalization gain required for conversion to spline coefficients: 6 for
cubic (order 3), or 120 for quintic (order 5). The gain is fused into the
first pole's forward sweep on each axis; subsequent poles use `g = 1`.

Each chunk needs the filtered value immediately before it: its incoming
**carry**. Its final filtered value is the outgoing carry needed by the next
chunk.

A **run map** summarizes a whole chunk as `y_out = A*y_in + B`, where
`y_in` and `y_out` are its incoming and outgoing carries. For `m` forward
updates, `A = z**m`; `B` combines the contributions of that chunk's input
samples, including the gain. Thus `(A, B)` describes the chunk's effect on
the same filtered state `y`.
**Carry propagation** means determining these boundary values across chunks.
The reverse sweep uses the same idea with the traversal direction reversed.

To determine the carries in parallel, we use the prefix scan illustrated for
summation in [GPU Gems 3, §39.2.1 and Figure 39-2](https://developer.nvidia.com/gpugems/gpugems3/part-vi-gpu-computing/chapter-39-parallel-prefix-sum-scan-cuda).
Here addition is replaced by associative composition of the run maps:
for two consecutive chunks, let `y0` be the incoming carry, `y1` the value
after the first chunk, and `y2` the value after the second:

```text
y1 = A1*y0 + B1
y2 = A2*y1 + B2 = (A2*A1)*y0 + (A2*B1 + B2)
```

The combined chunk therefore has summary `(A2*A1, A2*B1 + B2)`.
This reduction of first-order recurrences to scans is
derived in [Blelloch, *Prefix Sums and Their Applications*, §1.4.1](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~guyb/papers/Ble93.pdf#page=14).

The five shuffle rounds use `__shfl_up_sync`; `__syncwarp` separates shared
memory handoffs, as described in [*Using CUDA Warp-Level Primitives*](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/using-cuda-warp-level-primitives/).
Staging separates coalesced global transfers from each lane's recurrence
accesses, analogous to **Coalesced Transpose Via Shared Memory** in
[*An Efficient Matrix Transpose in CUDA C/C++*](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/efficient-matrix-transpose-cuda-cc/).
Its **Shared Memory Bank Conflicts** section explains the related layout principle
behind our odd run lengths; our kernel changes the run partition rather than
padding a transpose tile.

After this new kernel was implemented, a search for pre-existing
implementations identified that this same sort of linear recurrence pattern
also comes up in the Mamba neural network architecture. For more about these
patterns for the Mamba use case, please see Sarnthein's
[*Linear Recurrences Accessible to Everyone*](https://safelix.github.io/blog/2024/linrec/).
A concrete example of the same pair-composition rule in production is Mamba's
[`SSMScanOp<float>`](https://github.com/state-spaces/mamba/blob/main/csrc/selective_scan/selective_scan_common.h)

### Kernel Dispatch Criteria

Dispatch to this kernel requires sufficient device shared memory as well as at
least 32 samples to provide sufficient work for the 32-lane warp and amortize
cooperation overhead. At an FP32:FP64 throughput ratio of 64:1, float64 uses
the staged path for lines of at least 512 samples, or at most 256
single-channel lines; otherwise serial boundary initialization can outweigh
the parallel recurrence. A cached per-device CUDA ratio scales these
restrictions on GPUs with stronger FP64, reaching the float32 shape rules at
4:1 or better. Missing or invalid ratios retain the 64:1 defaults. This
scaling is a heuristic; the measurements below use the unchanged RTX A6000
dispatch. Strided cases outside this dispatch use the segmented kernel;
remaining cases use the general fallback.

### Performance

Against the retained general kernel, contiguous-axis calls improved
**2.32–7.81x** for float32 (orders 3 and 5) and
**2.68x** for float64 (order 3) in the 512²/2048² cases.
For interleaved lines, the staged warp path improved **2.48–3.46x**
for float32 RGB/RGBA and **2.81x** for float64 RGB, compared
with the retained segmented kernel. These one-axis calls also include their
workspace initialization copy.

## Optimization 2: Block-parallel prefilter for strided axes

Commits: da0fbdce (kernel) and 81db51e2 (shared kernel documentation).

After introducing within-line parallelism for contiguous lines, Nsight
Systems identified the still-serial axis-0 prefilter as a major remaining
cost. The second cooperative kernel family extends within-line parallelism
to strided axes while preserving coalesced accesses across neighboring lines.

For a non-last axis of a C-contiguous workspace, a block handles 32 adjacent
lines and splits each line into runs. At a fixed position along the filtered
axis, adjacent lanes read neighboring values in dimensions after that axis
in the array's shape—for axis 0 of a 2D image, neighboring columns. This
preserves coalesced global accesses. Shared memory holds each run's affine
carry map; composing these maps supplies the
incoming state before each thread replays its run. This adds parallelism
within long lines without staging the entire strided axis.

This kernel reuses the first-order recurrence composition described above,
combining run summaries through shared memory and block barriers instead of
a warp shuffle scan. Mapping neighboring lanes to neighboring memory
locations follows the same coalescing principle described in the matrix
transpose reference; it does not stage or transpose the image data.

This local-summary, boundary-reconstruction, and replay pattern has direct
spline-specific prior art. [Nehab et al. (2011), §§1, 4.3, and 8](https://doi.org/10.1145/2070781.2024210).
compute bicubic and biquintic B-spline coefficients using blocked recursive
filters. [Chaurasia et al. (2015), §6.1 and §8](https://doi.org/10.1145/2790060.2790063)
explain the local-filter, boundary-aggregation, and recomputation steps and
apply them to bicubic B-spline interpolation. Both share the recurrence
decomposition used by our two cooperative kernel families. Their image-wide
tiled pipelines differ from this kernel's processing of each line within
one thread block. These references were discovered by literature search
after this implementation was complete.

Against the retained general kernel, complete one-axis calls improved
**2.70–6.71x** for float32 at 512²/2048² (orders 3 and 5), and
**3.49x** for float64 at 2048² (order 3). These isolated dispatch
comparisons include the initial copy into a supplied output workspace.

## Optimization 3: Reduce memory passes, metadata transfers, and transform setup

Commits: 15472ef9 (batch coordinates), 4525c8f0 (gain fusion),
dd568372 (general-kernel launch sizing), addde396 (workspace reuse),
869cd0bc (scalar metadata), and 87d6e0e2 (host rotation setup).

Fuse spline gain into the first causal pass. Filter initialized workspaces
in place from the first axis, reuse private padded arrays, and skip self-copies.
Caller inputs retain their existing ownership and output/dtype behavior.
Pass counts and dimensions as runtime scalar kernel arguments instead of
allocating and uploading a metadata array for each filtered axis. Tune the
general fallback's block size for contiguous and low-stride lines.

Batched interpolation omits known-zero coordinate terms and reuses outer batch
offsets. Rotation keeps host matrices on the host through affine setup,
avoiding device uploads followed immediately by host readbacks.

With cooperative kernels absent, the gain/workspace/metadata/launch updates
improved complete prefilter GPU-event timings **1.08–2.63x** and host-call
timings **2.67–2.84x** across six selected cases. This isolates the
supporting changes; the net rotation results below also include coordinate
and host-matrix setup improvements.

## Combined result summary

With all changes, complete prefilter calls improved **2.29–6.68x**
against `main` (`a3d57b6d`). Complete float32 rotations improved
**4.93–5.50x** for the two grayscale images and
**3.00x** for the batched RGB case. These are direct
branch-versus-main measurements; the individual ranges above use separate
controls and should not be multiplied.

| Measured call | Input / dtype / order | Main (ms) | Branch (ms) | Net speedup |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Complete `spline_filter` | `(64, 64)`, float32 / 3 | 0.247 | 0.079 | 3.15x |
| Complete `spline_filter` | `(512, 512)`, float32 / 3 | 0.294 | 0.081 | 3.61x |
| Complete `spline_filter` | `(2048, 2048)`, float32 / 3 | 1.844 | 0.276 | 6.68x |
| Complete `spline_filter` | `(512, 512)`, float32 / 5 | 0.388 | 0.090 | 4.29x |
| Complete `spline_filter` | `(512, 512)`, float64 / 3 | 0.359 | 0.157 | 2.29x |
| Batch-aware prefilter | `(2, 512, 512, 3)`, float32 / 3 | 0.490 | 0.106 | 4.64x |
| Complete `rotate` | `(1920, 1080)`, float32 / 3 | 1.767 | 0.321 | 5.50x |
| Complete `rotate` | `(1080, 1920)`, float32 / 3 | 1.546 | 0.314 | 4.93x |
| Complete `rotate` | `(2, 512, 512, 3)`, float32 / 3 | 0.888 | 0.296 | 3.00x |

Complete prefilter calls include allocation and required copies. Complete
`rotate` calls also include interpolation (angle 17°, `reshape=False`,
`mode="reflect"`, order 3).

### Measurements

RTX A6000, CuPy 14.2.0 and `cupyx.profiler.benchmark(max_duration=2.0)` with
ten warmups.

title: Image pyramid performance: reduce filtering, downsampling, and clipping overhead
body:
## Summary
Stacked on top of #1182, so please review and merge that one first

This change reduces the overhead of repeated Gaussian filtering, especially for
image pyramids and batch-processing workloads that reuse the same filter
parameters. Several other sources of overhead were addressed in image pyramids to give overall large improvement in 

### Motivation

#### Caching

A multidimensional Gaussian filter is implemented as a sequence of 1D
convolutions. Previously, each call regenerated an identical host-side kernel
for every filtered axis and copied it to the GPU. This fixed setup cost is
significant for small and medium images, repeated calls, and
`pyramid_gaussian`, where the same sigma is used at each pyramid level.

The new cache pays the coefficient-generation and host-to-device-copy cost on
the first use of a parameter combination. Later axes, pyramid levels, and
calls reuse the GPU kernel directly.

Similarly, `ndimage.zoom` previously copied its short sequence of zoom factors
to a new GPU array on every call. A pyramid performs one zoom per reduction,
so these tiny transfers contributed a fixed cost at every level. The bounded
factor cache now performs this transfer once per unique device/factor/dtype
combination.

The cache key includes the CUDA device ID so an array is never reused on the
wrong device. Both caches copy new entries on a private non-blocking stream
per device and wait only for that stream before publishing fully initialized
arrays. Cache misses therefore do not drain work already queued by the caller.
Cache hits need no CUDA event or GPU stream operation. Consumer streams are
tracked on the host, and evicted allocations remain alive until their queued
reads have completed.

In a later commit, the shared cache was extended to cover vendored Prewitt,
Sobel, and Laplace, plus public separable Sobel, Prewitt, Scharr, and Farid
filters.

#### Remove synchronization and improve efficiency of clipping

Higher-order interpolation previously synchronized to read the clipping range
and to decide whether constant padding expanded that range. Most clipping now
uses device-resident reductions and device-side decisions. Intermediate-sized
constant-mode inputs retain the old host-side short-circuit to avoid the
measured regression when `cval` is within the input range. A combined reduction
carries NaN-safe extrema and a NaN flag together, avoiding separate image scans
and the synchronization in CuPy's public `nanmin`/`nanmax` warning checks.
Float32 comparisons preserve subnormal extrema despite CuPy's flush-to-zero
compilation. All-NaN results retain their NaN behavior; this clipping path omits those
host-side warning checks. The constant-fill path retains the distinction
between NaN-propagating and NaN-ignoring output range checks based on the input.

A generic scalar CuPy reduction uses a single block. C-contiguous arrays of at
most 512 KiB use it directly to avoid staging overhead; strided inputs retain
the conservative 4096-element cutoff. Larger contiguous real inputs compute
partial ranges in parallel and merge them in the last finishing block of the
same kernel launch. Float16, complex, and strided inputs retain separate partial
and merge launches, including a separate incomplete-tail reduction when needed.
Both approaches read each image element once for the range computation; the
merge only reads the small arrays of partial results.

The terminal-level shape check also applies to finite layer limits, avoiding a
discarded reduction after the last useful layer.

## More details on individual changes made

### Caching-based improvements
- Cache generated 1D Gaussian kernels by CUDA device, sigma, derivative order,
  radius, and dtype.
  - Reuse the cached kernels in both `gaussian_filter` and `gaussian_filter1d`
    instead of rebuilding the NumPy coefficients and copying them to the GPU
    for every call and every filtered axis.
  - Store Gaussian coefficients in the filter's working dtype. Coefficients are
    still generated and normalized in NumPy's existing precision, then cast
    during the initial transfer. This avoids repeated `float64`-to-`float32`
    conversion kernels on cache hits, including two conversions per 2D
    `float32` pyramid reduction. The cache byte limit uses the stored dtype.
  - Initialize cacheable Gaussian kernels on a private non-blocking stream,
    waiting only for that stream before publishing them. This preserves safe
    cross-stream reuse without draining the caller's stream or adding per-hit
    event waits. Oversized kernels retain asynchronous same-stream behavior.
  - Keep cache memory bounded: the LRU holds at most 64 entries, and individual
    kernels larger than 1 MiB bypass the cache. Cached kernel data is therefore
    limited to approximately 64 MiB per process, plus evicted storage still
    needed by queued consumers. Completion events protect this storage from
    premature reuse; subsequent misses reclaim completed allocations.
- Cache the small device array of zoom factors by CUDA device, factor tuple,
  and dtype instead of rebuilding and copying it for every pyramid level.
  - Bound the zoom-factor cache to 128 tiny entries. Factor arrays use the
    same private initialization stream and allocation-lifetime protection as
    Gaussian coefficients, without per-hit CUDA operations.
- Cache fixed coefficients for vendored Prewitt, Sobel, and Laplace filters,
  and public separable Sobel, Prewitt, Scharr, and Farid filters. A shared
  64-entry cache keys coefficients by device, dtype, and magnitude normalization,
  using the same initialization and allocation-lifetime policy as the other caches.

### Miscellaneous Other Improvements
- Call the vendored `ndimage.gaussian_filter` directly from pyramid smoothing,
  using `axes` to exclude the channel axis while avoiding redundant wrapper
  work. Sigma sequences covering just the spatial axes now also work with
  `channel_axis`.
- Preserve negative-sigma validation in the pyramid APIs.
- Skip Gaussian pyramid reductions whose output shape would be unchanged,
  including when a finite `max_layer` exceeds the available pyramid levels.
- Improvements to min/max/NaN-detection and clipping
  - Keep resize/warp clipping bounds on the device for nonconstant modes and
    small or large constant-mode inputs. Higher-order pyramid interpolation
    benefits from this shared clipping path. Constant-fill range checks and
    clipping are fused, preserving unused `cval` and NaN behavior.
  - For constant-mode inputs larger than 512 KiB and at most 16 MiB, retain the
    host-side input range check so an in-range `cval` avoids output reductions.
    Inputs without NaNs use ordinary extrema and fused clipping when `cval`
    is outside the range; NaN-containing inputs fall back to combined ranges.
    This deliberately restores one or two host readbacks in this size band.
  - Compute NaN-safe minimum, maximum, and a NaN flag together in one scan of
    each image. Small images use one combined reduction kernel; larger images
    use parallel partial ranges followed by a merge. Strided arrays are reduced
    through views without copying the full image to flatten it. This replaces
    two separate reductions for nonconstant clipping and six for constant-mode
    clipping with one combined range computation per participating image when
    using the device-side path.
  - Add keyword-only `assume_finite=False` to `resize` and all four pyramid APIs.
    Opting in promises finite inputs and intermediates, selecting ordinary min/max
    reductions without NaN detection or host range checks. Generators forward the
    promise through every level without rescanning the initial image. Constant
    mode rejects nonfinite `cval` values when opting in; defaults are unchanged.
    Each API's Notes identifies this as a cuCIM-only extension and warns that
    violating the finite-value promise may skip output clipping.
  - Use the direct single-block reduction for C-contiguous arrays up to 512 KiB,
    independently of the 4096-element chunk size used for staged reductions.
    Other layouts retain the 4096-element direct cutoff. This reduces staging
    overhead for intermediate image sizes without assigning large images to a
    single block.

### Follow-up optimizations

The following measurements compare each update with its preceding implementation,
rather than measuring cumulative gains against `main`.

- **axis-0 Gaussian filtering.** Collapse unfiltered trailing dimensions of
  C-contiguous arrays into a 2D view for the existing shared-memory kernel.
  At 4096² RGB, the axis-0 Gaussian pass improved **2.25x** (1.54 to 0.68 ms),
  and the complete two-axis Gaussian call improved **1.54x** (3.12 to 2.02 ms).  
  Small cases were close to unchanged. A separate correctness fix also restores   
  copying computed filter results back to overlapping output buffers.
- **interior- and last-axis filtering.** View eligible C-contiguous nD arrays
  as independent leading rows, a filtered axis, and independent trailing values.
  A shared-memory tile packs small trailing strides into full warps; larger
  strides reuse the existing 3D kernel. Boundaries map only the filtered axis,
  preserving trailing components. Short axes and unsupported layouts retain
  the elementwise path. This extends the common `correlate1d`/`convolve1d`
  dispatch used by Gaussian, uniform, and separable edge filters; zero-weight
  taps retain the elementwise implementation's NaN/Inf behavior.
  Relative to `48cc7f00`, the 4096² RGB axis-1 Gaussian pass improved **2.34x**
  (1.44 to 0.62 ms), and the complete two-axis call improved **1.60x**
  (2.05 to 1.28 ms). Complete 4096² RGB Laplacian pyramids (`max_layer=6`) improved **1.33x**
  for order 1 and **1.07x** for order 3; Gaussian pyramids improved **1.08x**
  for order 3, while the already-fused order-1 path was unchanged.
  At 1024² RGB, complete public Sobel, Scharr, Prewitt, and Farid calls improved
  **1.07x–1.10x**; vendored uniform filtering improved **1.10x** and
  Gaussian–Laplacian **1.22x**, while vendored Sobel stayed close to unchanged.
  On 64×256×256 volumes filtered over all three axes, complete Gaussian,
  Gaussian–Laplacian, and public Sobel calls improved **1.50x**, **1.56x**,
  and **1.14x**, respectively.
- **per-level setup.** Pass `preserve_range=True` for already converted
  pyramid images and let Gaussian filtering allocate its output. Complete
  order-1 pyramids improved up to **1.14x**; the largest GPU-bound cases were
  close to unchanged.
- **smoothing and downsampling.** For eligible C-contiguous float32/float64
  inputs with even spatial dimensions, `downscale=2`, `order=1`, and scalar
  sigma from 0 through 4, combine Gaussian smoothing with adjacent-sample
  averaging in separable strided correlations. Each pass computes only retained
  samples; other inputs use the existing path. Boundary mapping is retained,
  but reassociation changes floating-point rounding. Complete Gaussian pyramids
  improved **2.08x** at 4096² grayscale, **3.34x** at 4096² RGB, and **2.28x**
  at 8192² grayscale with the default sigma.
- **Laplacian differences.** Reuse each resized buffer for its difference
  with the smoothed image, saving one allocation per reduced level. The input,
  smoothed image, and previous yields remain intact. Complete-call timings were
  near unchanged, within about 4% of the baseline.
- **range reduction.** Use a per-call completion counter and device fence
  so the last finishing block merges partial ranges without a second launch
  or a spin wait. Float16, complex, and strided inputs retain the staged fallback.
  Range-only GPU-event speedups were **1.15x–3.07x**, with host-call
  speedups of **2.43x–3.44x** across the measured float32/float64 cases.


## Benchmark Results

Refreshed on **2026-10-21**. These tables compare `main` (a3d57b6d) with
Pyramid, including the interpolation base's spline kernels. Order-3 timings
were recorded at 686cf926, whose runtime code matches the current Pyramid
tip 4f8f8736 on interpolation base 81db51e2. Order-1 and standalone
Gaussian results are retained from ebeecbe6; those paths do not use the
spline prefilter. All results report cumulative gains over `main`, rather
than isolating this MR's changes relative to its interpolation base.

All table timings are GPU-event milliseconds for complete calls, with pyramid
generators fully materialized. Unless specified otherwise, inputs are float32,
`max_layer=6`, `downscale=2`, `preserve_range=True`, and `mode="reflect"`.

### `pyramid_gaussian`, order 1

Grayscale inputs. Geometric-mean speedups across eight sizes are **6.31x** for
GPU-event time and **7.35x** for host-call time. This path includes fused
smoothing/downsampling for eligible inputs, cached coefficients, and reduced
per-level setup overhead.

| Input shape | Before (ms) | After (ms) | Speedup |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 64 x 64 | 2.806 | 0.395 | 7.11x |
| 128 x 128 | 2.830 | 0.386 | 7.32x |
| 256 x 256 | 2.834 | 0.390 | 7.27x |
| 512 x 512 | 2.842 | 0.393 | 7.23x |
| 1024 x 1024 | 2.808 | 0.395 | 7.12x |
| 2048 x 2048 | 2.839 | 0.394 | 7.21x |
| 4096 x 4096 | 2.857 | 0.410 | 6.97x |
| 8192 x 8192 | 3.270 | 1.277 | 2.56x |

### `pyramid_gaussian`, order 3

Grayscale inputs. Geometric-mean speedups across eight sizes are **3.23x** for
GPU-event time and **4.14x** for host-call time. This path includes the
interpolation base's spline gain fusion, workspace copy removal, scalar
metadata arguments, and segmented-scan kernels for strided, contiguous, and
interleaved lines, plus Gaussian and clipping updates.

| Input shape | Before (ms) | After (ms) | Speedup |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 64 x 64 | 5.630 | 2.119 | 2.66x |
| 128 x 128 | 5.650 | 2.074 | 2.72x |
| 256 x 256 | 5.651 | 2.023 | 2.79x |
| 512 x 512 | 5.725 | 1.989 | 2.88x |
| 1024 x 1024 | 5.846 | 1.881 | 3.11x |
| 2048 x 2048 | 7.528 | 1.896 | 3.97x |
| 4096 x 4096 | 13.239 | 2.581 | 5.13x |
| 8192 x 8192 | 32.429 | 10.054 | 3.23x |

At 8192 x 8192, host-call time falls from 32.421 to 1.921 ms, while GPU-event
time improves 3.23x. The remaining large-image spline and filtering work still
limits device throughput.

### RGB and constant-padding coverage

RGB inputs use `channel_axis=-1`. Reflect-mode gains:

| Shape | Order-1 speedup | Order-3 before (ms) | Order-3 after (ms) | Order-3 speedup |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 128 x 128 x 3 | 7.78x | 5.859 | 2.111 | 2.78x |
| 512 x 512 x 3 | 7.78x | 5.917 | 2.093 | 2.83x |
| 2048 x 2048 x 3 | 7.48x | 10.681 | 2.147 | 4.98x |
| 4096 x 4096 x 3 | 5.05x | 23.805 | 7.932 | 3.00x |

Constant-mode order-3 cases cover spatial sizes 128, 512, 2048, and 4096. The
fills are the original input's min/max midpoint and `cval=2`, outside the
normalized input range. Fill membership is still checked per level.

| Layout | Fill | Default-path speedup range |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grayscale | midpoint | 2.15x–3.25x |
| Grayscale | outside | 2.45x–3.33x |
| RGB | midpoint | 1.79x–2.36x |

title: Fix custom-center rotation and channel offsets
body:
closes #1180

## Summary
This PR fixes two issues in `cucim.skimage.transform.rotate` when constructing
an affine transform for images with trailing channel or batch dimensions.

With a custom center and `resize=False`, the output shape remained `None`.
Appending the trailing dimensions raised
`TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'NoneType' and 'tuple'`:

```python
# image.shape == (100, 300, 3), an RGB image
rotated = rotate(image, 1.0, mode="edge", center=(0, 50))
```

With `resize=True`, the call completed but placed the spatial translation in
the channel-coordinate column of the larger affine matrix. Each channel
therefore received a different spatial offset, causing color separation:

```python
# image.shape == (100, 300, 3), an RGB image
rotated = rotate(image, 1.0, mode="edge", center=(0, 50), resize=True)
```

Initialize the spatial output shape to the input's first two dimensions, then
replace it with the computed bounds when resizing. Embed the 2D rotation in
the larger identity matrix with translation in its final column, preserving
independent channel and batch dimensions. The corrected shape and channel
behavior matches scikit-image.

Regression tests compare grayscale, RGB, and RGBA rotations with scikit-image
for orders 0 and 1. Additional tests check independent trailing dimensions
for orders 0, 1, and 3, with and without resizing.

title: Added marker-based watershed segmentation
body:
## Summary

This PR adds a GPU implementation of `cucim.skimage.segmentation.watershed`.
This resolves issues https://github.com/rapidsai/cucim/issues/49 and https://github.com/rapidsai/cucim/issues/89. The compact watershed implementation can act as
a superpixel method (there was a request for a different superpixel algorithm in https://github.com/rapidsai/cucim/issues/855)

The implementation replaces scikit-image's serial priority queue with a
parallel, cellular-automaton-style relaxation of path costs. For standard
watershed (`compactness=0`), each pixel carries a 64-bit key that is compared
lexicographically:

```text
key = (L, D)
L   = minimax path cost from a marker (the flooding level at which the pixel is reached)
D   = steps taken since the path last rose to level L
```

Every unlabeled pixel repeatedly takes the smallest key offered by its
neighbors:

```text
key(q) = min over neighbors p of  max((image[q], 1), (L(p), D(p) + 1))
```

`D` plays the role of scikit-image's first-in-first-out `age` tie-break, so the
keys reproduce scikit-image's flooding order: by value first, then
breadth-first within a level. This is the lexicographic watershed cost of
Lotufo & Falcão (ISMM 2000, DOI 10.1007/0-306-47025-X_37), written explicitly
as `C = [M, d]` by Felkel et al. (Comput. Graph. Forum 2001, DOI
10.1111/1467-8659.00495). A sequential FIFO queue keeps `d` implicitly; a
parallel relaxation has to store it. Packing both into one 64-bit integer
makes key comparisons and in-place updates single 64-bit operations.

Once the keys converge, each pixel takes the label of its lowest-key neighbor,
and labels are resolved by pointer jumping along these parent links to the
markers.

Because a key strictly increases along every step, the relaxation has a single
fixed point and every update order reaches it. The kernels can therefore
update keys in place without synchronization, including a shared-memory
block-asynchronous kernel, and still produce deterministic labels that are
identical across kernels and runs.

For compact watershed, the priority also includes a distance penalty from the
source marker:

```text
priority = image[pixel] + compactness * euclidean_distance(pixel, marker)
```

This cost depends on which marker a pixel is reached from, so the fixed point
is no longer unique and compact watershed uses a double-buffered (Jacobi)
relaxation of labels, keys and source coordinates instead. Keys use the same
`(priority, D)` layout, and candidates with equal priority are ranked by the
offering neighbor's key, approximating scikit-image's tie-break.

## Features

- Supports seeded watershed on CuPy arrays (n-dimensional, fewer than 2**31
  elements).
- Supports marker arrays, `markers=None` (local-minima markers), and integer
  marker generation.
- Supports masks (any non-zero mask value is inside the mask).
- Supports integer connectivity.
- Supports standard watershed with `compactness=0`.
- Supports compact watershed with `compactness > 0`.
- Supports `watershed_line` via post-processing.
- Preserves marker dtype (and negative marker values) in the output.
- Deterministic results for every kernel.
- A shared-memory block-asynchronous kernel is used by default for standard
  watershed on images with at most three dimensions of size greater than one
  (dimensions of size one are dropped and 1D images are processed as a single
  row).
- Adds benchmark coverage for 2D and 3D watershed cases.
- Adds `cucim.skimage.util.regular_grid` and `regular_seeds`.

## Kernels

1. **Block-asynchronous key relaxation (default for standard watershed with at
   most three dimensions of size > 1)**

   Each thread block loads a 16x32 (2D), 8x8x8 (3D) or 1x512 (single-row,
   e.g. 1D) tile plus a one-pixel
   halo of keys into shared memory. It relaxes the tile in place until no key
   in the tile improves, or until `inner_iterations` local iterations (64 in
   2D, 32 in 3D) have run. It then writes improved keys back to global memory.
   Launches repeat until no block improves any key; the flag is read back
   every 4 launches (launches past convergence are cheap because every tile
   is skipped). Each tile records the last launch in which it improved a key.
   A block exits immediately unless its own tile or a neighboring tile
   improved in the previous or current launch, so late launches only touch
   the tiles around the moving flood front.

   Standard watershed always runs on an equivalent shape: dimensions of size
   one have no in-bounds neighbors and are dropped (with connectivity clipped
   to the remaining dimensions), and a 1D image is processed as a single row.
   This lets such images use this kernel (e.g. a 1D signal of 100,000 samples
   takes 4.3 ms instead of 56.9 ms), and both kernels still break exact ties
   identically.

2. **Global key relaxation (standard watershed with four or more dimensions of
   size > 1, or `use_block_async=False`)**

   Each launch performs one in-place relaxation step for every pixel whose
   neighbors improved in the previous or current launch, tracked with a
   one-byte launch stamp per pixel. The convergence flag is read back only
   every `convergence_check_interval` launches (default 8) to limit
   host<->device synchronization.

   Both kernels converge to the same unique keys, so `use_block_async` only
   affects speed.

3. **Label resolution**

   Each pixel's parent is its first neighbor (in a fixed order) holding the
   smallest key. One kernel then resolves the parent chains: each thread
   walks its own chain for up to 16 steps per launch, replacing every pointer
   it passes with its grandparent (path halving, a form of pointer jumping),
   and writes the marker's label once it reaches it. Most images need one or
   two launches, and a chain as long as the image only a few.

4. **Compact watershed**

   A double-buffered relaxation reads labels, keys and source coordinates
   from one set of buffers and writes to another, swapping each iteration.
   This keeps the result deterministic. A double-buffered per-pixel
   "changed in the previous sweep" flag lets pixels whose neighbors did not
   change skip the neighbor scan. Pixels that did not change also skip the
   copy between buffers, because the output buffer already holds their
   value. Only the moving flood front is streamed through memory, and every
   sweep's result is unchanged.

5. **Watershed lines**

   After convergence, a non-marker pixel becomes a line pixel (label 0) if a
   neighbor with a different label was reached earlier (a smaller key), with
   ties broken by label value.

## Relation to Prior Work

The implementation combines published ideas with a few choices of its own; it
does not implement any single published algorithm. The `watershed` docstring
lists the references.

- **Model:** marker-controlled watershed by flooding (Meyer & Beucher 1990;
  Beucher & Meyer 1993), with scikit-image's priority-queue semantics.
- **Path cost:** the lexicographic `(f_max, steps within the level)` cost of
  Lotufo & Falcão (2000), written as `C = [M, d]` by Felkel et al. (2001).
  Labels are the root labels of the optimum-path forest of the image
  foresting transform (Falcão, Stolfi & Lotufo 2004).
- **Parallel relaxation:** in the spirit of the Ford-Bellman
  cellular-automaton watersheds of Kauffmann & Piché (2008, 2010), which relax
  a summed path cost with synchronous double-buffered updates.
- **Block-asynchronous tiling:** follows Section 4.2 of Quesada-Barriuso, Heras
  & Argüello (2013), the method NVIDIA NPP's (unseeded) 2D watershed
  implements. Their watershed is unseeded and updates each tile in synchronous
  steps with the halo held fixed; on plateaus this misplaces watershed lines,
  which their artifact-free variant (Section 4.3) corrects with a plateau
  distance. Here keys are updated in place, plateaus are ordered by `D`, and
  the unique fixed point makes the result independent of scheduling.
- **Label resolution:** each pixel's parent is its lowest-key neighbor, and
  parent chains are resolved by
  [pointer jumping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointer_jumping), as in the
  path-reducing GPU watershed of Yeghiazaryan & Voiculescu (WACV 2018).
- **Skipping quiet regions:** pixel-level active sets have precedent in GPU
  shortest paths (Harish & Narayanan 2007) and cudaIFT (Gonçalves et al.
  2019); the tile-level launch stamps were not found in the watershed work we
  checked.
- **Specific to this implementation:** `D` is stored explicitly (Felkel et al.
  note that a FIFO queue keeps it implicitly) and packed with the f_max cost
  into one 64-bit integer, so the relaxation has a unique fixed point that any
  update order reaches. cudaIFT, the closest GPU work found, has no such term
  and only matches the sequential cost map, not the labels.

## Testing

This PR adds watershed tests covering standard and compact watershed, masks,
connectivity, marker handling (arrays, integer counts, `None`, negative
labels), watershed lines, dtype preservation, and 1D/2D/3D/nD inputs. Many
cases are adapted from scikit-image's own watershed tests and assert exact
equality with scikit-image's expected output. Tolerances remain only where
scikit-image's own tests use them, and for compact watershed.

Additional tests check that:

- The global and block-asynchronous kernels produce identical labels for 2D
  and 3D inputs, all connectivities, small and odd shapes, and
  `inner_iterations=1`.
- Every region is connected to its marker.
- Results match scikit-image exactly on smooth random 2D and 3D images
  (and to within 0.5% of pixels for compact watershed).
- `convergence_check_interval` does not change results.
- Inputs are validated (e.g. NumPy inputs, a non-default `offset`, and
  unsupported `use_block_async=True` requests, which warn and fall back to the
  global kernel).

## Compatibility With scikit-image

The cuCIM implementation follows the scikit-image `watershed` API.

API differences:

- Inputs must be CuPy arrays; NumPy arrays and Python `list`/`tuple` markers
  are rejected.
- `connectivity` must be an integer; an ndarray footprint is not accepted.
- `offset` is accepted for signature compatibility but only the default
  (`None`) is supported; any other value raises `NotImplementedError`.
- A few cuCIM-only keyword-only arguments are added: `use_block_async`,
  `inner_iterations`, and `convergence_check_interval`. They only affect
  performance, not the result.

Result differences:

- Standard watershed matches scikit-image except where neighboring pixels are
  tied in both `L` and `D`. There, a fixed neighbor order decides instead of
  the full priority-queue insertion order. Typical cases are pixels
  equidistant from two markers on a plateau, and quantized images with large
  plateaus.
- Images are processed in single precision (float32), so float64 inputs whose
  values differ only beyond float32 precision are treated as ties.
- Compact watershed keeps, for each pixel, the source marker it was first
  reached from with its final priority. It differs more from scikit-image near
  region boundaries and can leave small groups of pixels disconnected from the
  rest of their region.
- Watershed lines are computed after flooding rather than during it, so line
  pixels can differ.

Pixel agreement with scikit-image on the scikit-image gallery examples (see
images below) and synthetic data:

| Case | Standard watershed | Compact watershed |
|:--|--:|--:|
| Two overlapping circles (distance transform) | 99.93% | |
| Coins, foreground/background markers | 100.00% | |
| Coins, 468 grid seeds | 99.88% | 98.56% (compactness=0.01) |
| Coins, `markers=468` | | 88.87% (compactness=0.001) |
| Eagle, uint8 gradient | 99.36% | |
| Human mitosis nuclei | 99.99% | |
| Astronaut, `markers=250` | | 95.71% (compactness=0.01) |
| Smooth random 2D (4- and 8-connectivity) | 100.00% | 99.77% (0.01), 100.00% (1.0) |
| Smooth random 3D | 100.00% | 99.96% (0.01) |
| Random 2D quantized to 16 levels | 97.28% | |

(Image comparisons will be attached in a follow-up comment)


## Benchmark Results

### Performance Notes

Watershed runtime is data dependent. Because this implementation is iterative,
the number of iterations required to converge depends on image content, marker
placement, mask shape, plateau size, and compactness settings.

In particular:

- Large flat regions take more iterations to converge, since the flood must
  cross them step by step.
- The block-asynchronous kernel performs many of these steps per launch in
  shared memory, which reduces global memory traffic and the number of
  launches by roughly an order of magnitude compared with the global kernel.
- Compact watershed has additional distance-priority work and always uses the
  global (double-buffered) kernel, which skips pixels away from the flood
  front.

Benchmark results on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 are tabulated below. Representative
device speedups versus the scikit-image CPU implementation are about 40-160x in
2D and 65-540x in 3D for standard watershed (default kernel), and about 25-45x
in 2D and 130-275x in 3D for compact watershed, depending on input shape and
settings.

Benchmarks were run with:

```bash
python cucim_segmentation_bench.py -f watershed -i <shape> -d float32 -t 3
```

The benchmark uses fixed-seed synthetic blob data (`rng=5`) for reproducible
inputs. For these PR-summary runs, sparse zero-valued separator planes/lines
were added to avoid one dominant connected foreground component:

- 2D: zero rows/columns every 128 pixels
- 3D: zero planes every 32 voxels

Standard 2D and 3D watershed is benchmarked with both the block-asynchronous
kernel (`use_block_async=True`, the default for 2D/3D) and the global kernel
(`use_block_async=False`). Compact watershed always uses the global kernel.

Hardware:

- GPU: NVIDIA RTX A6000
- CPU: Intel(R) Core(TM) i9-10980XE CPU @ 3.00GHz

Times are means in milliseconds. Speedup is `CPU host mean / GPU device mean`.

### 2D Watershed, Compactness 0

title: Port the Python bindings to nanobind, ship cp312-abi3 wheels, and use the C++11 string ABI
body:

4. If your pull request is not ready for review but you want to make use of the

5. If your pull request is ready to be reviewed without requiring additional
   work on top of it, then remove the `[WIP]` label (if present) and replace
   it with `[REVIEW]`. If assistance is required to complete the functionality,

   same PR. If the assistance is done by members of the rapidsAI team, then no

   person(s) assisting to commit to their personal fork of the project. If that

   merged.

6. Once all work has been done and review has taken place please do not add
   features or make changes out of the scope of those requested by the reviewer
   (doing this just add delays as already reviewed code ends up having to be
   re-reviewed/it is hard to tell what is new etc!). Further, please do not
   rebase your branch on main/force push/rewrite history, doing any of these

Many thanks in advance for your cooperation!

-->


This PR moves the `cucim.clara` Python bindings from pybind11 to nanobind and builds `_cucim` against the CPython 3.12 stable ABI. CI then builds one `cp312-abi3` wheel and one Python-version-independent conda package per CUDA version and architecture, and tests them on Python 3.12, 3.13, and 3.14. The PR also removes `_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=0`, so libcucim, its plugins, and `_cucim` use the default C++11 string ABI of libstdc++.

Closes #1029.
Closes #1163.

## Related issues and PRs

None of these is closed. This PR uses no closing keyword for them, and GitHub closing keywords do not close pull requests.

- **#1151** (open issue) proposes Cython bindings built as `cp311-abi3`, a version-independent conda package, stable artifact names, and one build per CUDA version and architecture. This PR delivers those packaging goals with nanobind and `cp312-abi3`. `main` dropped Python 3.11 in #1177, and [a comment on #1151](https://github.com/rapidsai/cucim/issues/1151#issuecomment-5610886602) explains why nanobind is preferred. Two of #1151's non-goals do not hold here. This PR changes libcucim's string ABI (#1163), and it changes some Python behavior (see "Release notes"). The `rapidsai/ci-imgs` cleanup in #1151 is not done, because it belongs to that repository. Closing #1151 is up to its author.
- **#1153** (open PR, based on #1152's branch `codex/cython-abi3`) reduces the build matrix. Commit 7 cherry-picks its one commit unchanged, and commit 8 fixes the docs build that it did not update. Once this PR merges, #1153 is superseded but stays open until someone closes it.
- **#1152** (open PR) is the Cython migration. Commit 6 adapts its conda recipe change. This PR replaces its binding approach, so it is superseded in the same way.

## Who is affected

- **Python users of `cucim.clara`.** Members of the scoped enums `CacheType`, `DeviceType`, and `FileHandleType` no longer support `int()` or `__index__()`. `DLDataTypeCode` members still support both, because the new binding makes `DLDataTypeCode` an `enum.IntEnum`. Boolean arguments accept only `True` and `False`, and path and text arguments are stricter. See "Release notes" for the full list. cuCIM's own `test_image_cache.py` used `int(cache.type)` and needed a one-line change per assertion, so downstream code may need the same change.
- **C++ code that links libcucim**, including out-of-tree plugins, must be rebuilt. This is an intentional C++ ABI break.
- **Packaging.** Wheels are tagged `cp312-abi3`. The conda package is built once on Python 3.12 and installs on Python 3.12 and later. Each PR pipeline builds 4 conda Python packages and 4 wheels instead of 12 of each. The test jobs are unchanged.

## Commits

Review the PR commit by commit.

1. **Add regression tests for the cucim.clara binding surface.** `test_bindings.py` and `test_bindings_cuimage.py` pin what callers of `_cucim` observe. Tests that need no generated image are in `test_bindings.py`, so they also run where `imagecodecs` is missing (aarch64 wheel jobs). On the pybind11 build, every test passes except `test_profiler_config_keyword`, which crashes the interpreter.
2. **Port the Python bindings from pybind11 to nanobind.** `python/pybind11` becomes `python/nanobind`, built with nanobind 3.1 and `nanobind_add_module(... STABLE_ABI ...)`. pybind11, its 2.11 patch, and pybind11_json are removed. This commit kept pybind11's conversions in `python/nanobind/compat.h`. Commit 5 removes its string caster, and commit 10 removes the file.
3. **Tag cucim wheels cp312-abi3 and audit the stable ABI.** `setup.py` sets `py_limited_api` to `cp312`. `ci/validate_wheel.sh` fails if there is no `cp312-abi3` wheel, and it runs `abi3audit --strict`.
4. **Use the C++11 string ABI.** This commit removes all seven `_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=0` settings and the old-ABI branch of `ImageMetadata`. One setting was a PUBLIC compile definition on `cucim::cucim`, which forced the old ABI on every consumer.
5. **Use nanobind's stock string caster and take paths as std::filesystem::path.** Text parameters accept only `str`, and path parameters use nanobind's `stl/filesystem.h`. `docs/source/api.rst` gains a "Path and text arguments" section.
6. **Make the cucim conda package independent of the Python version.** This is Michael Sarahan's recipe change from #1152 (`1a07dd7a`), adapted to Python 3.12 and without its Cython build changes.
7. **Reduce ABI3 build matrix.** Michael Sarahan's commit from #1153, cherry-picked unchanged with `-x`. Conda and wheel builds keep the lowest Python per CUDA version and architecture, and the CI scripts use `--stable` artifact names.
8. **Download the stable conda artifact in the docs build.** `ci/build_docs.sh` downloads the conda package too, and #1153 did not change it. Without this commit, the docs jobs look for a per-Python artifact that no job uploads.
9. **Use the canonical SPDX notice in ci/build_wheel.sh.** `verify-copyright` requires it because commit 7 changes the file.
10. **Use nanobind's own enum and bool behavior and remove compat.h.** Enums use `nb::enum_`, and `DLDataTypeCode` keeps `nb::is_arithmetic()`. Boolean parameters take `bool`, and conversions use `nb::cast`. Two new `docs/source/api.rst` sections document the changes. This follows [review feedback](https://github.com/rapidsai/cucim/pull/1188#discussion_r4395286056) that slightly preferred the breaking change to the compatibility shims.
11. **Update .github/CODEOWNERS.** `python/nanobind` is owned by `@rapidsai/cucim-python-codeowners` as well as `@rapidsai/cucim-cpp-codeowners`.
12. **Update conda/recipes/cucim/meta.yaml.** The host requirement `python ={{ py_abi_min }}` becomes `python {{ py_abi_min }}.*`, matching the `python-abi3` line. Conda's `MatchSpec` treats both forms as `python=3.12`.
13. **Update conda/recipes/cucim/meta.yaml.** The run requirement `python >=3.12` becomes `python`, and `python-gil` stays. `python-abi3` supplies the Python 3.12 lower bound, as described in "Packaging and build".

Commits 11 to 13 apply jakirkham's review suggestions.

## Release notes

The `cucim.clara` bindings use nanobind instead of pybind11 and are built against the CPython 3.12 stable ABI. One `cp312-abi3` wheel installs on Python 3.12, 3.13, 3.14, and 3.15. Public names are unchanged.

A probe recorded 183 cases on `main` (pybind11, `8a67a731`) and on this branch, and every change below comes from that comparison. The probe and the tests cover only the calls they make.

**Compatibility note**

**Equality with integers is preserved.** Members of `CacheType`, `DeviceType`, and `FileHandleType` compare unequal to integers in both the previous pybind11 bindings and this branch. For example, `io.Device("cuda").type == 2` remains `False`. `DLDataTypeCode` members continue to compare equal to their corresponding integers. For example, `DLDataTypeCode.DLUInt == 1` remains `True`. The new binding uses `enum.IntEnum` to preserve this behavior.

**Breaking changes**

- **Enums are classes from Python's `enum` module.** `cache.CacheType`, `io.DeviceType`, and `filesystem.FileHandleType` are `enum.Enum` classes. `DLDataTypeCode` is an `enum.IntEnum`.
  - `int(member)` and `operator.index(member)` raise `TypeError` for `CacheType`, `DeviceType`, and `FileHandleType`. Use `member.value`.
  - An unknown value, such as `DeviceType(99)`, raises `ValueError`. pybind11 returned an unnamed `<DeviceType.???: 99>` member.
  - `repr(member)` is `DeviceType.CUDA` instead of `<DeviceType.CUDA: 2>`. `str()` and `format()` still give `DeviceType.CUDA`.
  - Members of the three `Enum` classes hash by name instead of by value.
  - `DLDataTypeCode` members are now `int` instances and support `<` and `>`.
- **Boolean arguments accept only `True` or `False`.** pybind11 also accepted `None` and numbers such as `numpy.bool_`, `0`, `1`, and `1.0`. Pass `bool(value)` instead.
  - `read_region(drop_last=, shuffle=)`, `filesystem.CuFileDriver(no_gds=, use_mmap=)`, and `CuImageIterator(ending=)` raise `TypeError` for other values.
  - `CuImage.cache(record_stat=)` and `CuImage.profiler(trace=)` read these values from `**kwargs`, so they raise `RuntimeError: std::bad_cast`.
  - `pread` requires the read-only flag in a buffer's `__array_interface__` or `__cuda_array_interface__` data tuple to be a `bool`, and raises `RuntimeError` otherwise. NumPy and CuPy set a `bool`. `pwrite` does not read the flag.
- **Path and text arguments are stricter.** A `bytearray` path raises `TypeError`. So does a path with an embedded NUL character, where pybind11 cut the path at the NUL and opened the shorter path. Text arguments that are not paths, such as `dim_order`, device names, and the `filesystem.open` flags, raise `TypeError` for `bytes` and `bytearray`.
- **Some error messages changed.** Exception types are unchanged.
  - A call that matches no signature reports "incompatible function arguments" instead of "incompatible constructor arguments".
  - A value that fails to convert inside a binding still raises `RuntimeError`, with the message "std::bad_cast". pybind11 reported "Unable to cast Python instance of type ... to C++ type '?'". Examples are `CuImage.cache("per_process", capacity="1")` and a `read_region` location that is not an integer.

**Fixes and additions**

- `CuImage.profiler(trace=True)` no longer crashes the interpreter. The pybind11 binding released the GIL and then read its keyword arguments.
- `read_region` accepts a NumPy `int64` array for `location`. pybind11 checked only for buffer format `q`, and NumPy reports `l` on 64-bit Linux.
- `DLDataType(code, bits, lanes)` also accepts a plain integer `code` that names a member, such as `1`.
- Path arguments accept `os.PathLike` objects. A file name that is not valid UTF-8 can be passed as `bytes` or as an `os.fsdecode()` string.

`docs/source/api.rst` documents the enum, boolean, path, and text changes.

## C++ ABI break

- Exported functions that take or return `std::string` now use `std::__cxx11::basic_string`, so their mangled names change.
- `ImageMetadata` always stores `dims_` and `coord_sys_` as `std::pmr::string`. This changes its layout.
- The `cucim::cucim` CMake target no longer exports the definition, so consumers compile with their compiler's default ABI.

A binary built with `_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=0` against an older libcucim references string symbols that libcucim no longer exports. It fails at load time or on the first call. Even where no string crosses the boundary, such a binary can disagree on the `ImageMetadata` layout. Don't mix libcucim or plugin binaries from before and after this change in one process. Python users of the wheel need no action, because the wheel bundles libcucim, the plugins, and `_cucim`. The cucim conda package requires the libcucim package of the same version.

## Packaging and build

- nanobind (`>=3.1.0,<3.2.0a0`) is a build dependency in `dependencies.yaml`.
- The conda and wheel builds in `pr.yaml` and `build.yaml` use the `matrix_filter` that cuDF and cuVS use, which keeps the lowest Python per CUDA version and architecture. With the current matrix, that is Python 3.12.
- The conda package is built with `python_version_independent: true` against `python-abi3`. Its build string is `cuda<major>_cp312_abi3_…`.
  - The recipe's run requirements list `python` and `python-gil` without a version.
  - The Python 3.12 lower bound comes from `python-abi3 3.12`, whose run_exports add `cpython >=3.12` and `_python_abi3_support 1.*`. This was checked in the conda-forge build `he1d15d4_3`.
  - A package built locally at `17319017` depended on `python >=3.12` from the recipe at that time, plus `cpython >=3.12`, `_python_abi3_support 1.*`, and `python-gil`, with no `python_abi` pin. No package was built locally from commits 12 and 13, so their package metadata is not verified here.
- `ci/build_python.sh`, `ci/build_wheel.sh`, `ci/test_python.sh`, `ci/test_wheel.sh`, and `ci/build_docs.sh` name the Python artifacts with `rapids-artifact-name --stable`.
- `./run` copies only `_cucim.abi3.so`. Python imports a stale `_cucim.cpython-3XX-*.so` in preference to an abi3 module, so a leftover build output would shadow the new module.
- `nanobind_add_module` uses `PROTECT_STACK` and `NOMINSIZE`. Without them, nanobind adds `-fno-stack-protector` and `-Os` after the conda hardening flags.
- `LICENSE-3rdparty.md` and `3rdparty/` list nanobind and robin-map instead of pybind11 and pybind11_json.

## Validation

The branch includes `main` at `b715b157` (#1190), which skips `cucim.skimage` tests when GitLab rate-limits sample-data downloads. Below commit 10, the tree differs from `17319017` only by the seven files that #1190 changes.

**Hosted CI at `17319017`** (commits 1 to 9, before #1190):

- All 12 package builds pass: conda C++, conda Python, and wheel, each for CUDA 12.9 and 13.3 on amd64 and arm64, all on Python 3.12. The docs build and style checks also pass.
- 5 of 7 test jobs pass:
  - Conda tests on Python 3.12 (amd64, CUDA 12.2) and 3.14 (amd64, CUDA 13.0).
  - Wheel tests on Python 3.12 (amd64), 3.13 (arm64), and 3.14 (amd64).
- The other 2 test jobs fail, conda on Python 3.13 (arm64, CUDA 13.3) and wheels on Python 3.12 (arm64, CUDA 12.2). In each, every failure is a `cucim.skimage` test that got HTTP 429 from GitLab: 21 failed or errored tests in one job and 39 in the other. #1190 fixes this.

**Hosted CI at `1596499e`** (commit 10, with #1190). All 35 check runs of [run 40776096307](https://github.com/rapidsai/cucim/actions/runs/40776096307) passed. They include the 12 package builds, the docs build, and all 7 test jobs. This description does not report hosted CI for commits 11 to 13.

**Local, at commit 10.** All local checks ran on one x86_64 machine (i9-13900K, RTX A6000) with GCC 14.4 and CUDA 13.3, in conda environments.

- **Build.** A full `./run build_local all release` at commit 9 with #1190 succeeds. Its only warnings are four `-Wclobbered` warnings in cuslide's `libjpeg_turbo.cpp`, which this PR does not change. At commit 10, the five binding sources recompile with no warnings.
- **Tests.** The in-tree build runs `pytest tests/unit tests/performance` in `python/cucim` with the one `cp312-abi3` module:
  - Python 3.12 and 3.13: 164 passed, 5 skipped.
  - Python 3.14: 161 passed, 5 skipped, 3 xpassed. The 3 xpassed are cases of `test_read_random_region_cpu_memleak` marked xfail for #1043. No pybind11 build was tested on 3.14, so this PR does not claim to fix #1043.
  - The updated enum and bool tests fail 6 times against the commit-9 build, so they detect the change.
- **Behavior.** The probe gives the same output for commit 10 on Python 3.12, 3.13, and 3.14. Against commit 9, it differs only in enum `int()`, `operator.index()` and `repr()`, boolean arguments, and conversion messages.
- **pre-commit.** `pre-commit run --hook-stage manual --all-files`, as CI runs it, passes on a clean clone.
- **Docs.** `sphinx-build -b dirhtml` succeeds with the same 5 warnings at commits 9 and 10.

**Local, at earlier commits.** None of these was rerun at commit 10.

- **Wheel, commit 5.** The wheel built on Python 3.12 and repaired with `auditwheel` passes `ci/validate_wheel.sh`: pydistcheck, `twine check --strict`, the tag check, and `abi3audit --strict`. Installed on Python 3.12, 3.13, and 3.14, it passes the test suite of that commit.
- **Conda, `17319017`.** libcucim and cucim conda packages build from clean clones with conda-build 26.9.1. The cucim package built once for Python 3.12 installs and passes `tests/unit` and `tests/performance` on Python 3.12, 3.13, and 3.14. The recipe before commit 6 produces a package that can't be installed on 3.13 or 3.14.
- **CI artifact routing, `17319017`.** A script expands each job's matrix with shared-workflows' jq program. Every conda test, wheel test, and docs job downloads an artifact that a build uploads, built on a Python no newer than its own. Without commit 8, the docs jobs fail this check.
- **String ABI, commits 4 and 5.** None of the compile commands sets `_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI`. `nm` shows that libcucim, the plugins, and `_cucim` import only `std::__cxx11` string symbols. Before commit 4, libcucim imported 23 old-ABI string symbols.
- **End to end, commit 4.** Opening a TIFF, `read_region` for a region, a pyramid level, and batches (compared with tifffile), and `cucim convert` with readback all pass.

## Not validated

- Hosted CI results for commits 11 to 13 (`67b37775`), which this description does not report. Commit 11 changes only `.github/CODEOWNERS`, and commits 12 and 13 change the conda recipe's Python requirements.
- Local wheel and conda package builds from commit 10 or later. Commit 10 changes only the binding module, its tests, and the docs.
- The CI wheel platform. The local wheel was repaired as `manylinux_2_39`, and CI builds `manylinux_2_28` wheels.
- A pip-only environment. Local tests ran in conda environments.
- nanobind versions other than 3.1.0.
- C++ consumers of libcucim outside this repository.

## Historical performance measurements

These numbers are from commit 4, measured against `main` at `8a67a731`. They were not rerun after commits 5 to 10. Commits 6 to 9 change only packaging and CI. Commits 5 and 10 change argument conversion for strings, paths, enums, and booleans, and the benchmark calls few of those.

- Property access (`shape`, `dims`, `dtype`, `resolutions`, `spacing()`, `channel_names`) took 1.1 µs instead of 2.1 µs, 45% less. This is associated with the nanobind build, which also differs from the pybind11 build in LTO and default flags.
- `img.metadata` took 6.3 µs instead of 7.3 µs, 14 to 16% less. This is associated with commit 4, which changes both the C++ string ABI and the `ImageMetadata` member layout.
- A 16x16 `read_region` took 17.8 µs instead of 20.0 µs, 11% less. The difference was clear in the second run only.
- For opening a file, cold start, full-image JPEG and deflate reads, threaded tile reads, the batched iterator, and GPU reads, these runs did not establish a reliable improvement or performance equivalence.

<details>
<summary>Benchmark method and full results (commit 4)</summary>

Three trees were built with `./run build_local all release` in one conda environment (Python 3.12.16, GCC 14.4, CUDA 13.3, nvImageCodec 0.9.0, NumPy 2.5.4, CuPy 14.2.0):

- main at `8a67a731`, pybind11, `_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=0`.
- The control, this branch at commit 3, nanobind, `_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=0`.
- This branch at commit 4, nanobind, C++11 string ABI.

Each measurement is a fresh process pinned to performance cores. The build order rotates every round. For the 7-round workloads, one build goes first one extra time. Every process checks that libcucim, `_cucim`, and the plugins load from its own build tree, and the outputs match across builds. The libcucim tile cache is off, and the files are in the page cache.

Lower is better. Each value is the median over processes, with the min to max range and the process count. Each process reports the median of 7 to 15 samples after warmup. "None measurable" means that the ranges overlap or that a Mann-Whitney test gives p ≥ 0.05. It does not mean that the builds perform the same.

| Workload (data) | main (pybind11) | commit 4 | Change | Associated build change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `import cucim` + first `CuImage(path)`, cold process | 543 ms (536 to 572, n=15) | 542 ms (535 to 557, n=15) | none measurable | |
| `CuImage(path)`, 4096x4096 JPEG TIFF | 46.2 µs (43.7 to 48.2, n=7) | 45.5 µs (44.0 to 47.5, n=7) | none measurable | |
| `img.metadata` (JSON to dict) | 7.3 µs (7.3 to 7.4, n=7) | 6.3 µs (6.2 to 6.4, n=7) | **−14%** (rerun −16%) | string ABI and `ImageMetadata` layout commit −18%, nanobind build +3 to +4% |
| `shape`, `dims`, `dtype`, `resolutions`, `spacing()`, `channel_names` | 2.1 µs (2.0 to 2.3, n=7) | 1.1 µs (1.1 to 1.1, n=7) | **−45%** (rerun −45%) | nanobind build |
| 16x16 `read_region` + `np.asarray`, tiny JPEG TIFF | 20.0 µs (18.2 to 21.3, n=7) | 17.8 µs (16.5 to 18.8, n=7) | −11% in both runs (run 1 p=0.004 with overlapping ranges, run 2 p=0.001) | nanobind build |
| Full-level `read_region` 4096x4096, JPEG | 46.4 ms (45.6 to 47.4, n=7) | 46.6 ms (45.7 to 47.8, n=7) | none measurable | |
| Full-level `read_region` 4096x4096, deflate | 60.0 ms (59.0 to 65.4, n=7) | 59.8 ms (59.0 to 61.6, n=7) | none measurable | |
| 256 tiles of 256x256 via `ThreadPoolExecutor(8)`, JPEG | 6.99 ms (6.78 to 7.48, n=7) | 6.76 ms (6.66 to 6.96, n=7) | none measurable (−3% and −5% in the two runs, ranges overlap) | |
| Batched iterator, 256 random 256x256 patches, `num_workers=8`, `batch_size=32` | 22.9 ms (22.3 to 24.3, n=7) | 22.8 ms (22.3 to 24.0, n=7) | none measurable | |
| GPU `read_region(device="cuda")` 4096x4096 JPEG, synchronized | 45.4 ms (43.9 to 47.7, n=7) | 45.3 ms (44.3 to 45.8, n=7) | none measurable | |

A profile of the `metadata` work shows about 25% fewer allocator samples after commit 4. This fits C++11 strings that store short JSON keys and values inline, but the mechanism is inferred, not measured directly.

In a `perf` profile of the threaded JPEG tile scan, 76% (pybind11) and 80% (nanobind) of on-CPU samples are in the cuslide plugin, mostly JPEG decoding. The binding modules hold 0.8% and 0.5% of on-CPU samples. These percentages are not the total binding overhead, and they are not fractions of wall time.

Limitations:

- One machine and one Python version (3.12).
- A desktop with other processes running. The load average was 4.5 to 6, and GPU utilization from other processes and the display was 42% before and 82% after the run. Pinning and interleaving reduce the effect.
- Synthetic TIFFs from `python/cucim/tests/util/gen_image.py`. The deflate file is 185 KB because the pattern compresses well.
- Locally built conda binaries, not CI wheels.
- The pybind11 build links with LTO. The nanobind build does not, and it strips the module. "The nanobind build" means the binding together with its default build settings.
- The `cucim convert` CLI is not benchmarked because it uses OpenSlide and tifffile rather than the bindings.

The benchmark scripts and raw measurements (339 processes over two runs) are not part of this PR and can be shared on request.

</details>

## Binding build-mode comparison at `67b37775`

[A separate study](https://github.com/rapidsai/cucim/pull/1188#issuecomment-6508514243), run on October 29, 2026 at `67b37775`, compared three nanobind configurations with byte-identical libcucim and plugin binaries: linked with `STABLE_ABI` (this PR), linked with the full API, and split mode. Its results support keeping the current build.

- No image-read speedup was demonstrated for either alternative in the tested workloads.
- The full-API build's keyword-argument call latency was about 5 to 9% lower, 6 to 11 ns per call. Uneven load on the sibling CPU thread makes the exact size uncertain.
- 1,250 timed processes completed. On every variant, the tested `cucim.clara` tests gave 139 passed and 1 skipped.

The study used local builds on CPython 3.12.16 on one desktop machine. It does not validate production wheel or conda packaging at `67b37775`, and it is separate from the historical measurements above.

## Pre-existing issues found, not fixed here

These issues also occur on `main`.

- Installed wheels contain two copies of libcucim. The plugins use the copy that `auditwheel` grafts, so they bypass a cache configured from Python. Current nightly wheels have the same layout.
- The `CuFileDriver.pread` and `pwrite` bounds check ignores `buf_offset`, so a nonzero offset can access memory past the end of the buffer.
- Calling `repr`, `metadata`, or `save()` on a closed `CuImage` crashes.
- `read_region(..., device="cuda")` on a TIFF that is not JPEG-compressed aborts with "Unsupported compression method".
- Concurrent reads with a small per-process tile cache can crash in `PerProcessImageCache::remove_front`. The crash happened in 4 to 7 of 20 runs on each build.

Assisted-by: Claude Code

title: Skip tests when GitLab rate-limits sample data downloads
body:
## Description

Closes #1189.

Since October 19, 2026, GitLab.com limits unauthenticated traffic to 60
requests per hour per IP address
([announcement](https://about.gitlab.com/blog/rate-limit-change-2026/)). Tests
that download scikit-image sample data from GitLab (`eagle`, `brain`,
`cells3d`, and reference arrays for the rank filter, footprint and restoration
tests) now fail in CI with `429 Too Many Requests`. scikit-image only turns
`ConnectionError` into a skip, so the `HTTPError` raised for a 429 fails the
test, and `test_rank.py`, which fetched its reference data at import time, fails
to collect.

This PR is a workaround that skips these tests when the data cannot be
downloaded, while we decide where else to host the data (about 16 MB in total):

- `fetch()` and a new `load_sample_data()` helper in
  `cucim.skimage._shared.testing` skip the test if the download fails.
- A 429 is not retried. GitLab asks clients to wait until the hourly window
  resets, so pooch's retries 1 to 3 seconds apart cannot succeed. After the
  first 429, later downloads in the session are skipped without a request.
  Other failures (e.g. a dropped connection) are still retried 3 times.
- Data shared by several tests is loaded in module-scoped fixtures, and the
  rank filter reference data is loaded only by the two tests that use it.

With every download returning 429 and an empty cache, the affected tests make
one request in total and skip instead of failing. On `main`, each of these tests
downloads the data itself, with 4 attempts. Tests that don't need the data
still run.
