title: Fix misc bugs in `cucim.skimage.measure.regionprops_table`
body:
## Summary

This PR fixes bugs in cuCIM's batch region properties
(`regionprops_table(..., batch_processing=True)`, which calls
`regionprops_dict`). This includes wrong coordinates and pixel counts on label
images of 2³² or more pixels. It also fixes two closely related bugs: one in
the per-label path (`batch_processing=False`) and one in cuCIM's vendored
`binary_fill_holes`. The bugs were found while writing a technical explainer
of the batch implementation and while optimizing it.

Each bug has its own commit with its own tests, so the commits can be reviewed
one at a time (22 commits, listed at the end). The branch is based on `main`
(a0e27d1e) and does not depend on the `intensity_median` PR.

## Is the bug also in scikit-image?

**None of the bugs fixed here is present in scikit-image 0.26.** Every fix
either makes cuCIM return what scikit-image returns, or fixes a cuCIM-only
property, parameter, option or vendored function that has no scikit-image
counterpart. In every case where a scikit-image counterpart exists, the fixed
cuCIM result now matches it, apart from the rounding of `intensity_std` (see
"Not addressed here").

The one bug with an upstream history is the sign of `orientation` for ±45°
regions. scikit-image fixed it in 0.21 (scikit-image PR #6836, "Sign error fix
in measure.regionprops for orientations of 45 degrees"), but both cuCIM paths
still had the old sign.

### Fixes that restore agreement with scikit-image

Examples are from the commit messages and tests; "spacing (2, 2)" values are
for a test image with two ellipses.

| Commit | Properties | cuCIM path | Before → after (= scikit-image) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `orientation` | batch and per-label | `cp.eye(10)`: −π/4 → π/4 |
| 2 | `eccentricity` | batch | single-pixel region: NaN → 0 |
| 3 | `intensity_std` | batch | constant float32 region of 0.1 or 1000.3: NaN → 0 |
| 6 | `centroid`, `centroid_weighted` | batch | spacing (2, 2): `centroid-0` 28 → 40 |
| 7 | `centroid_weighted` | per-label | region starting at row 3, spacing 2: 7.95 → 10.95 |
| 8 | `area_bbox`, `extent` | batch | spacing (2, 2): `area_bbox` 493 → 1972 |
| 9 | `moments_normalized`, `moments_weighted_normalized` | batch | spacing (2, 2): `moments_normalized-2-0` 0.179 → 0.045 |
| 9 | `moments_hu`, `moments_weighted_hu` | batch | non-unit spacing: values → `NotImplementedError` |
| 10 | `area_convex`, `solidity` | batch | spacing (2, 2): `area_convex` 373 → 1492 |
| 11 | `perimeter`, `perimeter_crofton` | batch | spacing (2, 2): 73.9 → 147.9; anisotropic spacing: values → `NotImplementedError` |
| 14 | `area_filled` | batch | filled pixel count → filled area (× pixel area) |
| 16 | `area_filled`, `image_filled` | batch | labels not in raster order: [36, 4, 36] → [36, 36, 4]; touching regions: [128, 0] → [64, 64] |
| 18 | `bbox`, `centroid`, `centroid_local`, moments and properties derived from them | batch | (65537, 65536) image, region on the last row: `bbox` rows [0, 1) → [65536, 65537) |
| 22 | `intensity_min`, `intensity_max` | batch | float64 image of uniform values in [0.1, 1): off by up to 1.7e-9 (minimum) and 2e-8 (maximum), rounded to float32 → the exact pixel values |

Notes:

- **Spacing (commits 6–11, 14).** `regionprops_dict` did not pass `spacing`
  to these functions (or, for the perimeters, did not scale the result),
  although scikit-image applies it. The `NotImplementedError`s are the ones
  scikit-image and cuCIM's per-label path already raise.
- **Per-label `centroid_weighted` (commit 7).** This is the only spacing bug
  that was also in cuCIM's per-label path. `RegionProperties.centroid_weighted`
  added the bounding-box start without multiplying it by the spacing;
  scikit-image uses `slc.start * spc`.
- **`intensity_std` (commit 3).** The one-pass variance
  `(sumsq − mean²·count) / count` can round to a small negative number for a
  constant region, and `sqrt` then returns NaN. It is now clipped at 0, using a
  comparison rather than CUDA's `max` (which is `fmax`). That way, regions that
  contain NaN or ±inf still return NaN, as `numpy.std` does.
- **Images of 2³² or more pixels (commit 18).** See "Images of 2³² or more
  pixels" below.
- **float64 minima and maxima (commit 22).** The batch kernel combines the
  threads' partial minima and maxima with `atomicMin` and `atomicMax`. For
  `double`, these are CuPy's overloads (`cupy/_core/include/cupy/atomics.cuh`),
  whose compare-and-swap loops compare with `fminf` and `fmaxf`, the
  single-precision functions, so every stored value was rounded to float32
  and could even lie outside the region's range. CuPy's development version
  (October 2026) still has them. CUDA has no native atomic minimum or maximum
  for `double`, so the shared kernel preamble now defines
  `cucim_atomic_min` and `cucim_atomic_max`: CUDA's `atomicMin` and
  `atomicMax` for every other type, and for `double` a compare-and-swap loop
  that compares in double precision. The fix in CuPy itself would be to use
  `fmin` and `fmax` there.
- **Filled properties (commit 16).** scikit-image fills each region's holes on
  its own crop. The batch path filled the union of all labels and relabeled it
  with `measure.label`, so values came back in the wrong order and touching
  regions were merged. See "Filled-region properties" below.

### Fixes without a scikit-image counterpart

| Commit | What | Before → after |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | `pixels_per_thread` kernel parameter (batch only) | 128–255 overflowed the `int8_t` per-thread counters: `num_pixels` of a 64 × 64 region was 4294963200 (128) or 0 (255) → 4096 |
| 5 | `axis_lengths` (cuCIM-only property) | `properties=["axis_lengths"]` alone: `KeyError` → works |
| 12 | `copy_output_to_host=True` (cuCIM-only option) with `batch_processing=False` | `TypeError` for `centroid_weighted` with more than one region → works |
| 13 | docstrings of `regionprops_perimeter`, `regionprops_perimeter_crofton` (batch module) | said `perimeter` skips the boundary along the image edge; both perimeters count it |
| 15, 17 | vendored `ndimage.binary_fill_holes` | `structure` was ignored with the default `origin` and `axes` → it is used |
| 16 | `label_filled`, `num_pixels_filled` (cuCIM-only properties) | relabeled values and a one-pixel padding (22 × 22 output for a 20 × 20 input); `num_pixels_filled` requested alone was the unfilled count → input label values and shape, filled count |
| 19 | `feret_diameter_max` of a label value that does not occur (batch only) | `RuntimeError: No coordinates to process` → 0 |
| 20 | `regionprops_centroid` (batch module) with `num_pixels` already in `props_dict` | `TypeError: Wrong number of arguments` → works |
| 21 | `regionprops_centroid`, `regionprops_centroid_local` (batch module) | region of 2³² or more pixels: wrapped `uint32` count, centroid row 2.1e9 → 32768 |
| 23 | `inertia_tensor_eigenvectors` (cuCIM-only property) | the returned vectors were not eigenvectors of `inertia_tensor` (each eigenvector's components were reversed) → the columns are the eigenvectors, in the order of `inertia_tensor_eigvals` |

Commit 15 is a bug in cuCIM's vendored copy only. SciPy and
`cupyx.scipy.ndimage.binary_fill_holes` (CuPy 14.2) use the structuring
element. No cuCIM function passed a `structure` to the vendored version
before commit 16, whose per-label fallback does. Commit 17 completes commit
15: the fast non-iterative algorithm labels the background with the
structuring element, which is only valid for centrosymmetric 3 × 3 (× 3)
structures that contain the center and all face neighbors. Other structures
now use SciPy's iterative algorithm.

The batch path returns a row for every label value 1 … `max_label`, also for
values that do not occur (scikit-image returns only the labels present). Such
rows have an area of 0, so commit 19 returns 0 for their
`feret_diameter_max`, as for their `area_convex`, `perimeter` and axis
lengths. Before, any label image with a gap in its label values made
`regionprops_table` fail when `feret_diameter_max` was requested.

`regionprops_dict` computes centroids from the raw moments, so commits 20 and
21 only affect direct calls of the two helper functions.

`cupy.linalg.eigh` returns each batch of eigenvectors as the columns of a
(K, ndim, ndim) array. To put them in the descending order of
`inertia_tensor_eigvals`, `regionprops_inertia_tensor_eigvals` reversed axis 1
(the components of every eigenvector) instead of axis 2 (the eigenvectors).
For an ellipse rotated by 30°, `T @ v` gave (−10.8, 25.2) instead of
56.9 · (0.511, 0.860). The eigenvalues were correct. Commit 23 reverses the
columns; the first eigenvector is then along the region's shortest axis (the
largest eigenvalue of the inertia tensor).

## Behavior changes users may notice

- **`orientation`.** Regions whose inertia tensor has equal diagonal entries
  (±45°) change sign, in both paths. The values now match scikit-image ≥ 0.21.
- **New errors in batch mode, matching scikit-image and the per-label path:**
  - `moments_hu` and `moments_weighted_hu` raise `NotImplementedError` with
    non-unit spacing;
  - `perimeter` and `perimeter_crofton` raise it with anisotropic spacing.
- **Spacing.** Batch values of the properties in commits 6–11 and 14 change
  whenever the spacing is not 1.
- **`label_filled`.** It now has the shape and the label values of the input,
  with no padding and no relabeling.
- **`feret_diameter_max` of absent label values** is 0 instead of an error.
- **`inertia_tensor_eigenvectors`** returns actual eigenvectors (as columns).
- **`bbox` dtype for images of 2³² or more pixels** is `uint64` (it was
  `uint32` with wrapped values).
- **Speed.** The filled-region properties are slower than before (next
  section), because the old implementation did not compute per-region fills.

## Filled-region properties (commit 16)

How the batch computation works:

1. The label image is padded and its background labeled with full
   connectivity, as `binary_fill_holes` does with the `3**ndim` structuring
   element that scikit-image uses. Every background component except the one
   touching the padding is a hole.
2. For each hole, the largest and smallest neighboring labels are found with a
   grey dilation and erosion. A hole with a single neighboring label is filled
   with that label. For that region, this is exactly what scikit-image's
   `binary_fill_holes` on the region's crop gives.
3. scikit-image treats other labels as background. A label's result can
   therefore differ from step 2 only if:
   - (a) it borders a hole that also borders other labels, or
   - (b) a connected component of another label sits in one of its holes with
     no background in between. Such a component touches the label, and its
     bounding box lies strictly inside the label's bounding box.

   Labels matching (a) or (b) are recomputed one at a time with
   `binary_fill_holes` on their crop, as `robust_perimeter` does for close
   labels. The test is conservative: a flagged label may not need the
   recomputation, but every label that needs it is flagged. Test (b) uses the
   bounding box of the component, not of the whole label, because the other
   components of a nested label can lie anywhere.

`num_pixels_filled`, `area_filled` and `image_filled` are all computed from
this one result.

`area_filled` timings, with the number of labels each version gets wrong
compared with scikit-image 0.26:

| Input | Labels | Recomputed per label | `main` (ms) | this PR (ms) | Wrong on `main` | Wrong here |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| tiles 2160 × 3840, 32 × 32 | 1024 | 0 | 5.8 | 16.0 | 1024 | 0 |
| tiles 2160 × 3840, 127 × 128 | 16256 | 0 | 5.7 | 15.8 | 16256 | 0 |
| `binary_blobs` 4096² | 240 | 0 | 9.6 | 20.4 | 0 | 0 |
| 4 intensity levels 2048² | 1864 | 121 | 4.0 | 109.9 | 1864 | 0 |

Setup:

- RTX A6000, CuPy 14.2, `regionprops_dict(labels, properties=["area_filled"])`.
- GPU time is the mean of 20 runs of `cupyx.profiler.benchmark`.
- Inputs:
  - **Tiles:** rectangular regions that all touch each other.
  - **`binary_blobs`:** `blob_size_fraction=0.02`, `volume_fraction=0.5`,
    labeled.
  - **4 intensity levels:** Gaussian-smoothed (σ = 8) uniform noise, split
    into 4 levels at its 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles. The connected
    components of each level are labeled, giving many regions nested inside
    others with no gap.

Most of the added cost on images that need no recomputation comes from the
extra full-image passes: the background labeling, the grey dilation and
erosion, and the connected-component labeling for test (b). Test (b) alone
adds about 3 ms on the tilings. On the intensity-levels image, the call takes
11.2 ms when the recomputation is skipped, against 110.3 ms with it. Each of
the 121 recomputed labels therefore costs about 0.8 ms, because the fallback
loops over labels on the host. Batching that fallback would be a separate
performance change.

## Images of 2³² or more pixels (commits 18 and 21)

The batch bounding-box, centroid and moments kernels unravel each pixel's
raveled index into coordinates in their coordinate type. That type was
`uint32` whenever every axis is shorter than 2³², so on larger images the
raveled index wrapped. Commit 18 chooses `uint64` coordinates when the image
has 2³² or more pixels, in one helper (`_get_coord_dtype`) used by all four
call sites. Commit 21 does the same for the pixel counts of the two centroid
helpers, which were always `uint32`; the other count kernels already chose
their type from the image size.

Smaller images keep 32-bit coordinates and counts, whose integer divisions
are much faster. Their generated kernels are unchanged: the sources of all
57 kernels that `regionprops_dict` builds for 2D and 3D inputs with `uint8`,
`int32` and `int64` labels (all non-convex properties) are identical before
and after the commits.

Checked on a (65537, 65536) `uint8` label image (4.3 GB) with a `uint8`
intensity image, outside the test suite:

- Five regions before, straddling and after raveled index 2³² (one with a
  hole) were compared with the same regions in a crop of a few rows around
  them, with the crop offset added back to `bbox` and the centroids.
- 14 properties were compared, among them `bbox`, `centroid`,
  `centroid_weighted`, `centroid_local`, `moments_central`,
  `moments_weighted_central`, `inertia_tensor`, `intensity_mean` and
  `intensity_max`.
- Before commit 18 there were 16 mismatches, all for the two regions past
  2³². There are none after it.
- A region of 2³² + 65521 pixels gets the exact `bbox` and centroid, with
  either the moments or the coordinate sums.

Two properties still cannot be computed on such an image with 48 GB of GPU
memory (see "Not addressed here").

## Tests

New tests:

- **Kernels:** `test_eccentricity_single_pixel_batch`,
  `test_intensity_std_constant_regions`, `test_intensity_std_nonfinite`,
  `test_num_pixels_large_pixels_per_thread`,
  `test_intensity_min_and_max_float64_exact` (float64 minima and maxima
  equal to scikit-image's exactly; the existing min/max tests used
  `assert_allclose`), `test_inertia_tensor_eigenvectors` (T·v = λ·v,
  orthonormality and descending order, 2D and 3D, with and without
  spacing)..
- **Batch `regionprops_dict` vs. scikit-image:**
  - `test_regionprops_dict_spacing` (2D and 3D, isotropic and anisotropic
    spacing, 10 properties);
  - `test_regionprops_dict_perimeter_spacing`,
    `test_regionprops_dict_hu_spacing_not_implemented`,
    `test_regionprops_dict_area_filled_spacing`,
    `test_regionprops_dict_axis_lengths`.
- **Filled regions:** `test_regionprops_dict_filled`, with 8 cases: labels not
  in raster order, touching, nested with a gap, nested and touching, nested
  with another component elsewhere, a ring open through a diagonal gap, a hole
  between two labels, and 3D. Also `test_regionprops_dict_filled_random`,
  `test_label_filled` and `test_fill_holes_by_label_tiling_is_exact`.
- **Both paths:** `test_orientation_continuity` (ported from scikit-image),
  `test_orientation_diagonal_batch_matches_regionprops`,
  `test_centroid_weighted_offset_spacing`,
  `test_centroid_weighted_copy_to_host`.
- **Vendored ndimage:** `test_binary_fill_holes_structure`,
  `test_binary_fill_holes_iterative_structure`.
- **Absent labels and helpers:** `test_feret_diameter_max_absent_label`,
  `test_centroid_reuses_num_pixels`.
- **Images of 2³² or more pixels:**
  `test_regionprops_dict_coordinates_beyond_2_32_pixels` and
  `test_centroid_region_of_2_32_pixels`. Each uses a 4.3 GB label image and
  is skipped when less than 8.6 GB of GPU memory is free. They take about 2 s
  each on an RTX A6000.

The expected values in the existing `test_orientation` were updated to
scikit-image 0.26's.

Every commit except the docstring one adds at least one test that fails
without its fix. For the filled-region commit, this was checked against
`main`'s implementation: all 8 `test_regionprops_dict_filled` cases fail
there. A few tests guard against regressions that `main` did not have.
For example, `test_intensity_std_nonfinite` checks that clipping the variance
keeps NaN for regions with NaN or inf values.

title: Add intensity_median region property
body:
## Context

This MR implements kernels for efficient batch computation of the `intensity_median` region property via `cucim.skimage.measure.regionprops_table`. We can reuse an efficient CUB segmented sort as the core of the implementation. We chose here to pre-compile the needed CUB wrappers as a nanobind extension module rather than use `cuda.compute` from Python. This was done primarily to avoid fairly high JIT compilation cost (~12 seconds per data type) for `cuda.compute`. CuPy's own JIT costs occur only the first time a function is called and .cubin files are cached to disk for reuse from future sessions. `cuda.compute` does not have that disk caching mechanism so the costs would be payed each time a process is run. By precompiling the kernels up-front we pay the cost only once when the package is compile with no JIT cost at all for these CUB segmented sorts.

## Summary

The implementation adds a hybrid GPU strategy controlled by the module-level
`hybrid_size_threshold` value in
`cucim.skimage.measure._regionprops_gpu_intensity_kernels`. The default
threshold is `128000`, and users can monkeypatch it for benchmarking or tuning.

The segmented sort is provided by a new compiled extension,
`cucim.skimage._cucim_skimage_cpp_ext`, built with nanobind against the stable
ABI.


## Motivation

The original batch path rejected `intensity_median`, forcing users away from
the fast GPU batch regionprops implementation. A direct loop over
`cp.median` for every labeled region is simple and robust, but it performs
poorly when there are many small regions because each label requires a separate
median operation.

Sorting all labeled regions together with CUB's segmented sort avoids the
many-small-regions overhead of separate `cp.median` calls. For very few very
large regions, however, `cp.median` can still be faster than sorting the packed
segmented array.

The hybrid mode addresses both cases:

- regions with `num_pixels <= hybrid_size_threshold` use
  `cub::DeviceSegmentedSort::SortKeys` through the optional nanobind CUDA
  extension;
- larger regions fall back to `cp.median` on the packed per-label intensity
  view.

The current flow is:

1. Pack foreground intensities into one contiguous segment per label. A single
   elementwise kernel uses one atomic write cursor per label, so no sort by
   label is needed (values within a segment are unordered, which the
   subsequent sort does not care about). For floating-point inputs the
   same kernel records which labels/channels contain NaN.
2. Select labels with `count <= hybrid_size_threshold`.
3. Sort those selected packed ranges using
   `cub::DeviceSegmentedSort::SortKeys`.
4. Extract each selected region's median from the sorted packed values
   (averaging the two middle values for even-sized regions).
5. Fill any remaining larger regions with `cp.median`.
6. Set the median to NaN for segmented-sort regions/channels that contained a
   NaN, matching NumPy/scikit-image NaN propagation.

## API additions

`regionprops_table` (and the internal `regionprops_dict`) gain a
`disable_nan_check=False` option (ignored when `batch_processing=False`).
Set it to `True` to skip the NaN bookkeeping in steps 1 and 6 when the input
is known to be NaN-free.


## Compiled extension

- Sources live in `python/nanobind/skimage/` and are built by
  `python/CMakeLists.txt` as the `cucim_skimage_cpp` target, producing
  `cucim/skimage/_cucim_skimage_cpp_ext.abi3.so`. It uses the same
  `nanobind_add_module(... STABLE_ABI NB_STATIC PROTECT_STACK NOMINSIZE)`
  options as the `cucim.clara` extension, so the wheel stays `cp312-abi3`.
- `segmented_sort.cu` has no binding-library dependency; argument
  validation throws `std::invalid_argument`, which nanobind surfaces as
  `ValueError`.
- `CUDA_VISIBILITY_PRESET hidden` is set on the target because
  `nanobind_add_module()` only hides C++ symbols; without it the CUB/libcu++
  instantiations are exported from the module (71 dynamic symbols vs 7).
- `CUDA_STANDARD` follows `CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD`.
- Bindings are provided for `uint8`, `uint16`, `float32` and `float64` keys:
  a `segmented_sort_keys_temp_storage_bytes_<dtype>` size query plus
  "offsets" and "begin/end ranges" sort variants. The sorts take raw device
  pointers, a caller-provided `temp_storage` buffer and an optional
  `stream_ptr`, and are enqueued asynchronously (no host synchronization).
- The extension is optional at runtime: if it cannot be imported, every
  region falls back to `cp.median`.

## Build system: following RAPIDS conventions

The CUDA extension is the first CUB-based code in the cuCIM Python build, so
its CMake setup deliberately follows the conventions used by cudf, cuml and
cuvs rather than introducing cuCIM-specific mechanisms:

- **rapids-cmake bootstrap.** `cmake/RAPIDS.cmake` and
  `cmake/rapids_config.cmake` are copied from those projects
  (`RAPIDS.cmake` is byte-identical across all three). `rapids_config.cmake`
  reads `VERSION` and a new `RAPIDS_BRANCH` file (`main`) to select the
  rapids-cmake branch, and `ci/release/update-version.sh` now keeps
  `RAPIDS_BRANCH` up to date, as cudf's does.
- **CCCL via rapids-cmake.** CCCL is fetched with `rapids_cpm_cccl()`
  (currently CCCL 3.6.0) instead of using whichever CCCL ships with the CUDA
  Toolkit, so every CUDA version builds against the same RAPIDS-pinned CCCL.
  The version lookup is `EXACT`, so an older toolkit CCCL is never picked up
  silently. This matches cudf's `python/cudf/udf_cpp`, the closest analogue
  (a Python-side CUDA module that calls `rapids_cpm_cccl()` directly).
  No CCCL install rules are generated, so nothing extra is installed.
- **CUDA architectures via `rapids_cuda_init_architectures`.** As in every
  cudf/cuml/cuvs CMake project (including their Python ones), it is called
  before `project()`. Builds default to the RAPIDS architecture list (for
  CUDA 13: `75-real 80-real 86-real 90a-real 100f-real 120a-real 120`), which
  is what CI wheel and conda builds get; `CUDAARCHS=NATIVE` (or
  `CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES`) overrides it for faster local builds.
  Previously only nvcc's default (`sm_75` + PTX) was built.
- **Size and build time.** With the RAPIDS architecture list the extension is
  about 10.1 MB (9.3 MB of device code, ~2.9 MB compressed) and
  `segmented_sort.cu` takes about 130 s to compile; a single-architecture
  build is about 1.9 MB. See "Sort algorithm" below for why this is larger
  than the earlier `DeviceSegmentedRadixSort` version (4.0 MB, ~50 s).

## Alternative considered: `cuda.compute`

An earlier iteration of this PR also offered a `cuda.compute` (CCCL Python,
`cuda-cccl` / `cccl-python`) backend for the segmented sort, selectable via an
`intensity_median_backend` option. It was tested and then removed because of
its JIT compilation cost: `cuda.compute` compiles the sort kernels on the
first call in each new Python process and has no persistent on-disk kernel
cache, so every new process pays that cost again. The precompiled extension
has no such cost.

Measured with `cuda-cccl` 1.1.1 on an RTX A6000, calling
`regionprops_table(..., properties=["intensity_median"])` on a 1024×1024
image in three separate fresh processes (results were consistent across
processes):

| call in a fresh process | `cuda.compute` | CUB extension |
|---|---:|---:|
| first call (`float32`, 256 regions) | ~9.8-10.4 s | ~120 ms |
| repeat call, same inputs | ~2.1-2.3 ms | ~1.8-2.4 ms |
| new region count (4096 regions) | ~14 ms | ~14 ms |
| first call with a new dtype (`uint16`) | ~9.1 s | ~2.9 ms |

Compiled kernels are reused within a process (repeat calls and new problem
sizes are fast), but each additional key dtype triggers another ~9 s
compilation, and all of it is repeated in the next process.

Once warmed up, the two backends produced identical results and similar
throughput. This comparison was made while the extension still used
`cub::DeviceSegmentedRadixSort`; `cuda.compute`'s `segmented_sort` wraps
`cub::DeviceSegmentedSort`, which showed up as a small, consistent
difference for the many-small-regions cases (end-to-end, median of three
interleaved runs; differences within ~5-7% are run-to-run noise):

| image | grid cell | dtype | channels | extension, radix sort (ms) | `cuda.compute` (ms) | ratio |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1024² | 16 | float32 | 1 | 2.81 | 2.56 | 0.91 |
| 1024² | 64 | float32 | 1 | 1.65 | 1.61 | 0.98 |
| 1024² | 128 | float32 | 1 | 1.62 | 1.73 | 1.07 |
| 1024² | 64 | uint8 | 1 | 1.43 | 1.60 | 1.12 |
| 1024² | 64 | float32 | 3 | 2.25 | 2.37 | 1.05 |
| 2048² | 16 | float32 | 1 | 7.74 | 6.84 | 0.88 |
| 2048² | 64 | float32 | 1 | 3.77 | 3.63 | 0.96 |
| 2048² | 128 | float32 | 1 | 3.87 | 3.92 | 1.01 |
| 2048² | 64 | uint8 | 1 | 3.19 | 3.34 | 1.05 |
| 2048² | 64 | float32 | 3 | 5.51 | 4.77 | 0.87 |

`cuda.compute` was ~10% faster for the smallest-region grids (and the
3-channel 2048² case), while the radix-sort extension was faster for
`uint8`. This led to switching the extension itself to
`cub::DeviceSegmentedSort` (next section), which captures that benefit
without any JIT cost.

## Sort algorithm: `cub::DeviceSegmentedSort`

The extension originally used `cub::DeviceSegmentedRadixSort` and now uses
`cub::DeviceSegmentedSort`. The CUB documentation's guidance on choosing
between them:

> DeviceSegmentedRadixSort is optimized for significantly large segments
> (tens of thousands of items and more). Nevertheless, some domains produce
> a wide range of segment sizes. DeviceSegmentedSort partitions segments into
> size groups and specialize sorting algorithms for each group. This approach
> leads to better resource utilization in the presence of segment size
> imbalance or moderate segment sizes (up to thousands of items). This
> algorithm is more complex and consists of multiple kernels. This fact leads
> to longer compilation times as well as larger binaries sizes.

Label images typically have exactly that wide range of region sizes, and
the segmented-sort path only handles regions up to `hybrid_size_threshold`.
End-to-end batch `intensity_median` timings (RTX A6000, `sm_86` builds of
both variants with CCCL 3.6.0, mean of two interleaved rounds per build;
"grid" images have uniform regions of ~cell² pixels, "heavy-tailed"
images have N labels with a Pareto-distributed size distribution):

| image | labels | dtype | ch | radix sort (ms) | segmented sort (ms) | ratio |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1024² | grid, cell 16 | float32 | 1 | 2.77 | 2.52 | 0.91 |
| 1024² | grid, cell 64 | float32 | 1 | 1.58 | 1.54 | 0.98 |
| 1024² | grid, cell 128 | float32 | 1 | 1.65 | 1.63 | 0.99 |
| 1024² | grid, cell 256 | float32 | 1 | 1.95 | 1.97 | 1.01 |
| 1024² | grid, cell 64 | uint8 | 1 | 1.43 | 1.39 | 0.97 |
| 1024² | grid, cell 64 | float32 | 3 | 2.19 | 1.99 | 0.91 |
| 1024² | heavy-tailed, 500 | float32 | 1 | 2.75 | 2.70 | 0.98 |
| 1024² | heavy-tailed, 5000 | float32 | 1 | 3.61 | 2.93 | 0.81 |
| 1024² | heavy-tailed, 5000 | uint16 | 1 | 2.96 | 2.49 | 0.84 |
| 2048² | grid, cell 16 | float32 | 1 | 7.60 | 6.81 | 0.90 |
| 2048² | grid, cell 64 | float32 | 1 | 3.83 | 3.57 | 0.93 |
| 2048² | grid, cell 128 | float32 | 1 | 3.96 | 3.93 | 0.99 |
| 2048² | grid, cell 256 | float32 | 1 | 4.05 | 4.00 | 0.99 |
| 2048² | grid, cell 64 | uint8 | 1 | 3.29 | 3.28 | 1.00 |
| 2048² | grid, cell 64 | float32 | 3 | 5.49 | 4.79 | 0.87 |
| 2048² | heavy-tailed, 500 | float32 | 1 | 5.16 | 5.14 | 1.00 |
| 2048² | heavy-tailed, 5000 | float32 | 1 | 4.93 | 4.37 | 0.89 |
| 2048² | heavy-tailed, 5000 | uint16 | 1 | 4.09 | 3.70 | 0.90 |

`DeviceSegmentedSort` was never meaningfully slower (worst case 1.01, within
run-to-run noise of up to ~6%) and up to 19% faster, 6.5% faster on
geometric mean. The gains are largest for mixed region sizes, many small
regions and multichannel images; large uniform regions (cell 256, ~65k
pixels) are a tie, consistent with the CUB guidance.

As the CUB documentation warns, the trade-off is binary size and build time:

| build | radix sort | segmented sort |
|---|---:|---:|
| `sm_86` only: module size | 0.87 MB | 1.9 MB |
| RAPIDS arch list: module size (compressed) | 4.0 MB (1.15 MB) | 10.1 MB (2.9 MB) |
| RAPIDS arch list: `.cu` compile time | ~53 s | ~133 s |

Splitting `segmented_sort.cu` into one translation unit per key type
(`uint8`, `uint16`, `float32`, `float64`) was tried to reduce CI build time
through build parallelism, but was not kept because of the size increase
(RAPIDS architecture list, 16 parallel jobs):

| | single `.cu` (kept) | four per-dtype `.cu` files |
|---|---:|---:|
| build wall time | ~133 s | ~62 s |
| module size | 10.1 MB | 12.4 MB |

The size increase comes from the CUB kernels that do not depend on the key
type (the three-way partition that groups segments by size) being compiled
into every translation unit.

Correctness: in addition to the test suite, both variants were compared
against the pure `cp.median` path on heavy-tailed label images (region sizes
1 to ~230k pixels) for `uint8`/`uint16`/`float32`/`float64`, 1 and 3
channels, with duplicate values, signed zeros and NaNs; all 48
configurations matched exactly. Note that `DeviceSegmentedSort` uses
comparison-based merge sorts for small and medium segments, so the order of
NaNs within a segment is unspecified. This does not affect results: regions
containing a NaN get a NaN median from the NaN check, and with
`disable_nan_check=True` the caller asserts that there are no NaNs.

## Implementation Notes

- `uint8` and `uint16` intensities are sorted in their native dtype; all
  other dtypes are sorted after conversion to the output dtype.
- Median output dtype is `cp.promote_types(intensity_image.dtype, cp.float32)`,
  matching the convention used by other GPU intensity measurements.
- Multichannel intensity images are handled by sorting each channel's packed
  values separately.
- CUB's temporary storage is allocated in Python from CuPy's memory pool
  (sized by the extension's size query) and shared across channels, so
  repeated calls reuse pooled memory and respect any user-configured CuPy
  allocator. An earlier version of the wrapper called
  `cudaMalloc`/`cudaStreamSynchronize`/`cudaFree` on every sort; removing
  that reduced end-to-end batch `intensity_median` time by roughly 5-13% for
  single-channel and 13-26% for 3-channel `float32` images (1024² and 2048²
  grids, RTX A6000).
- Regions larger than the hybrid threshold fall back to `cp.median`.
- `hybrid_size_threshold = 128000` is intentionally a simple initial heuristic.


## Benchmarks

The benchmark script verified CPU/GPU numerical agreement before timing. Inputs
below were generated from a binary image with horizontal and vertical zero-valued
bands, then labeled. The intensity image was `float32`.

Results:

Shape `(1024, 1024)`:

| case | regions | median pixels/region | max pixels/region | scikit-image CPU (ms) | cuCIM GPU (ms) | speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `grid:16` | 4096 | 225 | 225 | 185.28 | 3.34 | 55.48x |
| `grid:64` | 256 | 3969 | 3969 | 21.44 | 2.16 | 9.95x |
| `grid:128` | 64 | 16129 | 16129 | 12.46 | 1.99 | 6.26x |
| `grid:196` | 36 | 38025 | 38025 | 11.02 | 2.17 | 5.08x |
| `grid:384` | 9 | 97665 | 146689 | 9.91 | 3.14 | 3.15x |
| `mixed:2:8:128` | 289 | 2511 | 14641 | 21.52 | 2.14 | 10.06x |
| `mixed:2:16:160` | 144 | 5265 | 25281 | 15.12 | 1.99 | 7.59x |
| `mixed:2:32:256` | 81 | 10465 | 50625 | 12.66 | 2.10 | 6.03x |
| `mixed:16:32:320` | 64 | 11297 | 57121 | 11.81 | 2.11 | 5.59x |

Shape `(2048, 2048)`:

| case | regions | median pixels/region | max pixels/region | scikit-image CPU (ms) | cuCIM GPU (ms) | speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `grid:16` | 16384 | 225 | 225 | 735.47 | 8.82 | 83.39x |
| `grid:64` | 1024 | 3969 | 3969 | 84.23 | 4.04 | 20.85x |
| `grid:128` | 256 | 16129 | 16129 | 50.31 | 4.10 | 12.28x |
| `grid:196` | 121 | 38025 | 38025 | 46.45 | 3.83 | 12.14x |
| `grid:384` | 36 | 146689 | 146689 | 41.21 | 7.83 | 5.26x |
| `mixed:2:8:128` | 625 | 5207 | 16129 | 68.12 | 4.18 | 16.29x |
| `mixed:2:16:160` | 361 | 9425 | 25281 | 57.05 | 4.12 | 13.83x |
| `mixed:2:32:256` | 169 | 20769 | 65025 | 46.82 | 3.78 | 12.39x |
| `mixed:16:32:320` | 144 | 22601 | 101761 | 45.99 | 3.99 | 11.51x |

title: Improve performance of regionprops_table
body:
This branch is on top of the bug fixes in #1196, so please review and merge that PR first. The unique commits for this branch start with b55beb3.

This MR is a performance refactoring of much of `regonprops_table`. The commits here are the results of allowing Opus 5.5 to iterate on improvements to the existing batch kernels. The results of these updated implementations are unchanged up to floating-point rounding, except that the perimeters move closer to scikit-image's; every commit was checked against the outputs of that branch (see "Testing"). 

Each commit is one optimization, so they can be reviewed (and reverted)
separately. 


## Summary

| # | Commit | What it changes | Main effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Keep each label run's statistics in registers | all label-run kernels | 2.4–8.6× faster moment, bbox and intensity passes |
| 2 | Count pixels, bounding boxes and intensity statistics together | `regionprops_dict`, intensity functions | intensity group 1.2–1.5× faster |
| 3 | Compute centroids without an order-2 moments pass | `regionprops_dict` | basic group 1.7–2.1×, area/bbox/centroid 4.2× faster |
| 4 | Sum unweighted moments of each run in integers | raw moments kernel | moments group 2.0× (2D), 1.4× (3D) faster |
| 5 | Combine the last runs of a warp's lanes before the atomics | all label-run kernels | 1.7–22× faster where atomics collide (large regions) |
| 6 | Measure perimeters and Euler numbers per label in one pass | perimeter, Crofton perimeter, Euler number | boundary group 24–170× faster; perimeters now agree with scikit-image to 1e-15 |
| 7 | Update only the last coordinate's power sums per pixel | raw moments kernel | weighted group up to 1.28× faster |
| 8 | Read 4 and 8-byte labels and images with 16-byte loads | label-run loop, intensity and weighted moments kernels | intensity passes 1.3–3.2× faster on large images; label passes 1.3–1.8× with 4/8-byte labels |
| 9 | Do not cast the label image to a smaller integer type | `regionprops_dict` | 1.03–1.56× for every group |
| 10 | Let lanes in holes of a region join the warp's group | label-run loop | 1.6–6.2× faster on large regions with holes |
| 11 | Unravel boundary-kernel coordinates in 32 bits when possible | perimeter, Crofton perimeter, Euler number | boundary group 1.12–1.21×, all properties 1.04–1.08× faster |

Overall, measured back to back against #1196 (see "How it was measured" below for the inputs and groups):

| Input | Labels | Group | Before (ms) | After (ms) | Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3840x2160/16 | 1024 | basic | 2.417 | 0.194 | 12.46× |
| 3840x2160/16 | 1024 | moments | 3.367 | 0.293 | 11.49× |
| 3840x2160/16 | 1024 | intensity | 0.821 | 0.190 | 4.32× |
| 3840x2160/16 | 1024 | weighted | 3.350 | 0.529 | 6.33× |
| 3840x2160/16 | 1024 | boundary | 12.431 | 0.337 | 36.89× |
| 3840x2160/16 | 1024 | all | 18.980 | 1.137 | 16.69× |
| 3840x2160/64 | 16256 | basic | 2.526 | 0.196 | 12.89× |
| 3840x2160/64 | 16256 | moments | 3.558 | 0.303 | 11.74× |
| 3840x2160/64 | 16256 | intensity | 0.909 | 0.227 | 4.00× |
| 3840x2160/64 | 16256 | weighted | 3.570 | 0.709 | 5.04× |
| 3840x2160/64 | 16256 | boundary | 95.486 | 0.433 | 220.52× |
| 3840x2160/64 | 16256 | all | 101.918 | 1.495 | 68.17× |
| 192x192x192/4 | 498 | basic | 3.772 | 0.210 | 17.96× |
| 192x192x192/4 | 498 | moments | 3.706 | 0.243 | 15.25× |
| 192x192x192/4 | 498 | intensity | 0.685 | 0.180 | 3.81× |
| 192x192x192/4 | 498 | weighted | 3.762 | 0.358 | 10.51× |
| 192x192x192/4 | 498 | boundary | 12.841 | 0.210 | 61.15× |
| 192x192x192/4 | 498 | all | 19.868 | 0.798 | 24.90× |
| 8192^2 g=1 | 220219 | cca | 53.356 | 1.960 | 27.22× |
| 8192^2 g=1 | 220219 | moments | 50.673 | 6.561 | 7.72× |
| 8192^2 g=1 | 220219 | intensity | 15.216 | 1.859 | 8.19× |
| 8192^2 g=16 | 882 | cca | 24.481 | 0.686 | 35.69× |
| 8192^2 g=16 | 882 | moments | 23.052 | 1.722 | 13.39× |
| 8192^2 g=16 | 882 | intensity | 5.716 | 1.072 | 5.33× |
| 8192^2 g=None | 1 | cca | 46.196 | 0.686 | 67.34× |
| 8192^2 g=None | 1 | moments | 43.624 | 1.588 | 27.47× |
| 8192^2 g=None | 1 | intensity | 13.423 | 1.453 | 9.24× |

The convex-hull properties (`area_convex`, `image_convex`, `solidity`,
`feret_diameter_max`) are not covered in this branch: they still loop
over the host and will be optimized in a subsequent follow-up.

## How it was measured

- **Hardware.** NVIDIA RTX A6000 (CUDA 13, CuPy 14.2).
- **Timing.** Median GPU time (CUDA events) of 20 runs of `regionprops_dict`
  with `cupyx.profiler.benchmark`, after warm-up, 16 pixels per thread (the
  default of `regionprops_table`), `max_label` passed in. Each comparison
  runs both versions back to back (`ab.sh`: stash, measure, unstash,
  measure) and reports the best of 3 medians. From commit 8 on, the warm-up
  runs the same call for at least 0.3 s first: the GPU lowers its clocks
  when idle, and short warm-ups left some large-image timings up to 2×
  too slow.
- **Inputs.**
  - `3840x2160/16` and `3840x2160/64`: tilings of disks, ellipses, squares
    and plus shapes (1024 and 16 256 labels; about 19% foreground), float32
    intensities. `192x192x192/4`: the 3D equivalent (498 labels).
  - `8192^2 g=1`, `g=16`: random binary images of density 0.5 (blocks of
    g × g pixels), labeled with full connectivity (220 219 and 882 labels).
    `g=None`: one region covering the whole image. These stress the atomics.
- **Groups.**
  - basic: label, area, bbox, centroid, extent, equivalent_diameter_area
  - moments (2D): moments_hu, inertia_tensor_eigvals, axis_major_length,
    axis_minor_length, orientation, eccentricity; (3D): moments_central,
    inertia_tensor_eigvals, axis_major_length, axis_minor_length
  - intensity: intensity_mean, intensity_std, intensity_min, intensity_max
  - weighted: centroid_weighted, moments_weighted_hu (2D) /
    moments_weighted_central (3D)
  - boundary: perimeter, perimeter_crofton, euler_number (2D); euler_number
    (3D)
  - all: the union of the above
  - cca (8192² only): area, bbox, centroid; moments: moments_central;
    intensity: intensity_mean, intensity_std


## Agent-generated summaries for individual commits and benchmark results

### 1. Keep each label run's statistics in registers

The label-run kernels split the raveled image into chunks of
`pixels_per_thread` pixels, one per thread. Each thread accumulates the
statistics of each run of equal labels and adds them to the per-label
outputs with atomics. The accumulators were per-thread arrays with one entry
per possible run, indexed by the run number. Because that index is only known
at run time, the arrays were placed in local memory:

| Kernel (16 pixels per thread) | Local memory before | after | Registers before | after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| pixel counts | 48 B | 0 | 34 | 28 |
| bounding boxes, 2D / 3D | 288 / 416 B | 0 | 40 / 40 | 39 / 38 |
| raw moments order 2, 2D / 3D | 1184 / 3488 B | 0 | 40 / 40 | 40 / 50 |
| raw moments order 3, 2D / 3D | 2080 / 8224 B | 0 | 40 / 44 | 56 / 64 |
| intensity sum and sum of squares | 288 B | 0 | 38 | 36 |
| intensity min and max | 160 B | 0 | 33 | 20 |

All label-run kernels now share one loop (`_get_label_run_loop`) that keeps
only the current run's accumulators in scalar variables and flushes them with
atomics when the label changes and after the last pixel. The atomics issued
are the same as before (one set per run). The moments kernel also loads the
bounding-box offset of the run once per run instead of once per pixel.

| Input | Labels | Group | Before (ms) | After (ms) | Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3840x2160/16 | 1024 | basic | 2.410 | 0.483 | 4.99× |
| 3840x2160/16 | 1024 | moments | 3.384 | 0.650 | 5.21× |
| 3840x2160/16 | 1024 | intensity | 0.840 | 0.340 | 2.47× |
| 3840x2160/16 | 1024 | weighted | 3.370 | 0.715 | 4.71× |
| 3840x2160/16 | 1024 | boundary | 11.983 | 11.234 | 1.07× |
| 3840x2160/16 | 1024 | all | 18.593 | 12.392 | 1.50× |
| 3840x2160/64 | 16256 | basic | 2.544 | 0.459 | 5.54× |
| 3840x2160/64 | 16256 | moments | 3.579 | 0.657 | 5.45× |
| 3840x2160/64 | 16256 | intensity | 0.920 | 0.336 | 2.74× |
| 3840x2160/64 | 16256 | weighted | 3.588 | 0.725 | 4.95× |
| 3840x2160/64 | 16256 | boundary | 94.315 | 90.402 | 1.04× |
| 3840x2160/64 | 16256 | all | 101.536 | 91.188 | 1.11× |
| 192x192x192/4 | 498 | basic | 3.770 | 0.482 | 7.82× |
| 192x192x192/4 | 498 | moments | 3.714 | 0.433 | 8.58× |
| 192x192x192/4 | 498 | intensity | 0.690 | 0.286 | 2.41× |
| 192x192x192/4 | 498 | weighted | 3.779 | 0.474 | 7.97× |
| 192x192x192/4 | 498 | boundary | 12.867 | 12.083 | 1.06× |
| 192x192x192/4 | 498 | all | 20.030 | 12.812 | 1.56× |
| 8192^2 g=1 | 220219 | cca | 55.688 | 48.185 | 1.16× |
| 8192^2 g=1 | 220219 | moments | 51.182 | 45.548 | 1.12× |
| 8192^2 g=1 | 220219 | intensity | 12.184 | 12.362 | 0.99× |
| 8192^2 g=16 | 882 | cca | 24.700 | 22.158 | 1.11× |
| 8192^2 g=16 | 882 | moments | 22.904 | 20.958 | 1.09× |
| 8192^2 g=16 | 882 | intensity | 5.712 | 5.281 | 1.08× |
| 8192^2 g=None | 1 | cca | 47.105 | 44.025 | 1.07× |
| 8192^2 g=None | 1 | moments | 44.216 | 44.304 | 1.00× |
| 8192^2 g=None | 1 | intensity | 13.308 | 14.038 | 0.95× |

The 8192² images change little: there, the time goes into the atomics (one
set per run, and in the single-region image all of them on the same
addresses), which this commit does not change.

### 2. Count pixels, bounding boxes and intensity statistics together

`regionprops_dict` ran separate label-run passes for the pixel counts, the
bounding boxes, the intensity sums (and squares) and the intensity minima and
maxima. Since a pass costs about the same for any number of statistics (once
they are kept in registers, commit 1), it now:

- counts the pixels in the bounding-box pass, or, when no bounding box is
  needed, in the intensity pass;
- computes the intensity sums, minima and maxima in one pass
  (`_regionprops_intensity`, which `regionprops_intensity_mean`,
  `regionprops_intensity_std` and `regionprops_intensity_min_max` now call).

The intensity kernel had never been generated with both sums and minima or
maxima (both code fragments declared a variable `v`); a new test checks the
one-pass statistics against the separate functions.

Measured back to back against commit 1 (best of 3 medians of 20 runs):

| Input | Labels | Group | Before (ms) | After (ms) | Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3840x2160/16 | 1024 | basic | 0.480 | 0.450 | 1.07× |
| 3840x2160/16 | 1024 | intensity | 0.326 | 0.215 | 1.52× |
| 3840x2160/16 | 1024 | all | 12.473 | 12.489 | 1.00× |
| 3840x2160/64 | 16256 | basic | 0.454 | 0.456 | 1.00× |
| 3840x2160/64 | 16256 | intensity | 0.345 | 0.241 | 1.43× |
| 3840x2160/64 | 16256 | all | 95.576 | 97.428 | 0.98× |
| 192x192x192/4 | 498 | basic | 0.486 | 0.446 | 1.09× |
| 192x192x192/4 | 498 | intensity | 0.293 | 0.200 | 1.46× |
| 192x192x192/4 | 498 | all | 13.009 | 13.358 | 0.97× |
| 8192^2 g=1 | 220219 | intensity | 12.348 | 10.111 | 1.22× |
| 8192^2 g=16 | 882 | intensity | 5.327 | 4.164 | 1.28× |
| 8192^2 g=None | 1 | intensity | 13.105 | 10.829 | 1.21× |

The other groups do not use these passes and stay within ±4% (run-to-run
variation).

### 3. Compute centroids without an order-2 moments pass

`centroid` and `centroid_local` depend on `moments`, whose required order is
2, so requesting a centroid ran a bounding-box pass and an order-2 raw moments
pass (9 float64 accumulators and atomics per run in 2D, 27 in 3D) for what are
first moments.

- When no other requested property needs the raw moments, the integer
  coordinates are summed in the pass that counts the pixels and divided by
  the counts (`_regionprops_centroid_from_sums`). `centroid_local` subtracts
  `count × bbox_min` from the sums first, exactly, in uint64. The global
  centroid then needs no bounding boxes either. When the moments are
  computed anyway (e.g. with `moments_hu`), the centroids still come from
  them.
- The moment order is now taken from the properties computed from the raw
  moments; `moments`/`moments_weighted` require order 2 only when requested
  themselves. So `centroid_weighted` alone uses order-1 weighted moments.
- The counting/bounding-box/coordinate-sum pass is a new helper,
  `_regionprops_label_pass`, which `regionprops_bbox_coords` now also uses.

The centroids from coordinate sums differ from the moment-based ones by at
most 2e-16 (relative). A new test checks that both paths agree, including
NaN for absent labels; `test_regionprops_dict_spacing` already compares the
new paths (each centroid property requested alone) with scikit-image.

Measured back to back against commit 2:

| Input | Labels | Group | Before (ms) | After (ms) | Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3840x2160/16 | 1024 | basic | 0.452 | 0.244 | 1.85× |
| 3840x2160/16 | 1024 | weighted | 0.719 | 0.718 | 1.00× |
| 3840x2160/16 | 1024 | all | 12.552 | 12.454 | 1.01× |
| 3840x2160/64 | 16256 | basic | 0.452 | 0.215 | 2.10× |
| 3840x2160/64 | 16256 | weighted | 0.724 | 0.728 | 0.99× |
| 3840x2160/64 | 16256 | all | 98.707 | 95.129 | 1.04× |
| 192x192x192/4 | 498 | basic | 0.449 | 0.268 | 1.68× |
| 192x192x192/4 | 498 | weighted | 0.475 | 0.479 | 0.99× |
| 192x192x192/4 | 498 | all | 12.959 | 13.110 | 0.99× |
| 8192^2 g=1 | 220219 | cca | 48.371 | 11.660 | 4.15× |
| 8192^2 g=16 | 882 | cca | 22.319 | 5.349 | 4.17× |
| 8192^2 g=None | 1 | cca | 42.844 | 10.044 | 4.27× |

`centroid_weighted` alone (best of 3 medians): 0.504 → 0.371 ms
(3840x2160/16), 0.486 → 0.349 ms (192³), 46.2 → 34.8 ms, 21.1 → 15.7 ms and
41.9 → 30.9 ms on the three 8192² images (1.33–1.39×). The weighted group
does not change because `moments_weighted_hu` needs order 3.

### 4. Sum unweighted moments of each run in integers

The raw moments kernel computed every term (e.g. `c0 * c1 * c1`) and its
per-run sum in double precision, and multiplied the local coordinates by the
spacing for every pixel. On GPUs with low FP64 throughput (1/64 of FP32 on the
RTX A6000) this arithmetic dominated the kernel.

- For unweighted moments the terms are products of integer local
  coordinates, so the per-run sums are now 32-bit or 64-bit unsigned
  integers, chosen from the image shape so that a run of `pixels_per_thread`
  pixels cannot overflow (`_get_moments_accum_c_type`; double is kept for
  images too large for 64 bits). They are exact and converted to double once
  per run.
- The spacing factor of each moment is applied once per run, when adding the
  sums to the outputs (unweighted and weighted moments).

Unweighted moments without spacing are bit-identical to before. A new test
checks that the three accumulator types give the same moments.

Measured back to back against commit 3:

| Input | Labels | Group | Before (ms) | After (ms) | Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3840x2160/16 | 1024 | moments | 0.654 | 0.331 | 1.98× |
| 3840x2160/16 | 1024 | weighted | 0.720 | 0.716 | 1.01× |
| 3840x2160/16 | 1024 | all | 12.401 | 12.200 | 1.02× |
| 3840x2160/64 | 16256 | moments | 0.662 | 0.322 | 2.06× |
| 3840x2160/64 | 16256 | weighted | 0.703 | 0.726 | 0.97× |
| 3840x2160/64 | 16256 | all | 95.456 | 95.618 | 1.00× |
| 192x192x192/4 | 498 | moments | 0.430 | 0.306 | 1.41× |
| 192x192x192/4 | 498 | weighted | 0.475 | 0.477 | 1.00× |
| 192x192x192/4 | 498 | all | 13.027 | 12.773 | 1.02× |
| 8192^2 g=1 | 220219 | moments | 47.949 | 47.794 | 1.00× |
| 8192^2 g=16 | 882 | moments | 21.852 | 21.460 | 1.02× |
| 8192^2 g=None | 1 | moments | 42.560 | 41.989 | 1.01× |

The weighted moments still use double precision (the intensities are
floating point), and the 8192² images are bound by atomics.

### 5. Combine the last runs of a warp's lanes before the atomics

In a large region, every thread's last (often only) run has the same label,
so the 32 lanes of a warp added their statistics to the same addresses. These
atomics dominated the label-run kernels on large regions: 42 ms for the
moments of an 8192 × 8192 image that is one region, against 0.3 ms for the
3840 × 2160 tilings.

- After its loop, each lane compares the label of its last run with the next
  lane's (a shuffle and a ballot). Consecutive lanes with the same label form
  a group, and their accumulators are combined with a segmented shuffle
  reduction (`cucim_warp_reduce`, for sums, minima and maxima); only the
  first lane of each group issues the atomics. Runs that end inside a
  thread's pixels are still flushed directly.
- The lanes taking part are computed from the number of threads, not from
  `__activemask()`, so the `_sync` intrinsics get an exact mask in a partial
  last warp.
- The scan stops at the offset that the longest group of the warp needs
  (from the ballot), so warps with short groups do one or two shuffle steps
  instead of five. Without this, and before commit 4, the extra float64 adds
  of the reduction made the moments kernel up to 20% slower on the tilings
  (FP64 runs at 1/64 rate on the RTX A6000).
- Each label-run code fragment now also lists its accumulators and how they
  are combined.

A new test compares counts, bounding boxes, coordinate sums and intensity
statistics with NumPy for 5 label dtypes (including the 8- and 16-bit shuffle
overloads), 3 values of `pixels_per_thread` (partial last warp) and label

### 6. Measure perimeters and Euler numbers per label in one pass

The batch perimeter, Crofton perimeter and Euler number filtered the binary
image (an erosion and a 3 × 3 convolution, or the 2 × 2 (× 2) configuration
codes), assigned each pixel to the largest label within one pixel (a grey
dilation), and summed coefficients per label. That is wrong for regions
within two pixels of another region, so with `robust_perimeter=True` (the
default) a search for such regions (two 5 × 5 dilations and two label
reversals with `map_array`) was followed by a host loop recomputing each of
them on its crop. With many labels the loop dominated: 95 ms for the three
properties with 16 256 labels.

The configurations are now computed from "has the same label as this pixel"
instead of "is foreground", so every region is measured as in isolation, as
scikit-image does on each region's image, in one label-run pass per property:

- **perimeter:** for a border pixel of label L (a pixel of L with a 4- or
  8-connected neighbor outside L or outside the image), the coefficient is
  looked up from the border pixels of L among its 3 × 3 neighbors (a 5 × 5
  neighborhood, loaded only for border pixels).
- **Crofton perimeter and Euler number:** each 2 × 2 (2 × 2 × 2) window that
  contains pixels of L adds the coefficient of L's configuration in that
  window, counted by the first of those pixels in raster order. Windows
  partly outside the image count, as scikit-image pads with background. The
  coefficient of the empty window is 0 in every table, so only windows that
  contain L matter; that of the full window is 0 too, so interior pixels are
  skipped.

The per-pixel coefficients are summed by the label-run loop (registers and
warp aggregation from commits 1 and 5). The coefficient tables are now
float64, as in scikit-image: they were float32, which put the perimeters off
by up to 4e-8 (relative); they now agree with scikit-image to about 1e-15 on
the test images. The Euler coefficients are summed as integers.

The three properties no longer depend on the bounding boxes, the close-label
search is gone, and `robust`/`labels_close` (and the `robust_perimeter`
argument of `regionprops_dict`) are kept for compatibility but unused.
`_find_close_labels` is only used by the tests now. A new test compares each
label of touching random label images (4 granularities, 2 dtypes) with
scikit-image's `perimeter` (4 and 8 neighborhoods), `perimeter_crofton` (2 and
4 directions) and `euler_number` (2D connectivity 1 and 2, 3D connectivity 1
and 3) applied to that label alone.

The previous implementation with `robust_perimeter=False` (no close-label
search, inexact near other regions) took 6.08, 16.36 and 3.52 ms on the same
three inputs, so the new kernels are also 11–30× faster than that.

### 7. Update only the last coordinate's power sums per pixel

Within a row of the image only the last coordinate varies, so a moment is
`M[a, b] = Σ w·c0^a·c1^b = c0^a·T[b]` (2D), with the power sums
`T[e] = Σ w·c1^e` over the row's pixels (`c0^a·c1^b·T[c]` in 3D). The raw
moments kernel now updates only the `order + 1` power sums per pixel instead
of every moment (10 terms in 2D and 20 in 3D for order 3), and expands them
into the run's moments when the row changes and at the end of the run. This
matters for the weighted moments, which are summed in double precision.

The expansion must happen before the run's moments are combined across the
warp (commit 5), so the label-run loop gets a `finish` fragment that runs at
the end of each run, before the warp reduction and the flush. (Expanding in
the flush instead lost the pending row of every lane but the first of each
group; the existing moment tests fail with 327 errors in that case.)

expansion costs about as much as it saves. The unweighted moments (integer

### 8. Read 4 and 8-byte labels and images with 16-byte loads

Each thread of a label-run kernel reads `pixels_per_thread` consecutive
labels (and intensities), so each load instruction of a warp reads 32
locations `pixels_per_thread` elements apart. For 4 and 8-byte elements the
cache lines a warp works on (2–4 KB per array) no longer fit in the L1 cache
with many warps per SM, and lines were fetched several times.

A new `cucim_sequential_reader` reads a thread's elements with 16-byte loads
when they are at least 4 bytes, 16-byte aligned and the thread has
`pixels_per_thread` pixels (otherwise one element at a time). It extracts
the elements from the chunk with shifts and selects, so that the chunk stays
in registers and the loop body is not duplicated. It is used for the labels
in the label-run loop and for single-channel intensity images in the
intensity and weighted moments kernels. For 1 and 2-byte labels the
extraction cost more than it saved in label-only passes (pixel counts
0.18 → 0.26 ms with uint8 labels in a first version), so these are still
read one at a time. A new test checks that misaligned views (scalar path)
give the same results as aligned copies.

### 9. Do not cast the label image to a smaller integer type

`regionprops_dict` cast the label image to the smallest unsigned type that
holds `max_label` (e.g. int32 → uint16) so that the passes would read fewer
bytes. The cast reads and writes the whole image: on the 3840 × 2160 tiling
it took 69 µs, more than the label-run pass of the basic group (57 µs,
from an Nsight Systems profile). With 4 and 8-byte labels read with 16-byte
loads (commit 8), it no longer pays off even for the calls with the most
passes ("all").

The labels are now cast only when the image has to be copied anyway (not
C-contiguous) or is not an integer image (e.g. bool). `label_filled` is
still returned with the smallest unsigned type. A check of bool, int8,
int64, uint64 and Fortran-ordered int32 label images against scikit-image
(area, perimeter, Euler number, Hu moments, intensity, filled area) passed.

### 10. Let lanes in holes of a region join the warp's group

The warp aggregation (commit 5) combines the last runs of consecutive lanes
with the same label. A lane whose pixels are all background ended the group,
so in a large region with holes (e.g. the percolating component of the
random image with 16 × 16-pixel blocks, where a thread's 16 pixels often fall
in one background block) the groups stayed short and most atomics still
went to the same addresses: 10.6 ms for the moments of that 8192 × 8192
image, against 1.6 ms for one region without holes.

A lane without labeled pixels between two lanes whose last runs have the same
label now joins their group with identity values (0 for sums, +∞ or the
largest value for minima, −∞ or the lowest value for maxima). Lanes between
different labels stay apart: letting every empty lane join the next group
made the float64 scans longer and the tilings 3–7% slower in a first
version. The extra ballot and shuffles are skipped in warps where all or no
lanes have runs. The aggregation test gets a pattern with background blocks,
and intensities that are positive in odd and negative in even labels, so
that a wrong identity for the minimum or maximum fails the test (checked by
replacing each identity with 0).

run-to-run variation of these measurements (repeated runs of the moments
group gave 0.96–1.00×).

### 11. Unravel boundary-kernel coordinates in 32 bits when possible

The label-aware boundary kernels of commit 6 unraveled every labeled
pixel's raveled index into coordinates with 64-bit `%` and `/`, whatever the
image size. The other label-run kernels use 32-bit coordinates below 2³²
pixels (`_get_coord_dtype` on the bug-fix branch), since 64-bit integer
division is much slower. The boundary kernels now use 32-bit coordinates for
images of fewer than 2³¹ pixels, and 64-bit ones otherwise.

**Why signed.** These coordinates are signed `int`, hence the 2³¹ limit.
The first version used `unsigned int`, and NVRTC 13.3 (CuPy 14.2, sm_86)
produced an illegal memory access in one configuration only: 3D Euler
numbers of 4-byte labels with 10 pixels per thread, the default of
`regionprops_euler`.
- When every label and coefficient index was instrumented with a range
  check, the kernel ran correctly and no index was out of range.
- Signed 32-bit, 64-bit, or a `volatile` copy of the index all worked.

This points to code generation rather than an indexing error.

**Checks.**
- The signed version was compared with scikit-image's `perimeter`,
  `perimeter_crofton` and `euler_number` for 2 2D and 2 3D shapes.
- It covered 5 label types (`uint8`, `int16`, `int32`, `uint32`, `int64`),
  1–32, 40 and 64 pixels per thread, and both connectivities: 1700
  comparisons, all within 1e-12 (`boundary_matrix.py`).
- `test_boundary_kernel_coordinate_types` builds both coordinate types on
  small images. The 64-bit kernels are otherwise only used on images of 2³¹
  or more pixels.
- The (65537, 65536) image check passes with the 64-bit kernels.

### Incremental coordinates

moments) unravel every pixel's raveled index with `ndim - 1` integer

incrementing the coordinates (with carry) made no measurable difference

title: ci: Revert matrix_type overrides in for CUDA 13.4
body:

title: Update Euclidean distance transforms to efficiently support anisotropic extents
body:
The distance transform kernels were adapted from a third-party implementation that assumed isotropic shape. Whenever one axis is longer than the others we had to:
1. pad the image up to isotropic size
2. run the distance transform kernels
3. crop back to the original size

Whenever one axis is much longer than the others, this is very inefficient. There is nothing in the ideas behind the kernels that requires isotropic shape, but in some cases a transpose assumed both axes had equal size so the conversion is not fully trivial. I had Claude Opus 5.5 work on updating the existing kernels so we can run on truly anisotropic shape without introducing unnecessary additional intermediate buffers.


Every commit is one concern (2D and 3D are separate commits), and every change that is not a bug fix leaves the output **bit-for-bit unchanged** (compared on saved reference arrays after each change; the commit messages carry the per-change A/B numbers).


### Bug fixes

- **User-supplied `m1` whose band size is not a multiple of 32** gave wrong results (the 32 x 32
  transpose tiles skipped rows; error up to 320 against SciPy for `block_params=(6, 1, 1)` on
  288 x 288). The padded size is now a multiple of `32 * m1`.
- **In-place `indices` shape check:** the shape was compared with the *padded* shape, so every
  padded input raised "indices array has wrong shape". The cropped shape is used now.
- **`float64_distances` was never passed on** to `_pba_2d` / `_pba_3d`, so float32 distances were
  always computed and a float64 `distances` array raised. It is passed through now.
- **No background in the input:** the distances were arbitrary (>= 32768 in 2D, small values in
  3D). They are now infinite and `indices` negative, detected from the kernel results without a
  reduction or synchronization (documented in the docstring).
- **Arrays with 2**31 or more padded elements** raise a `ValueError` instead of overflowing the
  32-bit indices silently.
- **`sampling` validation:** the dimension is checked first, and a `sampling` that is not a scalar
  or one value per axis raises a `ValueError` instead of failing in the kernels.
- **float16 and complex images** now work in 2D (they failed when packed by the old elementwise
  kernel); they are converted to boolean as in 3D.
- **License header:** `pba_kernels_3d.h` now carries the PBA+ copyright and `Apache-2.0 AND MIT`
  tags like the 2D header.

### Performance tuning

- **Per-axis extents in the 2D kernels.** Each axis is padded only to the multiple that the bands
  and tiles need; the default block parameters are chosen from the first (m1) and second (m2) axis.
  No extra buffers (two image buffers, margin array of `2 * m1 * width`).
- **Per-axis extents in the 3D kernels** (`size_x`, `size_y`, `size_z`). x and y are padded to the
  tile size and z to the block height only. Two buffers are still enough.
- **Larger default `m3` in 2D** (largest power of two <= 16 and <= number of 32-wide tiles):
  1.2 to 1.3 times faster for 512² to 4096². With a pixel spacing in double precision the larger
  value is slower (the coloring kernel is limited by the double precision rate), so `m3` is at
  most 2 there (the previous default); a sweep of `m3` for sizes 256² to 8192² showed that the
  kernels without spacing, with `float32_spacing` and with `indices` still prefer 8 or 16.
- **Short, wide 2D images are processed transposed** (a transposed view that the kernels read; used
  only when no `indices` are requested, since ties between equidistant background pixels would be
  broken differently, and not when `block_params` is given). Limits: first axis <= 3072, second
  axis at least twice as long, <= 2**26 pixels. Up to 5x faster for 64 x 8192.
- **Cached kernels** (memoized per device, block size, type, and so on): 10 to 15 us less host time
  per call.
- **`sampling` checked with NumPy on the host** instead of `cp.unique(...).item()`: 0.2 to 0.35 ms
  less host time per call that has a `sampling`.
- **3D coordinates packed with the number of bits the shape needs.** A 64-bit integer was used as
  soon as one axis exceeded 1024; a 32-bit integer is now enough for most volumes below 2**31
  elements (e.g. 32 x 2048 x 2048): 1.5x faster and 1.5x less memory for such volumes.
- **The two phase-1 sweeps of the 2D kernels are fused** into `kernelFloodDownUp`: one launch less
  and the second sweep reads from cache (2 to 6% faster).
- **The first 2D and 3D kernels read the image** instead of a separate elementwise packing kernel:
  one pass over the coordinate arrays and one launch less. 8 to 18% faster. The image is read with
  its strides, so non-contiguous inputs need no copy.
- **Opt-in `float32_spacing`** (keyword-only, default `False`): float instead of double for the
  spacing and the distances computed with it. 2.6 to 4 times faster than double on GPUs with a low
  double precision rate; the distances differ from the default by about 1e-7 relative.

### Performance

RTX A6000, CuPy 14.2, `distance_transform_edt(image)` with float32 distances, random binary image
with 5% background pixels. GPU time per call (mean of 20 calls, 6 for the largest; best of 3
alternating runs of each version). "Before" is b715b157, "After" the tip of this branch. The
distances are identical (checked against SciPy for the tests and bit-for-bit between the versions
for the compared shapes).

**Anisotropic shapes, 2D**

| Shape | Before (ms) | After (ms) | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 256 x 4096 | 3.44 | 0.24 | 14.5x |
| 1024 x 4096 | 3.43 | 0.75 | 4.6x |
| 4096 x 256 | 2.33 | 0.22 | 10.6x |
| 512 x 8192 | 12.6 | 0.74 | 17.1x |
| 2048 x 8192 | 11.7 | 2.64 | 4.4x |
| 64 x 8192 | 13.3 | 0.14 | 93x |
| 40000 x 64 | 1034 | 0.54 | 1925x |

The time now follows the number of pixels (compare 1024² 0.32 ms, 4096² 2.5 ms below). Before, a
40000 x 64 image was padded to 40000² and used about 27 GB of memory pool.

**Anisotropic shapes, 3D**

| Shape | Before (ms) | After (ms) | Speedup | Memory pool before -> after |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 32 x 512 x 512 | 23.3 | 1.81 | 12.8x | 1536 -> 512 MiB |
| 64 x 512 x 512 | 22.3 | 2.58 | 8.6x | 1536 -> 512 MiB |
| 128 x 512 x 512 | 21.5 | 4.67 | 4.6x | 1536 -> 512 MiB |
| 512 x 64 x 64 | 11.2 | 0.61 | 18.3x | 1536 -> 512 MiB |
| 96 x 320 x 640 | 32.5 | 2.77 | 11.7x | 2512 -> 512 MiB |
| 64 x 1024 x 1024 | 179 | 8.9 | 20.1x | 9728 -> 1024 MiB |
| 32 x 2048 x 2048 | out of memory | 18.1 | | 2048 MiB |

**Isotropic shapes** (no padding was needed, so this is the effect of the tuning commits only)

| Shape | Before (ms) | After (ms) | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 64 x 64 | 0.149 | 0.117 | 1.28x |
| 512 x 512 | 0.249 | 0.165 | 1.51x |
| 1024 x 1024 | 0.466 | 0.315 | 1.48x |
| 2048 x 2048 | 1.23 | 0.84 | 1.47x |
| 4096 x 4096 | 3.53 | 2.49 | 1.42x |
| 8192 x 8192 | 11.3 | 9.42 | 1.20x |
| 32³ | 0.122 | 0.108 | 1.12x |
| 128³ | 0.552 | 0.512 | 1.08x |
| 256³ | 2.88 | 2.30 | 1.25x |
| 512³ | 20.4 | 16.6 | 1.23x |

For small images the call is limited by the host (launching 12 kernels in 2D, 6 in 3D); the
host time per call is 0.145 -> 0.113 ms for 64 x 64 and 0.09 -> 0.08 ms for 32³ (the same
runs).

**With `return_indices=True` and with a `sampling`**

| Case | Before (ms) | After (ms) | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| indices, 4096² | 3.96 | 2.90 | 1.36x |
| indices, 256 x 4096 | 3.58 | 0.75 | 4.8x |
| indices, 256³ | 4.05 | 3.49 | 1.16x |
| indices, 64 x 512 x 512 | 23.0 | 3.81 | 6.0x |
| sampling (1, 2.5), 1024² | 1.01 | 0.74 | 1.4x |
| sampling (1, 2.5), 4096² | 5.30 | 4.60 | 1.15x |
| sampling (1, 1, 2.5), 128³ | 1.40 | 1.17 | 1.20x |
| sampling (1, 1, 2.5), 256³ | 7.62 | 7.24 | 1.05x |
| `float32_spacing`, 4096² (new) | | 2.65 | 3.2x faster than the default with spacing |
| `float32_spacing`, 256³ (new) | | 1.98 | 3.7x faster than the default with spacing |

The transposed processing is not used for `indices`, so short, wide images gain less there.

### Tests

`morphology/tests/test_distance_transform.py` grows by about 590 lines. New or extended tests cover
anisotropic and strongly anisotropic shapes in 2D and 3D (against SciPy), the 2D orientation
(transposed) path, user-supplied `block_params` (including the band size and non-isotropic
cases), the padding and default-parameter helpers, the 3D coordinate encoding (including shapes
that need 64 bits and too-large inputs), the `ValueError` for too many elements, in-place
`distances` and `indices` (including the unpadded-shape case), `float64_distances`, no
background, input dtypes (NaN is foreground), non-contiguous inputs, `sampling` types and
validation, `float32_spacing`, repeated calls and the kernel cache.

### Not included

- Fusing the final distance computation into the last coloring kernel (upper bound 7.5 to 10% improvement).
- CUDA graph or fewer launches to cut the host cost of small images.
- float32 spacing as the default (an accuracy decision).

title: Complete scheduled cuCIM 26.12 deprecations
body:
This PR completes deprecations previously scheduled for removal in cuCIM 26.12 and aligns the morphology API with scikit-image’s removal of the separate `binary_*` functions. cuCIM retains the binary GPU kernels internally because they offer substantial performance benefits on boolean images.

The scheduled removals are:

- `rolling_ball(num_threads=...)`, replaced by `workers`.
- `remove_small_objects(min_size=...)`, replaced by `max_size=min_size - 1`.
- `remove_small_holes(area_threshold=...)`, replaced by `max_size=area_threshold - 1`.

The `remove_small_*` parameters become keyword-only, and their default `max_size` becomes 63 to preserve the original threshold behavior.

The public `binary_erosion`, `binary_dilation`, `binary_opening`, and `binary_closing` functions are deprecated in 26.12, with removal scheduled for 27.04. Their warnings provide migration instructions for the corresponding grayscale functions.

To preserve performance, grayscale morphology now dispatches suitable boolean inputs and outputs to private binary kernels, which stop scanning a neighborhood as soon as the result is known. This dispatch preserves grayscale boundary modes, footprint alignment and mirroring, footprint sequences, and output semantics. Large dense footprints retain separable filtering, avoiding the cost of scanning every footprint element in uniform regions. Other dtypes and incompatible border values retain the grayscale path.

Regression tests compare the dispatched results with scikit-image and cover deprecation warnings, migration recipes, boundary modes, footprints, array layouts, and output handling.

title: Faster `cucim.skimage.measure.label` performance
body:
This MR is the result of iterative agent driven refactoring of cuCIM's connected-component labeling. 2.6-6.6x performance improvements were obtained by adopting new kernels for the case of binary images with full connectivity. Other cases such as reduced connectivity or grayscale images have a more modest 1.1-1.4x performance improvement.

The docstring has been updated with references covering various optimizations that were previously proposed in the literature. Iterative improvement of performance based on measurements of the existing kernels and newer algorithms described in the literature was performed by Claude Opus 5.5.

Every commit is one optimization with an A/B measurement in its message, and every commit leaves the output of `label` **bitwise unchanged** (the labels are numbered by the raster order of the first pixel of each region, so all implementations must give identical arrays; the benchmark script checks a hash of every output against `main`).

### Results

RTX A6000, GPU time (mean of 30 calls, best of three alternating A/B rounds). "Before" is `main`. `label` of a boolean image, default (full) connectivity unless a
connectivity `c` is given.

| Case | Before (ms) | After (ms) | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| label random 4096^2 p=0.1 c=2 | 2.31 | 0.90 | 2.6x |
| label random 4096^2 p=0.5 c=1 | 2.50 | 2.23 | 1.1x |
| label random 4096^2 p=0.5 c=2 | 3.55 | 1.04 | 3.4x |
| label random 4096^2 p=0.9 c=2 | 4.00 | 0.88 | 4.5x |
| label blobs 4096^2 c=2 | 4.05 | 0.72 | 5.6x |
| label all foreground 4096^2 c=2 | 6.44 | 0.97 | 6.6x |
| label tiles 2160x3840 int32 (greyscale) | 2.07 | 0.95 | 2.2x |
| label random 512^2 p=0.5 c=2 | 0.44 | 0.20 | 2.2x |
| label random 256^3 p=0.5 c=1 | 2.65 | 1.86 | 1.4x |
| label random 256^3 p=0.5 c=3 | 5.82 | 0.92 | 6.3x |
| label blobs 256^3 c=3 | 5.23 | 0.84 | 6.2x |
| label serpentine 1024^2 c=1 | 0.49 | 0.23 | 2.1x |

The largest gains are for boolean images with the default (full) connectivity, which is
the common call, in 3D (5 to 6 times) and for dense 2D images (4 to 6 times). Connectivity 1 and greyscale (integer-valued) images use the pixel kernels and gain 1.1 to 2.2 times.

### What was changed

0. **Refactor.** The init and connect steps of `_label` move into `_connect` (and the offsets of the preceding neighbors into `_half_structure_dirs`), so that the following commits change the connect step in one place. No change in behavior.
1. **Path halving in the connect kernel.** `find` follows up to 4095 links in an all-foreground image because the paths are never shortened. Each step now also points the node at its grandparent (as in ECL-CC). 2D dense images 1.3 to 2.4 times faster.
2. **Coordinates once per pixel, neighbor offsets compiled into the kernel.** The connect kernel recomputed the pixel coordinates (a division and a modulo per axis) for each neighbor. It now decomposes the index once, and the kernel is generated (and cached) for the number of dimensions and the structure so that the offsets are constants. 3D images 1.7 to 1.8 times faster.
3. **Link each pixel to a preceding neighbor before the unions.** A new init kernel points every foreground pixel at its first foreground (and equal-valued) preceding neighbor without atomics (the atomic-free initial linking of Komura and Kalentev, used by KE and BKE). The unions then find most pixels already in a tree. Dense and winding regions gain the most (all-foreground 4096² 2.6 -> 1.6 ms).
4. **2 x 2 (x 2) blocks** for boolean input with full connectivity, as in BUF and BKE (Allegretti, Bolelli and Grana, 2020): all pixels of a block are neighbors, so a block is one node. Two kernels with one thread per block replace init and connect: block init writes a star tree per block and an occupancy byte, block connect joins two blocks if both have a foreground pixel on the sides that face each other (at most 4 or 13 unions per block instead of per pixel). The root of each region is still its first pixel, so the later steps and the labels are unchanged.
5. **Per-block count, collect and finalize** in the block path: a thread per block finds the root of its block, counts and collects the roots, and, after the sort, looks up the rank once and writes the label of its 4 or 8 pixels (instead of a binary search per pixel).
6. **Fewer host costs.** The shapes are scalar kernel arguments (no host-to-device copy) and the structuring element is cached. A call is partly host-bound (CPU 0.76 ms against GPU 0.87 ms for a 4096² image), so this saves 0.10 to 0.13 ms per call.
7. **Documentation.** The Notes of `label` say when the fast path is used (boolean input, 2D or 3D, full connectivity, `background` 0) and what falls back to the general implementation, and cite the papers behind the implementation (ECL-CC, Komura, BUF/BKE, and the 2024 review of GPU labeling). The implementation started from the one in CuPy, for which no literature reference was given; the Notes say so.
8. **Boolean images with `background=True`** keep the fast path (the image is inverted instead of being converted to an integer image by the subtraction of the background).

### Tests

- `measure/tests/test_label_blocks.py`: block path equal to scikit-image on random images of 1 to 3 dimensions, shapes that cut the blocks (odd sizes, size-1 axes), densities from 0.1 to 1.0; equal to the pixel kernels; the dispatch conditions; 64-bit labels on small images; a boolean image with `background=True` uses the blocks.
- A 342-image comparison of the block path with scikit-image (run once, outside the test suite) and the full `measure` test folder pass.

### Alternative Approaches Tried and not kept

- Full (two-pass) path compression instead of halving: connect of the serpentine 1.4 -> 3.3 ms.
- Linking in the init kernel with the old per-neighbor coordinate math: slower for sparse and 3D images (it became a gain once the coordinates were computed once, item 3).
- Skipping the union with the neighbor that init already linked: mixed (p=0.9 1.81 -> 2.11 ms).
- The binary-mode kernels for boolean input of the pixel path: 3D 7% faster but dense 2D 8% slower (the connect step is limited by contention between unions, not by instructions).
- Other launch block sizes for the block kernels: the CuPy default (128) is best.

title: Add marching cubes and mesh surface area
body:
This PR adds GPU implementations of `cucim.skimage.measure.marching_cubes` and `cucim.skimage.measure.mesh_surface_area` for CuPy arrays. This resolves https://github.com/rapidsai/cucim/issues/332.

`marching_cubes` extracts triangular isosurfaces from 3D volumes and follows the scikit-image API for the supported options, including `level`, `spacing`, `gradient_direction`, `step_size`, `allow_degenerate`, `method`, and `mask`. `method="lewiner"` (the scikit-image default) and `method="lorensen"` are implemented, and `method="vega"`, which is not in scikit-image (see below). The Lewiner mesh has exactly the same number of vertices and faces as scikit-image's on every volume tested, including noise volumes that contain millions of ambiguous cells.

`mesh_surface_area` computes the surface area of triangular meshes produced by `marching_cubes` using a CuPy reduction kernel.

On an RTX A6000 the GPU implementation is 14-17x faster than scikit-image for 64^3 volumes, 69-88x for 128^3, 113-175x for 192^3 to 384^3 volumes with a simple isosurface, and 290-590x for volumes with large, noisy isosurfaces (see Benchmark results).

## Differences from scikit-image

These are also listed in the docstring of `marching_cubes`.

- Supports additional, more modern `method=vega` in addition to the `method=lewiner` and `method=lorensen` approaches of scikit-image.
- The vertices and faces of `method="lewiner"` and `method="lorensen"` are the same sets as scikit-image's, in a different order.
- `normals` have the sign of scikit-image's, but a vertex on an edge gets the interpolated central-difference gradient of its two samples (scikit-image sums the gradients of the cells around it); `values` is the larger of the two sample values of the edge (scikit-image uses the range of the cells around the vertex). Neither is equal to scikit-image's. The reason is the vertex generation: one thread per crossed edge computes its vertex from the two samples at the ends of the edge, without visiting the cells around it. scikit-image accumulates the normal and the value of a vertex over every cell that emits it (up to four in 3D, and which cells do depends on the method's triangulation).
