Reproducing that would need an additional pass over the cells with atomic additions, which was not built or measured. The normal chosen is the usual one for a point on an edge: smooth and independent of how many cells share the vertex.
- `verts` is float32 and `faces` int32 (scikit-image returns float64 `verts` for a non-unit `spacing` and int64 `faces` with `allow_degenerate=False`).
- A volume that contains NaN raises a `ValueError`.
- The level is used as a float32 by the kernels.
- `allow_degenerate=False` can give different counts for volumes with samples equal to the level (scikit-image's vertices at samples have errors of about 1e-16, so it misses coincident vertices).
- `method="vega"` is not guaranteed to give a manifold mesh (some noisy volumes have edges shared by four triangles), although each cell has the topology of its trilinear interpolant.

## Implementation Approach

The implementation uses CuPy RawKernels and scan-based allocation: no kernel appends to an output with atomics, so the mesh is deterministic and every output array is allocated once at its final size. For one call the steps are:

1. **Validate and prepare.** Convert the volume to contiguous float32, check `level` against the data range and apply `step_size` by subsampling. The kernels index the nodes, cells and output arrays with 32-bit integers, and with 64-bit integers (compiled as a second variant of each kernel) when three times the number of nodes, cells, vertices or faces reaches `2**31`, which is a volume of about 715 million voxels (894³). Volumes of over 2 billion voxels were checked (a 1300³ sphere, all three methods). The vertex ids are `int32`, so a mesh with `2**31` or more vertices or faces raises a `ValueError`.
2. **Classify edges, one thread per grid node.** Each thread tests the three edges that leave its node (along the three axes) and writes a 3-bit crossing mask and the number of crossed edges (`uint8` each). With a `mask`, an edge only counts when it belongs to a cell whose mask is set.
3. **Number the crossed edges.** An inclusive scan over the per-node counts gives `node_scan`; the vertex id of a crossed edge is `node_scan[node] - popcount(mask[node] >> side)`. Scanning per node rather than per edge makes the scan 3x smaller, and no separate array of vertex ids is stored. All scans of `uint8` counts in the pipeline use a block scan (sums of blocks of 1024 counts, a scan of the block sums, and a scan inside each block with the block offset added), which gives the same values as `cp.cumsum` in half the time for 256^3 entries (0.17 ms against 0.34 ms); below about 2.6 million entries `cp.cumsum` is used because it is faster there. A small compaction kernel (one thread per node) writes the flat index of each crossed edge at its vertex id.
4. **Generate vertices, one thread per vertex.** Position by linear interpolation along the edge, a normal from the interpolated central-difference gradient, and the `values` output (the larger of the two edge values).
5. **Count triangles, one thread per cell.** `uint8` triangle counts, and a scan gives each cell's output offset.
6. **Generate faces, one thread per cell.** Triangle indices are looked up and written at the cell's offset, with the winding flipped for `gradient_direction`.
7. **`allow_degenerate=False`.** Zero-area faces are found in parallel, coincident vertices are merged with a lock-free union-find, and the vertex and face arrays are compacted with scans (a no-op early return when no face is degenerate).

The code shared by both methods (validation, `step_size`, the edge classification, numbering and compaction kernels, the vertex kernel, the volume and gradient helpers, and degenerate-face removal) is in `_marching_cubes_common.py`. Each method supplies its crossing test (`mc_crosses`, which is now the same for the three methods: a sample equal to the level is below it, as in scikit-image). `_marching_cubes_lorensen.py` holds the classic 256-entry triangle table and the Lorensen counting and face kernels (steps 5-6).

The Lewiner path replaces steps 5-6 as follows. The counting kernel looks up the case and configuration of each cell and resolves the ambiguous cases (3, 4, 6, 7, 10, 12 and 13) with the face and interior tests of the Lewiner algorithm, evaluated in double precision, in the same operation order as scikit-image where the values allow it (the count kernel reads the sample values and the level as float32, so a sample or level that is not exactly a float32 can be classified differently from scikit-image, which keeps the level as a double). This is done once per cell: the kernel stores the triangle count, a "needs a center vertex" flag, and the offset of the cell's edges in a single concatenated triangle table (a `uint16` per cell). A second kernel creates the center vertices (for the cells that need one) and writes them after the edge vertices in the same vertex, normal and value arrays. The face kernel is then a plain table lookup with no ambiguity tests and no double-precision work.

`method="vega"` is the marching cubes 33 implementation of Vega, Abache and Coll (J. Computer Graphics Techniques 8(3), 2019), whose interior test is corrected: it is made on a diagonal of the cell on the plane through the saddle point of the trilinear interpolant, so that the topology of the mesh does not depend on the orientation of the field (the Lewiner method gives different topologies for some cells and their mirror images), and it has the two patterns of the case 13.5.2. The counting kernel resolves each cell once, as for Lewiner, with the case selection of the MC33 C library of Vega and Abache (MIT; ported with the help of the CUDA port in the isoext project, MIT) and its 2310-entry lookup
table, and everything else is shared. The default stays `lewiner`, which matches scikit-image.

All methods support masks (in classification and counting), `step_size` and `spacing`.

Lorensen was implemented first because it is the simpler classic algorithm and provided the GPU data layout. The Lewiner path was added afterward to provide the topologically consistent behavior that scikit-image uses by default. Both methods are kept for API compatibility: `method="lorensen"` is part of the scikit-image API, and the Lorensen kernels are somewhat faster on noisy data (see below). The two meshes differ in topology (different Euler characteristic on noisy data, for example), not in watertightness: the classic table also gives meshes without open edges on the volumes tested.

## References and Licensing

Licenses and attributions were added for some reference codebases:

- CuMCubes, as a design reference for a per-node, three-axis vertex-id grid with count, vertex and face passes.
- The MC33 C library of Vega and Abache (MIT) and the isoext project of Guangyan Cai (MIT): the case selection and the lookup table of `method="vega"` are a port of the library's, made with the help of isoext's CUDA port, and are credited in `LICENSE-3rdparty.md` and in the file headers.
- NVIDIA Warp, as a design reference for allocating the output from prefix scans rather than atomic appends. The reference is the legacy native CUDA marching cubes (`warp/native/marching.cu`) of Warp versions 1.6.2 to 1.7.2, the releases under Apache-2.0 (Warp was relicensed on 2025-03-06 and replaced this implementation in version 1.8.0).

The kernel code does not come from any of th above projects. The Lewiner path (case tables, ambiguity tests, center vertex) is derived from the scikit-image implementation, which is also the behavioral reference for validation, output conventions and supported API semantics.

## Testing

Tests (120 in `test_marching_cubes.py`, `test_marching_cubes_kernels.py` and `test_marching_cubes_vega.py`) compare behavior against scikit-image across representative volumes and options: Lorensen and Lewiner, `allow_degenerate=True` and `False`, `step_size`, masks, spacing, gradient direction, and surface-area calculation.

The kernel-level tests check, for each of the 256 binary cases and the ambiguous branches (including center-vertex cases), that the face-generating kernels produce the triangles of a
Python port of scikit-image's reference selector. Noisy volumes (white and smoothed, with `level` 0 and 0.1) check that the Lewiner mesh has the same number of vertices and faces and the same surface area as scikit-image's. The 64-bit kernels are run on small volumes (by lowering the limit) and give meshes that are bitwise equal to the 32-bit ones, for the three methods, with and without a mask and with and without removal of the degenerate faces; a 900³ sphere (above the old limit) is checked against the radius and the area of the sphere (skipped when less than 16 GB of device memory is free).

The tests of `vega` check that the case selection equals that of the reference code (144 reference cells), that the topology of single cells and of closed random fields equals that of the trilinear interpolant on a finer grid, that it does not depend on the 48 symmetries of the cube, and the examples of the paper.

For `allow_degenerate=False` the geometry is preserved, but which of several coincident vertices survives (and so the exact vertex count in rare cases) can differ from scikit-image's sequential post-processing; for example, one extra vertex in 12.6 million on a 384^3 noise volume. This is noted in the docstring.

### Benchmark comparison with isoext (a GPU reference for `method="vega"`)

`method="vega"` has no scikit-image counterpart, so it was compared with [isoext](https://github.com/GuangyanCai/isoext) (MIT; PyTorch and Thrust), whose `vega` method is a port of the same MC33 C library, and with its `lewiner` method as another GPU implementation. Same RTX A6000 and float32 volumes, one library at a time. isoext: median of 20 calls of `isoext.marching_cubes` on a prebuilt grid (CUDA events); cuCIM: mean GPU time of 20 calls with `allow_degenerate=True`. cuCIM also validates the input and returns normals and values, which isoext does not. isoext 1.0.0 was built from a local checkout with CUDA 13.2 and PyTorch 2.14.1.

| Volume | Method | isoext (ms) | cuCIM (ms) | isoext / cuCIM |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| ellipsoid 128^3 | Lewiner | 1.86 | 0.46 | 4.0x |
| ellipsoid 128^3 | Vega | 1.76 | 0.47 | 3.7x |
| ellipsoid 256^3 | Lewiner | 6.85 | 1.44 | 4.8x |
| ellipsoid 256^3 | Vega | 7.02 | 1.42 | 5.0x |
| ellipsoid 384^3 | Lewiner | 15.50 | 4.06 | 3.8x |
| ellipsoid 384^3 | Vega | 16.24 | 4.06 | 4.0x |
| smooth noise 256^3 | Lewiner | 63.40 | 3.29 | 19.3x |
| smooth noise 256^3 | Vega | 73.30 | 3.20 | 22.9x |
| smooth noise 384^3 | Lewiner | 160.92 | 10.54 | 15.3x |
| smooth noise 384^3 | Vega | 195.50 | 10.36 | 18.9x |

(White noise 128^3, a stress test with almost every cell ambiguous: Lewiner 96.4 vs 4.5 ms, Vega 66.5 vs 1.6 ms.) The cause of the difference was not isolated; isoext fills a fixed-size triangle soup per active cell and welds the vertices with a global sort, while cuCIM numbers the edges with a scan.

Correctness: the `vega` meshes agree. On the ellipsoids all triangles are identical, and on the smooth-noise volume 7,414,288 of 7,414,355 triangles are identical (the 67 and 49 that differ are probably borderline single-precision tests, not investigated); areas and signed volumes agree to the printed digits. The `lewiner` meshes have the same vertices and areas, but only about 30% of the triangles are identical on the ellipsoid and smooth-noise volumes: for cells without ambiguity isoext splits the quadrilaterals along a different diagonal
than scikit-image does (cuCIM's triangulation equals scikit-image's).

## Benchmark results vs. scikit-image

RTX A6000 vs Intel i9-10980XE, scikit-image 0.26.0, CuPy 14.2.0, float32 volumes.
GPU times are the mean of 10 runs from `cupyx.profiler.benchmark` (after 3 warm-up runs) and do not include host-device transfers.
CPU times are the best of 2 runs (1 run when the first took over 2 s) over two benchmark sessions.
The meshes had the same number of vertices and faces on CPU and GPU in every row except `allow_degenerate=False` (see Testing).

**Ellipsoid** (the isosurface of `benchmarks/skimage/cucim_measure_bench.py`; about 0.1-0.6 M vertices):

| Volume | Method | CPU (True) | GPU (True) | Speedup | CPU (False) | GPU (False) | Speedup |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 64^3 | Lewiner | 5.6 ms | 0.40 ms | 13.9x | 6.8 ms | 0.44 ms | 15.4x |
| 64^3 | Lorensen | 5.8 ms | 0.35 ms | 16.6x | 6.7 ms | 0.39 ms | 17.1x |
| 128^3 | Lewiner | 31.8 ms | 0.46 ms | 68.6x | 37.6 ms | 0.49 ms | 77.4x |
| 128^3 | Lorensen | 33.5 ms | 0.41 ms | 81.2x | 37.5 ms | 0.43 ms | 87.8x |
| 192^3 | Lewiner | 93.8 ms | 0.79 ms | 118.0x | 105 ms | 0.80 ms | 130.2x |
| 192^3 | Lorensen | 96.8 ms | 0.70 ms | 138.0x | 108 ms | 0.73 ms | 148.8x |
| 256^3 | Lewiner | 208 ms | 1.43 ms | 145.4x | 229 ms | 1.50 ms | 152.3x |
| 256^3 | Lorensen | 220 ms | 1.40 ms | 157.1x | 241 ms | 1.39 ms | 172.8x |
| 384^3 | Lewiner | 699 ms | 4.37 ms | 159.9x | 722 ms | 4.37 ms | 165.0x |
| 384^3 | Lorensen | 700 ms | 4.20 ms | 166.6x | 766 ms | 4.37 ms | 175.4x |

(True / False is `allow_degenerate`.)

**Noisy volumes** (Gaussian-smoothed noise, sigma 3, level 0; white noise has
many ambiguous cells; the masked case has the top half of the volume enabled):

| Volume | Vertices | Faces | Method | CPU (True) | GPU (True) | Speedup | CPU (False) | GPU (False) | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| smooth noise 256^3 | 3.7 M | 7.4 M | Lewiner | 1647 ms | 3.29 ms | 501x | 2.45 s | 4.83 ms | 506x |
| smooth noise 256^3 | 3.7 M | 7.4 M | Lorensen | 1724 ms | 3.20 ms | 538x | 2.46 s | 4.82 ms | 510x |
| smooth noise 384^3 | 12.6 M | 25.1 M | Lewiner | 6.33 s | 11.24 ms | 563x | 8.26 s | 15.78 ms | 523x |
| smooth noise 384^3 | 12.6 M | 25.1 M | Lorensen | 6.24 s | 10.90 ms | 572x | 8.01 s | 15.56 ms | 515x |
| white noise 128^3 | 3.2 M | 7.2 M | Lewiner | 1385 ms | 4.55 ms | 304x | 1890 ms | 5.88 ms | 322x |
| white noise 128^3 | 3.1 M | 6.6 M | Lorensen | 1195 ms | 2.03 ms | 589x | 1810 ms | 3.28 ms | 551x |
| smooth noise 256^3, half masked | 1.9 M | 3.7 M | Lewiner | 779 ms | 2.64 ms | 295x | 1121 ms | 3.47 ms | 323x |
| smooth noise 256^3, half masked | 1.9 M | 3.7 M | Lorensen | 743 ms | 2.35 ms | 316x | 1043 ms | 3.18 ms | 328x |

On smooth data the methods take about the same time (Lewiner within about 5% of Lorensen). Lewiner is slower only when almost every cell is ambiguous
(white noise), where it takes about twice as long as Lorensen because of the double-precision ambiguity tests. `method="vega"` takes 1.55 ms for the 256^3 ellipsoid, 3.34 ms for the smooth noise 256^3 and 10.50 ms for 384^3 (Lewiner 1.45, 3.27 and 10.82 ms), and 1.56 ms for white noise 128^3 (Lewiner 4.38 ms, Lorensen 2.07 ms), because its tests are in single precision (same GPU and settings, `allow_degenerate=True`; not isolated).

**`mesh_surface_area`** (meshes from `marching_cubes` of the ellipsoid with `allow_degenerate=False`; the areas agree with scikit-image's):

| Volume | Vertices | Faces | CPU | GPU | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 64^3 | 8,536 | 17,068 | 1.24 ms | 0.051 ms | 24.3x |
| 128^3 | 34,640 | 69,276 | 5.21 ms | 0.093 ms | 56.0x |
| 192^3 | 78,536 | 157,068 | 11.44 ms | 0.170 ms | 67.3x |
| 256^3 | 139,872 | 279,740 | 20.68 ms | 0.447 ms | 46.3x |

### Effect of the optimizations in the commit history

The branch ends with separate commits for each optimization of the first working implementation (same GPU and settings, `allow_degenerate=True`, GPU time before and after the whole series; every step left the output bitwise unchanged):

| Volume | Lewiner before | Lewiner now | Lorensen before | Lorensen now |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| sphere 256^3 | 3.56 ms | 1.48 ms | 3.37 ms | 1.39 ms |
| smooth noise 256^3 | 6.71 ms | 3.27 ms | 4.34 ms | 3.23 ms |
| smooth noise 384^3 | 22.6 ms | 11.1 ms | 14.7 ms | 10.9 ms |
| smooth noise 256^3, half masked | 5.54 ms | 2.65 ms | 3.98 ms | 2.31 ms |
| white noise 128^3 | 34.7 ms | 4.46 ms | 1.79 ms | 2.10 ms |

The largest effects were resolving each Lewiner case once in the counting kernel (the white-noise face kernel went from 31 ms to under 1 ms), scanning per node instead of per edge (about 0.5-1 ms at 256^3), generating vertices with one thread per vertex, and scanning the counts in blocks (about 0.15-0.2 ms less for each scan of 256^3 entries).

title: Reuse the new reductions and fused passes across cucim.skimage
body:
## Context

**Depends on #1182 (spline interpolation optimizations) and #1183 (pyramid optimizations).** This PR is stacked on top of both, in that order; please review them first. Its diff here includes their commits until they merge, so review only the commits after the pyramid branch tip (`8d129f5f`).

## Motivation

The pyramid branch (#1183) introduced several optimizations that are not specific to image pyramids: one-scan combined extrema/NaN reductions with a single-launch final merge, a promise that inputs are finite, and fused elementwise passes that avoid full-sized temporaries and repeated scalar readbacks. Many other `cucim.skimage` functions repeat the same pattern (separate `min()`, `max()`, `isnan().any()`, each with a host readback). This stacked change moves the reductions into a shared module and reuses them in exposure, metrics, dtype conversion, histograms, CLAHE, Chan-Vese, phase correlation, and Li thresholding.

## Common implementation

`cucim.skimage._shared._reduction_kernels` owns the min/max/NaN accumulator, the NaN-ignoring and NaN-propagating policies, dispatch (direct, single-launch last-block, partial/merge), packed bounds, and the extrema/squared-error and error/normalizer reductions used by the metrics. Warp clipping (moved from the transform module, no duplicate left), exposure, metrics, dtype conversion, and Chan-Vese use it. Ordered comparisons preserve float32 subnormal extrema. The sign of zero in an extremum is unspecified and documented.

Dispatch cutoffs were measured on an RTX A6000. Contiguous bool, integer, float32, and float64 inputs use the single-launch kernel above 16384 elements; only contiguous float16 inputs of at least 128 KiB use CuPy's separate `min()` and `max()` (CUB when available, with an optional-import fallback), because float16 has no single-launch kernel. Chan-Vese's fused normalization and phase
correlation's NaN check stay next to their single callers; `threshold_li` reuses its local shifted maximum.

### Fused extrema against CuPy's separate reductions

Complete-call time on an RTX A6000, back to back, CuPy `min()` + `max()` + packing the results against the single launch (the last commit):

| Input | CuPy | Single launch |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| float32, 1 MiB / 32 MiB / 128 MiB | 41 / 116 / 401 us | 31 / 66 / 215 us |
| float64, 8 MiB / 32 MiB / 128 MiB | 92 / 213 / 602 us | 31 / 69 / 224 us |
| uint8, 32 MiB / 128 MiB | 108 / 393 us | 68 / 213 us |
| bool, 16 MiB | 184 us | 50 us |

With a NaN flag, the fused kernel is 1.7x-4x faster than `min()`, `max()`, and `isnan().any()` (3x-5.7x against `nanmin()`/`nanmax()`), and it reads the image once. At large sizes it reaches 560-640 GB/s, close to one CUB pass (570-670 GB/s). Below 16384 elements the direct one-block reduction is used; a 512 KiB uint8 image took 166 us there against 32 us single-launch, which is why the direct limit is an element count for extrema.

## Functional changes

### Intensity rescaling

Warp clipping continues to use NaN-ignoring bounds plus the NaN flag. `intensity_range(..., "image")` uses NaN-propagating bounds and transfers its packed min/max together in one host readback, preserving Python scalar return types and integer precision.
`rescale_intensity` reuses those bounds when both ranges request `"image"`. A further fused elementwise pass performs clipping, subtraction, division, multiplication, addition, and the output cast without full-sized temporaries. It keeps separately rounded operations, constant-image clipping, and NaN warnings; half-precision arithmetic retains the existing path.

Compared with the rebased statistics implementation before these review follow-ups, complete float32 rescaling improved as follows:

| Spatial size | Default ranges | Explicit input/output ranges |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 16 x 16 | 1.48x | 2.29x |
| 512 x 512 | 1.31x | 2.15x |
| 2048 x 2048 | 1.81x | 2.85x |
| 4096 x 4096 | 2.58x | 4.11x |

At 2048 x 2048, float64 improved 1.36x with default ranges and 1.63x with explicit ranges.

### Combined error and NRMSE reductions

`normalized_root_mse(..., normalization="min-max")` combines reference-image extrema and squared-error accumulation using the shared range accumulator and partial/merge staging. A fused device-side scalar calculation propagates NaNs and computes the final normalized error. This avoids the two full-sized subtraction/squaring temporaries and separate min/max scans. Inputs with
different strides are reduced through views rather than copied to flatten. Large contiguous Euclidean/mean NRMSE calls now use the same staging with error and reference sums instead of extrema. MSE uses it from 2048² elements, while Euclidean/mean NRMSE uses it from 1024²; smaller or noncontiguous inputs keep the existing path. Mean normalization retains the input dtype for its sum and
division.

The squared differences are formed in the promoted image dtype, as before, and summed in float64; the range subtraction also retains its previous dtype. Reduction order can change the last bits of floating-point sums.

Complete min-max NRMSE calls improved **1.25x-4.03x** (contiguous float32 RGB, 16 x 16 through 4096 x 4096). Large-image MSE and Euclidean/mean NRMSE gained further:

| Float32 size | MSE | Euclidean NRMSE | Mean NRMSE |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1024 x 1024 | Existing path | 1.71x | 1.54x |
| 2048 x 2048 | 1.20x | 1.62x | 1.89x |
| 4096 x 4096 | 2.02x | 2.48x | 2.88x |

At 2048 x 2048, float64 improved 1.52x, 2.15x, and 1.83x respectively. The cutoff keeps MSE on its original path at intermediate sizes where staging regressed; min-max NRMSE is unchanged by this follow-up.

### PSNR automatic range validation

For matching float32/float64 inputs, `peak_signal_noise_ratio` combines extrema and squared error in one staged reduction when `data_range` is not provided. Other dtypes retain packed extrema plus the existing MSE path. Validate both bounds and select the signed/nonnegative range on the host after one transfer, avoiding multiple scalar GPU comparisons/readbacks. Explicit data ranges, dtype warnings, validation errors, and NaN propagation retain their behavior. Negative float32 subnormals now select the signed range rather than being treated as zero by GPU comparison flush-to-zero behavior.

Complete automatic-range float32 calls improved 1.65x at 16 x 16, 1.03x at 512 x 512, 1.19x at 2048 x 2048, and 2.19x at 4096 x 4096 in the final follow-up measurements. Float64 at 2048 x 2048 improved 1.79x. Explicit-range calls also benefit from large-image MSE: 1.06x at 2048 x 2048 and 2.03x at 4096 x 4096 for float32, and 1.50x at 2048 x 2048 for float64; small explicit cases were unchanged.

### Histogram range and bin-bound reuse

Reuse the shared extrema helper for integer bin centers and floating histogram outer edges, including the default single-channel floating path. Keep integer endpoints on the host and pass them through single- and multichannel calls. Known integer ranges of up to 4096 bins use shared-memory block histograms with the offset applied in the counting kernel, avoiding `cp.bincount`'s redundant
extrema and negativity checks. Wider ranges retain the existing path. Contiguous inputs use `ravel()` to avoid a full copy.

Float bin-edge construction preserves the original dtype rounding. Constant and empty images, nonfinite range errors, signed offsets, normalization, and exceptional float32 ranges retain their behavior.

Complete-call GPU-event gains from the review follow-ups:

| Spatial size | Float32 histogram | Uint8 histogram |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 16 x 16 | 1.24x | 2.17x |
| 512 x 512 | 1.44x | 2.14x |
| 2048 x 2048 | 1.43x | 2.21x |
| 4096 x 4096 | 1.61x | 2.79x |

At 2048 x 2048, float64 improved 1.40x and signed int16 improved 2.53x.

### Batched CLAHE contextual histograms

`equalize_adapthist` uses the same known-bound integer histogram helper to count all contextual regions in one launch. This replaces the per-row `cp.bincount` loop and its repeated validation scans/readbacks. Compact bins use shared block counts; wider histograms use global atomics. Histogram clipping still runs on the host, and interpolation is unchanged.

For 64 contextual rows and 256 bins, the histogram component fell from 12.81 to 0.026 ms (4096 pixels per row) and 13.01 to 0.095 ms (262144 pixels per row). Together with the rescaling/conversion changes, complete float32 CLAHE improved 3.46x at 16 x 16, 3.38x at 512 x 512, 2.15x at 2048 x 2048, and 1.51x at 4096 x 4096. Float64 at 2048 x 2048 improved 2.00x. These complete calls include the remaining host clipping and interpolation costs.

### Phase-correlation scalar NaN checks

Combine the final NaN checks on the complex correlation peak and the two real amplitude statistics in one elementwise kernel, followed by one host decision. This replaces up to three separate scalar `isnan` operations and host readbacks. The error message and complex/mixed-precision NaN behavior remain unchanged; infinities are still handled separately by the existing error calculation. No FFT or registration algorithm changes are included.

The final NaN check alone improved **2.54x-2.67x** for finite statistics. Complete unmasked float32 registration calls improved **1.03x-1.08x** at 512 x 512 and 2048 x 2048, including the FFTs and peak search. When the first statistic is NaN, the check was within about 1.4 microseconds of the previous short-circuit path.

### Float-to-integer validation and conversion

Use packed, NaN-propagating image extrema for float-to-integer conversion in `util.dtype._convert`. Transfer the bounds together and evaluate the permitted `[-1, 1]` range on the host, replacing separate GPU predicates and up to two scalar readbacks. After validation, a fused elementwise pass scales, rounds, clips, and writes the integer output directly. Signed/unsigned and uniform/nonuniform variants keep their separately rounded arithmetic. Half-precision computation and the legacy uniform-uint64 error retain the old path. NaNs continue to suppress range validation errors.

Complete float32 conversion gains from the review follow-ups:

| Spatial size | `img_as_ubyte` | `img_as_int` |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 16 x 16 | 1.33x | 1.45x |
| 512 x 512 | 1.31x | 1.39x |
| 2048 x 2048 | 1.80x | 2.03x |
| 4096 x 4096 | 2.58x | 2.97x |

Float64 at 2048 x 2048 improved 1.69x and 1.90x respectively. Computing both extrema upfront costs more on early lower-bound rejection (148 to 232 microseconds at 4096 x 4096).

### Chan-Vese initialization normalization

Compute original-image extrema once, then fuse shifting and normalization in one elementwise pass. The zero-range decision stays on the GPU. This removes the two shifted-maximum reductions and their host conditional/readback, and avoids materializing the shifted image separately. Constant images remain zero after shifting, and nonfinite values retain their propagation behavior. The iterative segmentation solver is unchanged.

The normalization gain is larger than the gain for complete segmentation:

| Scope | Pre-change/current |
| --- | ---: |
| Initialization normalization only | 1.19x-2.48x |
| Complete segmentation, checkerboard initialization | 1.01x-1.05x |
| Complete segmentation, disk initialization | 1.06x-1.09x |

The complete float32 calls at 512 x 512 and 2048 x 2048 used `max_num_iter=10`: checkerboard ran all ten iterations, while disk converged after one. Initialization accounts for more of the shorter disk call; these results do not establish gains for longer solves. The smaller gains are sensitive to timing variation.

### `threshold_li` scalar initial-guess range validation

Reuse the shifted-image maximum when validating a scalar `initial_guess`, and reconstruct the original maximum only if the error message is needed. This removes one redundant maximum reduction and an unnecessary scalar GPU addition on valid guesses. Keep the shifted maximum rather than substituting `original_max - original_min`, preserving signed-integer subtraction behavior. The existing filtering, early returns, default tolerance calculation, and iterative update remain unchanged.

Scalar initial-guess validation alone improved **1.55x-1.74x**. Complete `threshold_li` calls with a scalar initial guess and explicit tolerance were close to unchanged: **0.98x-1.05x** in the common finite float32 sweep. The component speedup therefore has little effect on total thresholding time.

## Benchmark methodology and scripts

Measurements used an RTX A6000, `rapids-26.04-py313`, CuPy 14.2.0, and `cupyx.profiler.benchmark(max_duration=2.0)` with ten warmups.

title: Faster batch filled-region properties (`regionprops_table`: "area_filled", "label_filled")
body:
## Context

This PR builds on top of the regionprops bug fixes in !1196 and the regionprops performance improvements in !1198, in that order. Please review those first; until they merge, this PR's diff also contains their commits, so review only the commits listed under "Commits" below.

This PR speeds up the batch filled-region properties (`area_filled`, `num_pixels_filled`, `image_filled`, `label_filled` of
`regionprops_table(..., batch_processing=True)` / `regionprops_dict`). The bug-fix PR !1196 made them correct, filling each region's holes as scikit-image does, but 2–3× slower than `main`'s incorrect implementation, and 27× slower on an image of nested regions (4.0 → 109.9 ms), because of a per-label fallback (see "Filled-region properties" in `regionprops_batch_bugfixes_pr_description.md`). The performance PR did not change them. This PR is stacked on the performance PR (!1198).

The results are unchanged: on every benchmark input, `num_pixels_filled` equals scikit-image's for every label, and after every commit `label_filled` and the set of labels recomputed one by one are identical to those before the commit, on the benchmark inputs and on 60 random 2D and 3D images of nested regions.

## Summary

| # | Commit | What it changes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Fill the holes of all inexact labels in one canvas | the per-label fallback becomes one batched fill |
| 2 | Flag the inexactly filled labels in one kernel | replaces a loop of masked lookups over the neighbor offsets |
| 3 | Find the labels around each hole in one kernel | replaces a grey dilation, a grey erosion and contended `ufunc.at` scatters |
| 4 | Label the background and the labels' components together | one labeling instead of two when labels touch |
| 5 | Fill the crops of inexact labels in memory-bounded batches | the canvas of commit 1 is split so that nested labels cannot exhaust the device memory |
| 6 | Fill the holes of images of more than 2³¹ pixels | less memory per pixel, no 2³¹ limit on the canvas, and a canvas no wider than its boxes |

`area_filled`, GPU time against the performance PR:

| Input | Labels | Recomputed | Before | After | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| tiles 2160 × 3840, 32 × 32 | 8227 | 0 | 14.21 ms | 4.03 ms | 3.5× |
| tiles 2160 × 3840, 127 × 128 | 557 | 0 | 14.02 ms | 4.42 ms | 3.2× |
| `binary_blobs` 4096² | 240 | 0 | 19.50 ms | 6.01 ms | 3.2× |
| 4 noise levels 2048² | 3128 | 228 | 191.26 ms | 11.41 ms | 16.8× |
| 4 noise levels 192³ | 861 | 2 | 50.05 ms | 20.47 ms | 2.4× |

"Recomputed" is the number of labels whose filled region the batch fill cannot settle (nested or multiply-bordered holes). On the tilings and the blobs, the properties are now faster than `main`'s incorrect implementation was on similar inputs (5.8 and 9.6 ms in the bug-fix PR's measurements, on tilings of 1024 and 16 256 rectangles and the same blobs).

## How the batch fill works

(From the bug-fix PR, unchanged in substance.) The background of the image padded by one pixel is labeled with full connectivity; every background component except the one touching the padding is a hole. A hole bordered by a single label is filled with it, which is exactly scikit-image's result for that label. A label's result can differ only if (a) it borders a hole that also borders other labels, or (b) a connected component of another label touches it and lies strictly inside its bounding box; such labels are
recomputed with `binary_fill_holes` on their crop.

## Commits

### 1. Fill the holes of all inexact labels in one canvas

The recomputation was a host loop, about 0.8 ms per label: 188 of the 191 ms on the nested noise levels, with 228 such labels.

`_fill_holes_of_labels` now packs the crops (`label_image[bbox] == label`) into one canvas, with one background pixel around each (shelf packing, tallest first), copies them with one kernel, and fills all of them with one `binary_fill_holes` call. The background at each crop's border is connected to the canvas border through the gaps, so a crop's holes are exactly those it has on its own. The filled pixels of each crop are counted with the label-run count of a box-index image: `cupy.bincount` with weights contended on its few bins (30 ms for two boxes). `image_filled` takes views of the filled canvas. On the nested noise levels, the crops add up to 3.25 times the image.

| Input | Before | After | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| tiles 2160 × 3840, 32 × 32 | 14.21 ms | 14.29 ms | 1.0× |
| tiles 2160 × 3840, 127 × 128 | 14.02 ms | 14.15 ms | 1.0× |
| `binary_blobs` 4096² | 19.50 ms | 19.59 ms | 1.0× |
| 4 noise levels 2048² | 191.26 ms | 19.12 ms | 10.0× |
| 4 noise levels 192³ | 50.05 ms | 51.48 ms | 0.97× |

On the 192³ image the two recomputed labels each span the whole volume, so there is nothing to batch. Test: `test_fill_holes_of_labels_batch` compares every label of nested 2D and 3D label images with one `binary_fill_holes` call per crop.

### 2. Flag the inexactly filled labels in one kernel

Test (b) looped over the 3ⁿ − 1 neighbor offsets, each with masked lookups (a host synchronization each), built (label, component) pairs and took their unique values; test (a) dilated the mask of the multi-label holes. That took 28 ms on the 192³ image and 7 ms on the 2160 × 3840 tiling.

`_get_inexact_fill_labels_kernel` now does both: each pixel of a label A tests its neighbors and flags A if a neighbor is background in a multi-label hole (a), or belongs to another label's component whose bounding box lies strictly inside A's (b). Pixels of an already flagged label skip the test.

| Input | Before | After | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| tiles 2160 × 3840, 32 × 32 | 14.29 ms | 7.36 ms | 1.9× |
| tiles 2160 × 3840, 127 × 128 | 14.15 ms | 8.00 ms | 1.8× |
| `binary_blobs` 4096² | 19.59 ms | 19.53 ms | 1.0× |
| 4 noise levels 2048² | 19.12 ms | 13.91 ms | 1.4× |
| 4 noise levels 192³ | 51.48 ms | 22.97 ms | 2.2× |

The blobs do not touch each other, so test (b) does not run there.

### 3. Find the labels around each hole in one kernel

The largest and smallest label bordering each background component came from a grey dilation and a grey erosion of the whole image, scattered per component with `cupy.maximum.at` and `cupy.minimum.at` over every background pixel. Almost all of them belong to the component outside of the regions, so these atomics all went to one address: 14 ms on the 4096² blobs.

`_get_hole_neighbors_kernel` now does this: a background pixel in a hole adds the largest and smallest label among its neighbors to its hole's entry with atomics, and the outer component's pixels are skipped. The pixel coordinate and neighbor code is shared with the kernel of commit 2.

| Input | Before | After | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| tiles 2160 × 3840, 32 × 32 | 7.36 ms | 5.10 ms | 1.4× |
| tiles 2160 × 3840, 127 × 128 | 8.00 ms | 5.64 ms | 1.4× |
| `binary_blobs` 4096² | 19.53 ms | 5.67 ms | 3.4× |
| 4 noise levels 2048² | 13.91 ms | 12.40 ms | 1.1× |
| 4 noise levels 192³ | 22.97 ms | 20.49 ms | 1.1× |

### 4. Label the background and the labels' components together

When two labels touch, the image was labeled twice: the background (for the holes) and the labels (for test (b)). One labeling of the padded image with every value as its own class, the background included (`label(..., background=-1)`), gives both and costs 0.9–1.6 ms less than the two. A new kernel first checks whether any two labels touch; if not, only the background is labeled, as before. The component boxes are computed over the labeled pixels only, so the outer background component does not contend.

| Input | Before | After | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| tiles 2160 × 3840, 32 × 32 | 5.10 ms | 4.03 ms | 1.27× |
| tiles 2160 × 3840, 127 × 128 | 5.64 ms | 4.42 ms | 1.28× |
| `binary_blobs` 4096² | 5.67 ms | 6.01 ms | 0.94× |
| 4 noise levels 2048² | 12.40 ms | 11.41 ms | 1.09× |
| 4 noise levels 192³ | 20.49 ms | 20.47 ms | 1.0× |

Images whose labels do not touch (the blobs) pay 0.3 ms for the check and gain nothing; images of touching labels, common in segmentations, gain about 1 ms. This commit can be dropped without affecting the others if that trade-off is not wanted.

### 5. Fill the crops of inexact labels in memory-bounded batches

The canvas of commit 1 holds the sum of the crops, which can be far more than the image: for the concentric cubical shells of a 512³ `int16` label image (0.25 GiB, 255 crops of side 512, 510, ..., 4) it is `(5208, 514, 4745)` pixels, 59 GiB for the `bool` canvas and the `int32` box ids alone, so even `num_pixels_filled` or `area_filled` failed where the per-crop fallback worked (found in review).

`_fill_holes_of_labels` now splits the labels, largest crops first so that the crops of a batch have similar extents, until the canvas of each batch has at most `_canvas_pixel_limit()` pixels: a quarter of the free device memory (including the memory pool's free blocks) at 16 bytes per pixel (the canvas and box ids, the filled canvas, the temporaries of `binary_fill_holes` and the counted label image), and fewer than 2³¹ pixels. A crop larger than the limit is filled alone, as before the batch fill. With several batches `image_filled` returns copies, so each canvas is freed. Nothing changes when one batch is enough, as on all the inputs above. A 256³ `int16` shell image (64 labels, 32 MiB) needs a 7 GiB pool and takes 0.18 s warm. Test: `test_fill_holes_of_labels_batch` also runs with a 4000-pixel limit and a one-pixel limit (one crop per batch).

### 6. Fill the holes of images of more than 2³¹ pixels

The kernels already index with 64 bits, and the labelings return `int64` labels beyond 2³¹ pixels, so such images worked but needed more than 20 bytes per pixel. On a 48 GB GPU, a `uint8` image of 2³¹ + 2¹⁵ pixels with touching labels ran out of memory. Now:

- `_fill_holes_by_label` drops the padded image as soon as it is labeled, builds `label_filled` from the unpadded labels, and passes the component ids of the box pass as `int32` when they fit.
- The canvas holes come from one labeling of the inverted canvas (`_fill_canvas_holes`) instead of `binary_fill_holes`, which pads the canvas and assigns through a boolean mask (an 8-byte index per pixel). The result is identical, and 10-20 % faster on canvases of 1M to 17M pixels (1.19 to 0.92 ms for 1024², 5.23 to 4.33 ms for 4096², 7.24 to 6.45 ms for 256³).
- `_pack_crops` no longer makes the canvas wider than all its boxes side by side. One tall crop had a canvas of the width of a square, 23 times larger than the crop (found with the test below; it affected every size).
- The canvas is no longer limited to 2³¹ pixels.

Measured on 2³¹ + 2¹⁵ pixels (1 048 592 × 2048, `uint8`), with nested and ring labels on both sides of the 2³¹ mark, the `num_pixels_filled` of every label equal to the known values: no touching labels, peak pool 44 to 24 GiB; touching labels, out of memory to 38 GiB. A single inexact label whose crop has 2.15 × 10⁹ pixels (nested labels in a hole) is filled correctly and peaks at 40 GiB. These images were run by hand (they need more than 40 GB), not in the test suite; the new tests cover `_pack_crops`, and `_fill_holes_by_label` for `uint8`, `int16` and `int64` labels.

## How it was measured

- RTX A6000, CuPy 14.2, CUDA 13; scikit-image 0.26 for the exactness checks.
- `regionprops-perf/filled_bench.py` (not committed here): the GPU time of `regionprops_dict(labels, properties=["area_filled"], max_label=...)`, the median of 20 runs after 0.3 s of warm-up, and the number of labels whose `num_pixels_filled` differs from scikit-image's (0 for every input and commit).
- Inputs (`regionprops-perf/filled_inputs.py`):
  - **Tiles:** rectangles of 32 × 32 or 127 × 128 pixels covering a 2160 × 3840 frame, all touching.
  - **`binary_blobs` 4096²:** `blob_size_fraction=0.02`, `volume_fraction=0.5`, labeled; the blobs do not touch.
  - **4 noise levels:** Gaussian-smoothed uniform noise (σ = 8 in 2D, 4 in 3D) split into 4 levels at its 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles, with the connected components of each level labeled, so that many regions are nested in others with no gap.
- Equivalence: after each commit, `label_filled` and the labels recomputed one by one were compared with the previous commit's on these inputs and on 60 random 2D and 3D images of nested regions (smoothed noise levels with 5 % of the pixels set to background).

## Testing

- New test: `test_fill_holes_of_labels_batch` (2D and 3D, three canvas limits).
- The existing filled-region tests (`test_regionprops_dict_filled` with its 8 nested and touching cases, `test_regionprops_dict_filled_random`, `test_label_filled`, `test_fill_holes_by_label_tiling_is_exact`) pass after every commit.

title: Batch convex-hull region properties
body:
## Context

This PR builds on top of the regionprops bug fixes in #1196, the regionprops performance improvements in #1198 and the faster filled-region properties in #1208, in that order. Please review and merge those first; until they merge, this PR's diff also contains their commits, so review only the commits listed under "Commits" below.

The primary goal of this PR is to remove the per-label device↔host round trip through Qhull when computing convex-hull properties, by computing the hulls of all labels at once on the device. This is fully achieved for the 2D properties. In 3D, this PR reduces each label to a small set of candidate points on the device and moves them to the host in one transfer for all labels, but Qhull still runs once per label on the host; moving the 3D hull itself to the GPU is done in a follow-up PR (hull3d).

**Caveat on correctness.** I am not an expert in convex-hull algorithms, and the implementation was written with an AI agent. I have not proven it correct; I verified it empirically, against scikit-image's own results as the oracle. This is how much confidence the tests support:

- *Well supported:* `image_convex`, `area_convex`, `solidity` and `feret_diameter_max` equal scikit-image's (rtol 1e-12) in 2D and 3D, with and without anisotropic spacing, on the test inputs: blobs, large blobs, thin digital lines in random directions (nearly collinear hull edges), and random multi-component labels with absent labels and rows without pixels. These are fixed-seed tests that run in CI (`test_row_extents`, `test_area_convex_and_solidity_batch_2d`, `test_image_convex_batch_2d`, `test_convex_batch_3d`, `test_feret_diameter_max_batch_2d` and `_3d`). The 2D hull uses exact integer arithmetic, so near-collinear points are not a floating-point risk. Each commit was also compared on larger random campaigns (4056 2D and 929 3D regions for the areas and images, 803 3D regions for the Feret diameter); those campaigns were run by hand, and only the smaller fixed cases are in the test suite.
- *Weaker:* behavior outside those inputs is untested. That includes images much larger than the test images (the 64-bit coordinate path of images with an axis of 2³⁰ pixels or more is tested only by forcing it on a small image, `test_convex_batch_64bit_coordinates`), and adversarial shapes beyond thin lines. In 3D the hull itself comes from SciPy's qhull, as in scikit-image, so the risk is in the GPU candidate reduction (below), not in the hull.
- *No oracle:* for 3D regions whose voxel centers are coplanar, scikit-image's qhull fails, so there is nothing to compare with. The result there follows the definition in "Behavior changes", and `test_convex_flat_3d` checks it on a few constructed cases. 426 of the 3D regions in the random campaign were skipped for this reason.

This PR computes the convex-hull properties of the batch regionprops implementation (`regionprops_table(..., batch_processing=True)` / `regionprops_dict`) for all labels at once, instead of one convex image per label. It is stacked on the performance PR (`grelee/regionprops-batch-perf`), and follows the design in `regionprops_batch_convex_hull_design.md`.

The properties are `image_convex`, `area_convex`, `solidity` and `feret_diameter_max`. Before this PR they were the last batch properties that loop over the labels on the host, at 0.4–2 ms per label in 2D (slower than scikit-image on the CPU) and 3.5–5.7 ms per label in 3D.

Each commit is one step, with its own tests and A/B benchmark. All four properties now equal scikit-image's results wherever scikit-image succeeds,in 2D and 3D; see "Behavior changes".

## Summary

| # | Commit | What it changes | Main effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Find each region's first and last pixel in each row | new label-run pass (not used yet) | 0.23–0.34 ms per image |
| 2 | Compute 2D area_convex for all labels at once | 2D `area_convex`, `solidity` | 640–6600× faster; equal to scikit-image |
| 3 | Build the 2D hull chains without reading back vertices | 2D hull kernel | 2D `area_convex` 1.2–2.5× faster |
| 4 | Compute 2D image_convex for all labels at once | 2D `image_convex`, `regionprops_image` | 280–540× faster; equal to scikit-image |
| 5 | Compute 2D feret_diameter_max as scikit-image does | 2D `feret_diameter_max` | 590–9500× faster; now equal to scikit-image (was up to 2 pixels short) |
| 6 | Compute 3D convex images and areas for all labels at once | 3D `image_convex`, `area_convex`, `solidity` | 13–19× faster; equal to scikit-image |
| 7 | Compute 3D feret_diameter_max as scikit-image does | 3D `feret_diameter_max` | 6.7–12.6× faster; now equal to scikit-image |
| 8 | Test the 64-bit path of the batch convex-hull kernels | tests only | |

Overall, against `grelee/regionprops-batch-perf` (wall time of `regionprops_dict(labels, properties=[prop])`, see "How it was measured"):

| Input | Labels | `area_convex` | `solidity` | `image_convex` | `feret_diameter_max` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| tiles 2160×3840, 128×128 | 510 | 739 → 0.53 ms | 763 → 0.57 ms | 733 → 1.42 ms | 1091 → 0.59 ms |
| tiles 2160×3840, 32×32 | 8160 | 4135 → 0.52 ms | 3950 → 0.55 ms | 3714 → 14.1 ms | 8935 → 0.60 ms |
| `binary_blobs` 2048², 0.02 | 823 | 581 → 0.64 ms | 579 → 0.67 ms | 545 → 2.10 ms | 1088 → 0.82 ms |
| one label, 2160×3840 | 1 | 11.2 → 1.18 ms | 11.5 → 1.21 ms | 11.5 → 1.34 ms | 23.4 → 1.81 ms |
| `binary_blobs` 128³, 0.05 | 380 | 1473 → 105 ms | 1501 → 105 ms | 1444 → 105 ms | 2321 → 130 ms |
| `binary_blobs` 192³, 0.03 | 1029 | 4976 → 249 ms | 4814 → 249 ms | 4690 → 255 ms | 8597 → 296 ms |

That is 260–15000× faster in 2D, and 14–29× in 3D, where scipy's qhull now takes most of the time (about 0.2 ms per label, see "Not addressed yet").

Against scikit-image on the CPU (one run of `regionprops_table`):

| Input | Labels | Property | scikit-image (ms) | This PR (ms) | Speedup |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| tiles 2160×3840, 128×128 | 510 | `area_convex` | 688 | 0.53 | 1300× |
| | | `image_convex` | 673 | 1.42 | 470× |
| | | `feret_diameter_max` | 1201 | 0.59 | 2000× |
| tiles 2160×3840, 32×32 | 8160 | `area_convex` | 2703 | 0.52 | 5200× |
| | | `image_convex` | 2597 | 14.1 | 180× |
| | | `feret_diameter_max` | 4745 | 0.60 | 7900× |
| `binary_blobs` 2048², 0.02 | 823 | `area_convex` | 473 | 0.64 | 740× |
| | | `image_convex` | 464 | 2.10 | 220× |
| | | `feret_diameter_max` | 744 | 0.82 | 910× |
| one label, 2160×3840 | 1 | `area_convex` | 336 | 1.18 | 280× |
| | | `image_convex` | 327 | 1.34 | 240× |
| | | `feret_diameter_max` | 936 | 1.81 | 520× |
| `binary_blobs` 128³, 0.05 | 380 | `area_convex` | 6325 | 105 | 60× |
| | | `image_convex` | 7040 | 105 | 67× |
| | | `feret_diameter_max` | 45089 | 130 | 350× |
| `binary_blobs` 192³, 0.03 | 1029 | `area_convex` | 22220 | 249 | 89× |
| | | `image_convex` | 23111 | 255 | 91× |
| | | `feret_diameter_max` | `MemoryError` | 296 | |

The scikit-image times of the tilings, the 2048² blobs and the 128³ blobs are from the measurements in the design document (same inputs and machine). On the 192³ blobs, scikit-image's `feret_diameter_max` raises `MemoryError`: `pdist` over the marching-cubes vertices of the largest region needs 182 GiB.

## How it works

All the convex-hull properties come from one label-run pass that records, for every row of each region's bounding box, the first and last column of the region in that row (commit 1).

- **Why row extents are enough.** scikit-image's `convex_hull_image` takes the hull of each pixel's diamond points (its center ± 0.5 along each axis). The diamond points of a pixel between a row's first and last pixel lie on segments between those of the two ends, so the hull of the row ends' diamond points is the same polygon.
- **2D hull (commit 2).** One thread per label runs Andrew's monotone chain over these points, in doubled integer coordinates, so the arithmetic is exact. On each horizontal line only the leftmost and rightmost point can be a vertex, and the points come sorted by row, so no sort is needed. The result is a left chain and a right chain.
- **Area (commit 2).** One thread per row of each bounding box finds the row's pixel centers inside the polygon. They form one interval of columns, found from the chain edge at that row on each side with exact integer ceil and floor divisions. Centers on an edge are inside, as with scikit-image's `grid_points_in_poly(..., include_borders=True)`. The interval lengths are added per label.
- **Image (commit 4).** One kernel writes all convex images into one buffer from the row intervals.
- **Feret diameter (commit 5).** scikit-image's `feret_diameter_max` is the largest distance between the level-0.5 contour points of the convex image. For a binary image these are the diamond points of its boundary pixels, so the largest distance is reached at two vertices of the hull of the convex image's row ends. The same chain kernel builds that hull from the row intervals, and one warp per label takes the largest distance between the vertices.
- **3D (commits 6 and 7).** The same row extents give the 3D candidates: the vertices of the 2D hull of the candidate points in each plane (in doubled coordinates, the planes of the region and the planes halfway between them), built by the 2D chain kernel for all planes of all labels in two launches. scipy's `ConvexHull` builds each label's hull from these on the host (one transfer each way), and one thread per row intersects the row with the facets as scikit-image's half-space test does. The 3D Feret diameter needs no 3D hull: it is the largest distance between the candidates of the convex image.

## Commits

### 1. Find each region's first and last pixel in each row

A new label-run kernel, `_regionprops_row_extents`.
- **Layout.** The extents of all labels are stored in one flat array. Label l's rows start at the prefix sum of the bounding-box heights (planes × rows in 3D) of the labels before it.
- **Kernel.** Each thread scans 16 pixels of one row, so runs end at row ends. It updates each run's extents with one `atomicMin` and one `atomicMax`.
- **Cost.** The pass, including the prefix sum and the one host synchronization for the total, takes 0.23–0.34 ms on the benchmark inputs (16 pixels per thread was the best of 8, 16, 32 and 64).

Not used by any property yet. Test: `test_row_extents` compares it with NumPy for 2D and 3D, 4 label dtypes, 3 chunk sizes, labels with several components, empty rows and an absent label.

### 2. Compute 2D area_convex for all labels at once

`area_convex`, and so `solidity`, of 2D regions come from the hull of the row extents (see "How it works"). The other convex properties still use one convex image per label in this commit, as does everything in 3D.

The convex properties now depend on `bbox` instead of `image`, and `regionprops_dict` computes them in `_regionprops_convex`.

A/B against commit 1:

| Input | Labels | Property | Before (ms) | After (ms) | Speedup |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| tiles 2160×3840, 128×128 | 510 | `area_convex` | 737.1 | 0.86 | 854× |
| | | `solidity` | 724.6 | 0.88 | 826× |
| tiles 2160×3840, 32×32 | 8160 | `area_convex` | 3936.8 | 0.59 | 6665× |
| | | `solidity` | 4019.0 | 0.62 | 6439× |
| `binary_blobs` 2048², 0.02 | 823 | `area_convex` | 585.9 | 0.87 | 671× |
| | | `solidity` | 590.9 | 0.92 | 642× |
| one label, 2160×3840 | 1 | `area_convex` | 11.5 | 2.90 | 4.0× |
| | | `solidity` | 11.6 | 2.93 | 4.0× |
| `binary_blobs` 128³, 0.05 | 380 | `area_convex` | 1438 | 1404 | 1.0× (3D, unchanged) |

The single label as tall as the frame is the slow case of one thread per label: its 2160 rows are processed by one thread (2.35 ms of the 2.90 ms). Commit 3 shortens it.

**Exactness.** The result equals scikit-image's `area_convex` exactly (rtol 1e-12) on 4056 regions:
- 150 random `binary_blobs` images and 30 random multi-component label images, with and without random anisotropic spacing;
- 60 images of thin digital lines in random directions (nearly collinear hull edges).

Test: `test_area_convex_and_solidity_batch_2d` (exact against scikit-image for blobs, large blobs, thin lines and random multi-component labels with an absent label, with and without spacing).

### 3. Build the 2D hull chains without reading back vertices

One thread builds the hull of each label, so it waits for every memory read and every dependent instruction. On a straight boundary, each new point removed the previous (collinear) one, and the chain read the vertex below it back from global memory: about one memory latency per row.

- **Local filter.** A point that is not a strict turn with its neighboring   points cannot be a vertex, and is skipped before it reaches the chain. On straight and staircase boundaries this skips most points and most removals.
- **Between-row points.** A point on the line between two rows whose ends differ by at most 1 lies on or inside the segment between the rows' points, and is skipped without a cross product.
- **Registers.** The chain keeps its last two vertices in registers.
- **32-bit differences.** Coordinate differences are taken in 32 bits when the coordinates fit, and only the products in 64 bits.

Chain kernel alone (GPU time):

| Input | Commit 2 (ms) | Commit 3 (ms) |
|---|---:|---:|
| tiles 2160×3840, 128×128 | 0.386 | 0.055 |
| tiles 2160×3840, 32×32 | 0.123 | 0.023 |
| one label, 2160×3840 | 2.350 | 0.623 |

A/B against commit 2:

| Input | Labels | Before (ms) | After (ms) | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| tiles 2160×3840, 128×128 | 510 | 0.84 | 0.51 | 1.7× |
| tiles 2160×3840, 32×32 | 8160 | 0.59 | 0.49 | 1.2× |
| `binary_blobs` 2048², 0.02 | 823 | 0.87 | 0.61 | 1.4× |
| one label, 2160×3840 | 1 | 2.91 | 1.18 | 2.5× |

`area_convex`; the results are unchanged (the same 4056 regions match scikit-image exactly).

### 4. Compute 2D image_convex for all labels at once

One kernel writes all 2D convex images into one buffer, one thread per output pixel, from the row intervals of commit 2.
- **Output.** The tuple returned holds one array per label on that buffer:
  `cp.ndarray(shape, memptr=...)` costs about 1.6 µs per label on the host, against 6 µs for slicing and reshaping. At 8160 labels this host loop is most of the remaining 12.8 ms. Absent labels get an empty image, as before.
- **Exactness.** Equal to scikit-image's `image_convex` on the 4056 regions of commit 2.
- **Also changed.** `feret_diameter_max` in 2D takes these images instead of one `convex_hull_image` call per label (its computation is unchanged until commit 5). `regionprops_image(..., compute_convex=True)` uses the same path when the slices are the bounding boxes it computed itself.

A/B against commit 3:

| Input | Labels | Property | Before (ms) | After (ms) | Speedup |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| tiles 2160×3840, 128×128 | 510 | `image_convex` | 735.3 | 1.36 | 541× |
| | | `feret_diameter_max` | 1069.3 | 339.0 | 3.2× |
| tiles 2160×3840, 32×32 | 8160 | `image_convex` | 3808.9 | 12.80 | 298× |
| | | `feret_diameter_max` | 9273.2 | 5354.5 | 1.7× |
| `binary_blobs` 2048², 0.02 | 823 | `image_convex` | 554.5 | 1.96 | 282× |
| | | `feret_diameter_max` | 1111.2 | 526.8 | 2.1× |
| one label, 2160×3840 | 1 | `image_convex` | 11.3 | 1.32 | 8.5× |
| | | `feret_diameter_max` | 23.1 | 13.3 | 1.7× |

Test: `test_image_convex_batch_2d` (exact against scikit-image, empty images for absent labels).

### 5. Compute 2D feret_diameter_max as scikit-image does

The Feret diameter comes from the hull of the convex image's row ends (see "How it works"). This replaces, per label:
- an erosion;
- `argwhere` (one host synchronization);
- `pdist_max_blockwise` over the boundary pixel centers (one synchronization per block).

**Behavior change.** The result now equals scikit-image's (rtol 1e-12 on the 4056 regions of commit 2, with and without anisotropic spacing):
- it was up to about 2 pixels shorter, because it measured between pixel centers;
- a single pixel now has a diameter of 1, as in scikit-image, instead of 0 with a warning.

`regionprops_feret_diameter_max(images_convex)`, which takes arbitrary convex images, keeps its previous definition.

A/B against commit 4:

| Input | Labels | Before (ms) | After (ms) | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| tiles 2160×3840, 128×128 | 510 | 342.3 | 0.58 | 592× |
| tiles 2160×3840, 32×32 | 8160 | 5575.1 | 0.59 | 9498× |
| `binary_blobs` 2048², 0.02 | 823 | 530.6 | 0.81 | 654× |
| one label, 2160×3840 | 1 | 13.3 | 1.81 | 7.4× |

Test: `test_feret_diameter_max_batch_2d` (exact against scikit-image for blobs, thin lines and multi-component labels, with and without spacing).

### 6. Compute 3D convex images and areas for all labels at once

3D `image_convex`, `area_convex` and `solidity` no longer build one convex image per label.

1. **Candidates.** In doubled coordinates, the row ends' diamond points lie in the planes z = 2 × plane (the in-plane diamond points of that plane's row ends) and z = 2 × plane ± 1 (the row ends' centers). A vertex of the 3D hull is a vertex of the 2D hull of the points in its plane, so the 2D chain kernel builds these per-plane hulls for all planes of all labels in two launches: the region's planes as before, and the planes between them with a new `centers_only` mode on merged row extents.
2. **Hulls.** The candidates are copied to the host in one transfer, and `scipy.spatial.ConvexHull` runs once per label on them. If qhull fails for a label, that label falls back to `convex_hull_image`.
3. **Rows.** The facet equations are copied back in one transfer. One thread per row of each bounding box intersects the row with the label's facets: a voxel center p is inside if `n · p + b < 1e-10` for every facet, as in scikit-image. Each facet bounds x on one side, so the voxels inside form one interval. The images and areas then come from the row intervals as in 2D.

**Why the per-plane filter.** Without it (only the extreme points of each line), the largest region of the 128³ blobs had 98,778 candidates. With it, the largest has 3,757 and the median label 72.

**Exactness.** Equal to scikit-image's `image_convex` and `area_convex` (rtol 1e-12) on 929 3D regions:
- 120 random 32³ `binary_blobs` images;
- 20 random multi-component label images;
- 20 images of thin digital lines;
- random anisotropic spacing throughout.

426 regions were skipped because scikit-image's own qhull fails on them (see "Behavior changes").

A/B against commit 5:

| Input | Labels | Property | Before (ms) | After (ms) | Speedup |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `binary_blobs` 128³, 0.05 | 380 | `area_convex` | 1371.6 | 107.5 | 12.8× |
| | | `solidity` | 1399.4 | 106.8 | 13.1× |
| | | `image_convex` | 1437.3 | 108.3 | 13.3× |
| | | `feret_diameter_max` | 2287.1 | 919.3 | 2.5× |
| `binary_blobs` 192³, 0.03 | 1029 | `area_convex` | 4850.6 | 254.4 | 19.1× |
| | | `solidity` | 4807.7 | 255.2 | 18.8× |
| | | `image_convex` | 4801.7 | 257.6 | 18.6× |
| | | `feret_diameter_max` | 8300.2 | 3893.0 | 2.1× |

**Where the time goes.** Profiling the 192³ input: the qhull loop takes 0.27 s of 0.30 s, and the GPU steps and candidates 8 ms.
- `ConvexHull` costs 170–200 µs per call even for 58 points.
- Threads do not help: 16 threads reach 126 µs per call.

Tests:
- `test_convex_batch_3d`: exact against scikit-image wherever its hull succeeds, with and without spacing.
- `test_convex_flat_3d`: flat regions and single voxels.

### 7. Compute 3D feret_diameter_max as scikit-image does

scikit-image's 3D Feret diameter is the largest distance between the marching-cubes vertices of the padded convex image at level 0.5. These are the diamond points of its boundary voxels.

The candidates of commit 6, built from the convex image's row intervals:
- contain every vertex of the hull of those points;
- are among those points.

So the largest distance between them is the Feret diameter, and no second 3D hull is needed. The candidates are now gathered on the device (the qhull path copies them to the host in one transfer). One warp per label takes the largest spacing-scaled distance between its candidates.

This also merges the rows of neighboring planes by testing for empty rows, instead of relying on the sentinel values that the rows of convex images do not have.

**Behavior change.** Equal to scikit-image's result (rtol 1e-12, worst relative difference 4e-16) on 803 3D regions with random anisotropic spacing, where it was up to about 2 voxels shorter. Flat regions and single voxels: see "Behavior changes".

A/B against commit 6 (`area_convex`, `solidity` and `image_convex` unchanged, 1.0×):

| Input | Labels | Before (ms) | After (ms) | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `binary_blobs` 128³, 0.05 | 380 | 863.4 | 129.4 | 6.7× |
| `binary_blobs` 192³, 0.03 | 1029 | 3602.3 | 285.6 | 12.6× |

The remaining time is the qhull loop for the convex images that the Feret diameter is computed from.

Tests:
- `test_feret_diameter_max_batch_3d`: exact against scikit-image wherever its hull succeeds.
- `test_convex_flat_3d`: now also checks the Feret diameter of flat regions.

### 8. Test the 64-bit path of the batch convex-hull kernels

Images with an axis of 2³⁰ pixels or more store row extents and hull vertices in 64 bits. `test_convex_batch_64bit_coordinates` forces that path on a small image. The convex images, areas and Feret diameters are unchanged, in 2D and 3D.

## Behavior changes

- **`feret_diameter_max` equals scikit-image's** in 2D and 3D. It used to be up to about 2 pixels shorter, because it measured between pixel centers. A single pixel or voxel now has a diameter of 1, as in scikit-image, instead of 0 with a warning.
- **`image_convex`, `area_convex` and `solidity` equal scikit-image's** in 2D and 3D. Before, they matched only where cuCIM's `convex_hull_image` happened to agree.
- **Regions whose voxel centers are coplanar** (3D regions flat along an axis, single voxels):
  - scikit-image's qhull fails on them. It warns, returns an empty `image_convex` and an `area_convex` of 0, and its `feret_diameter_max` raises.
  - The batch path takes the hull of the diamond points instead. For a region flat along an axis, that is the 2D convex image of the squeezed region, as cuCIM's `convex_hull_image` computed before. The Feret diameter is that of the 2D slice for isotropic spacing only: the diamond points keep a half-voxel extent along the collapsed axis, which dominates for anisotropic spacing (an all-ones `(1, 2, 2)` label image with spacing `(10, 1, 1)` gives √102, against √5 for the squeezed slice).
- **A 2D label confined to a single row with gaps** (or a 3D label confined to a single line) now gets its gaps filled, as in scikit-image. Before, `convex_hull_image` squeezed the crop to 1D and returned it unchanged.
- **`regionprops_image(..., compute_convex=True)`** uses the batch path when it computes the bounding boxes itself. With explicit `slices`, it still calls `convex_hull_image` per label.
- **Unchanged.** `regionprops_feret_diameter_max(images_convex)` and `regionprops_area_convex(images_convex)` take arbitrary convex images and keep their previous definitions. Label images with more than 3 dimensions use the per-label path as before.

## How it was measured

- RTX A6000, CuPy 14.2, CUDA 13.2; scikit-image 0.26, SciPy 1.17.
- `regionprops-perf/convex_ab.py` (not committed): wall time of `regionprops_dict(labels, properties=[prop])`. The old per-label path synchronizes with the host once per label, so wall time is what matters. Each time is the smallest of at least 3 runs (and of as many as fit in 2 s) after a 0.3 s warm-up.
- `regionprops-perf/convex_compare.sh <base> <name>` (not committed) runs it at two commits back to back.
- Inputs: tilings of a 2160×3840 frame into 128×128 and 32×32 rectangles, labeled `binary_blobs` (`volume_fraction=0.25`) in 2D and 3D, and one label covering a 2160×3840 frame.
- `regionprops-perf/convex_skimage.py` (not committed): scikit-image's times (one run each, on the CPU of the same machine).
- Exactness scripts (session scratchpad): random `binary_blobs`, random multi-component labels and thin digital lines, compared with scikit-image region by region.

## Tried, not included

- **Loading 8 rows of extents at a time** in the chain kernel (commit 3), so that a thread waits for memory once per 8 rows. With batches of 1, 4, 8  and 16 rows, 1 or 4 was fastest; after the other changes of commit 3 the chain is bound by instruction latency, not by the row loads.

## Not addressed yet

- **3D hulls on the GPU.** In 3D, scipy's `ConvexHull` now takes most of the time: 170–200 µs per call regardless of size, so about 0.25 ms per label. The median label has only 58–72 candidates. An exact 3D hull on the GPU (one warp or block per label, integer arithmetic on the doubled coordinates) would remove the host loop. A gift-wrapping hull for this is added in a planned stacked PR.
- **Tall labels.** One thread per label still takes 0.62 ms for one label of 2160 rows. A warp per label for tall labels (each lane filters its own rows, then one chain over the survivors) would remove that; not implemented here
- **`image_convex` with many labels** is bound by creating one array per label on the host: about 1.6 µs per label, 13 ms for 8160 labels.

## Testing

- **New tests.** `test_row_extents`, `test_area_convex_and_solidity_batch_2d`, `test_image_convex_batch_2d`, `test_feret_diameter_max_batch_2d`, `test_convex_batch_3d`, `test_convex_flat_3d`, `test_feret_diameter_max_batch_3d`, `test_convex_batch_64bit_coordinates`.
- **Exactness checks against scikit-image.** 4056 2D regions (area, image and Feret diameter), 929 3D regions (image and area) and 803 3D regions (Feret diameter). All are exact; regions where scikit-image's qhull fails were skipped.

title: regionprops: batch 3D convex hulls
body:
## Context

This PR is the fifth in a stack of regionprops PRs. It builds on the regionprops bug fixes in #1196, the performance improvements in #1198, the faster filled-region properties in #1208 and the batch convex-hull work in #1209, in that order. Please review and merge those first; until they merge, this PR's diff also contains their commits, so review only the commits listed under "Commits" below.

**Caveat on correctness.** I am not an expert in convex-hull algorithms, and the implementation was written with an AI agent. I have not proven it correct; I verified it empirically, against QHull and scikit-image as the oracles. This is how much confidence the tests support:

- *Well supported:* the device hull's facets equal qhull's (merging qhull's coplanar triangles) on 228,869 faces over all labels of the 8 benchmark inputs, and on 2,686 more labels of random blobs, random label images and boxes (six seeds, each with all labels on warps, all on blocks and on the default split). End to end, the convex images, areas and Feret diameters equal scikit-image's on 929 (image and area) and 803 (Feret) 3D regions where its qhull succeeds. All the hull tests are exact integer determinants, so near-coplanar points are not a floating-point risk.
- *In CI:* only smaller fixed cases of this evidence run in the test suite: `test_convex_hull_candidates_3d`, `test_convex_hulls_3d` (facets against qhull, warp and block kernels, including a label more than 2¹³ voxels wide that takes the 64-bit scans), `test_convex_batch_3d_host_hulls` (the host fallback), and `test_convex_batch_3d_qhull` (the `convex_hull_3d="qhull"` option). The large comparisons were run by hand (`regionprops-perf/hull3d_check.py`).
- *Weaker:* the gift-wrapping kernel is intricate (pending-edge hash table, coplanar faces, a first face found by a supporting plane), and shapes that neither the benchmark inputs nor the random inputs produce are untested. Labels wider than 2¹⁹ − 2 voxels, or whose hull does not fit the kernel's buffers, are handed to qhull on the host, so the wrong-answer risk there is qhull's, not the kernel's. A single very large label is also slower than qhull (see below), and `convex_hull_3d="qhull"` is the escape hatch if a result is ever in doubt.

This PR computes the 3D convex hulls behind `image_convex`, `area_convex` and `solidity` of the batch regionprops implementation
(`regionprops_table(..., batch_processing=True)` / `regionprops_dict`) on the GPU, instead of with `scipy.spatial.ConvexHull` on the host for each label. It is stacked on the batch convex-hull PR (`grelee/regionprops-batch-convex`), which made every other step of these properties run on the GPU for all labels at once. It implements step 7 of `regionprops_batch_convex_hull_design.md`.

On that branch, 3D was bound by qhull: 170–200 µs per label, one label after the other. With this PR, the hulls of all labels are computed by one kernel. The results do not change: the facets equal qhull's (checked on about 229,000 faces), and the convex images equal scikit-image's wherever its qhull succeeds.

Images with many labels gain the most: 19–79× for `area_convex` end to end with 64 or more labels. **A single very large label is slower than before** (0.4× for one ball of radius 120, see "When the device is slower"), because one label's hull is computed by one block, one face after the other. For such images, `convex_hull_3d="qhull"` keeps the host hulls (commit 3).

## Summary

| # | Commit | What it changes | Main effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Gather each 3D hull candidate once | 3D hull candidates | about 8 % fewer points; 3D `area_convex` 1.06× faster |
| 2 | Compute 3D convex hulls on the GPU | 3D `image_convex`, `area_convex`, `solidity` | 4.5–79× faster on the inputs with 18 or more labels; 0.4× for one very large label |
| 3 | Add an option to compute the 3D hulls with qhull | `convex_hull_3d` keyword of `regionprops_table` and `regionprops_dict` | `"qhull"` keeps the host hulls: 2.5× faster than the device for one very large label |
| 4 | Spread the 3D Feret diameter of a label over many threads | 3D `feret_diameter_max` | 11× faster for the large blobs (1.61 s → 40 ms), 2.3× for the 64 balls; 11× for one very large ball (4.20 s → 374 ms) |

End to end, against `grelee/regionprops-batch-convex` with commit 1 (wall time of `regionprops_dict(labels, properties=[prop])`, see "How it was measured"):

| Input | Labels | Candidates per label (median / max) | `area_convex` | `image_convex` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `binary_blobs` 128³, 0.05 | 380 | 56 / 3,753 | 98.3 → 4.18 ms (23.5×) | 99.6 → 5.01 ms (19.9×) |
| `binary_blobs` 192³, 0.03 | 1029 | 46 / 5,277 | 241 → 5.28 ms (45.6×) | 242 → 7.16 ms (33.7×) |
| `binary_blobs` 256³, 0.1 | 81 | 556 / 10,836 | 137 → 14.3 ms (9.6×) | 138 → 14.9 ms (9.2×) |
| `binary_blobs` 256³, 0.2 | 18 | 2,121 / 12,971 | 75.5 → 16.8 ms (4.5×) | 75.5 → 17.2 ms (4.4×) |
| 512 balls in 256³, r ≈ 11 | 512 | 667 / 817 | 858 → 10.9 ms (78.7×) | 861 → 11.9 ms (72.5×) |
| 64 balls in 256³, r ≈ 25 | 64 | 2,606 / 3,102 | 383 → 20.3 ms (18.9×) | 386 → 20.8 ms (18.6×) |
| one ball in 256³, r ≈ 120 | 1 | 35,993 | 157 → 354 ms (**0.44×**) | 154 → 355 ms (**0.43×**) |
| one label, 192³ | 1 | 2,308 | 3.18 → 2.68 ms (1.19×) | 3.29 → 2.90 ms (1.13×) |

`solidity` follows `area_convex`. `feret_diameter_max` in 3D does not use the hull's facets; it gets faster where it computes the convex image (for example 868 → 18.1 ms for the 512 balls), and commit 4 makes it much faster for large labels.

## How it works

The candidates are those of the convex branch: for each plane of a label's bounding box, the vertices of the 2D hull of the plane's diamond points, and of the points between two planes (doubled integer coordinates). They include every vertex of the 3D hull.

**Gift wrapping, face by face.** The hull is built with gift wrapping (Chand and Kapur [1]):

- **Wrapping around an edge.** Given an edge a → b of a known face, every point lies within half a turn around the edge, so the sign of one 3D orientation test orders two points by angle. One pass over the points finds the point c rotated furthest, and with it the plane of the face on the other side of the edge.
- **Whole faces.** The points come from a voxel grid and have many coplanar subsets (on the larger benchmark inputs, about 60 % of the faces have more than 3 vertices). So the points in the new face's plane are collected, and their 2D hull (Jarvis march [2], in the projection along the normal's largest component) gives the face as a polygon. The wrap also counts the points at c's angle: if c is the only one, the face is the triangle a, c, b, and the second pass is skipped.
- **Pending edges.** Every edge of the hull belongs to two faces, which traverse it in opposite directions. An edge whose reverse has not been seen yet is pending, and wrapping around it finds a new face. The pending edges are kept in a hash table (open addressing, one probe per lane) with a stack for the order.
- **The first face.** The plane z = z_min supports the points, so wrapping around the line along x through the smallest point (in (z, y, x) order) gives a supporting plane. If it touches the hull only in an edge, a second wrap around that edge gives a face.

**Exact arithmetic.** All tests are integer determinants of coordinate differences. They take 64-bit products, or 32×32-bit products in the scans when the label is less than 8192 voxels wide. Labels wider than 2¹⁹ − 2 voxels would overflow 64 bits; they use qhull on the host as before. So would a label whose hull does not fit the kernel's buffers (2n faces and 3n edges for n points, the most a hull can have), which should not happen. The faces' planes are then converted to qhull-style facet equations (normalized, in undoubled coordinates), and the convex-image rows are computed by the existing kernel, with scikit-image's `n · p + b < 1e-10`
test.

**Work division.** One pass over a label's points per face, and the faces are found one after the other, so a label's time grows with
faces × points:

- A label of at most 1024 candidates gets one warp; 16 labels share a block.
- A larger label gets a block of 16 warps. All warps scan the points, and the first warp (the leader) builds the polygon, updates the pending edges and picks the next edge, while the others wait at a barrier.
- The scans load four points per thread before testing them, so that the loads overlap. The reductions shuffle the candidate's coordinates rather than reloading them.

**Provenance.** The kernel was written from the descriptions in [1] and [2], with general CUDA techniques (warp shuffles and votes, block reductions, an open-addressing hash table). No third-party convex-hull code was consulted. The CuACD paper [3] was read when considering the design. This kernel does not use its divide-and-conquer hull, two-lane hull groups, warp quicksort, direction-extreme prefilter or device heap allocator.

## Commits

### 1. Gather each 3D hull candidate once

A plane's left and right hull chains share their first (last) vertex when the plane's top (bottom) line has a single point, and both copies were gathered. A counting pass now skips the shared vertices before the points are gathered. About 8 % of the candidates were duplicates (4,219 of 49,646 in a random test set).

qhull and the Feret diameter do not depend on duplicates, but the device hull identifies vertices by index, so it needs distinct points. The new `test_convex_hull_candidates_3d` checks that the candidates are distinct diamond points that include every hull vertex (it fails before this commit).

| Input | Labels | Property | Before | After | Speedup |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `binary_blobs` 128³, 0.05 | 380 | `area_convex` | 105.8 ms | 99.4 ms | 1.06× |
| | | `feret_diameter_max` | 131.1 ms | 128.1 ms | 1.02× |
| `binary_blobs` 192³, 0.03 | 1029 | `area_convex` | 256.6 ms | 241.4 ms | 1.06× |
| | | `feret_diameter_max` | 286.2 ms | 278.9 ms | 1.03× |

### 2. Compute 3D convex hulls on the GPU

See "How it works". New tests:

- `test_convex_hulls_3d` compares the device facets with qhull's (merging qhull's coplanar triangles), with all labels on warps and all on blocks. It includes a label wider than 8192 voxels, for the 64-bit scans.
- `test_convex_batch_3d_host_hulls` lowers the size limit so that labels go to qhull on the host, and checks that the convex images do not change.

End-to-end timings are in the Summary. The hull stage alone (device kernel against a host loop of `ConvexHull` over the same candidates):

| Input | Labels | Faces | Device | qhull loop | Ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `binary_blobs` 128³, 0.05 | 380 | 9,469 | 1.97 ms | 97.8 ms | 49.5× |
| `binary_blobs` 192³, 0.03 | 1029 | 28,480 | 2.08 ms | 241 ms | 116× |
| `binary_blobs` 256³, 0.1 | 81 | 16,329 | 8.82 ms | 135 ms | 15.3× |
| `binary_blobs` 256³, 0.2 | 18 | 7,512 | 9.63 ms | 66.1 ms | 6.9× |
| 512 balls in 256³, r ≈ 11 | 512 | 110,440 | 4.83 ms | 931 ms | 193× |
| 64 balls in 256³, r ≈ 25 | 64 | 48,208 | 9.25 ms | 369 ms | 39.9× |
| one ball in 256³, r ≈ 120 | 1 | 8,405 | 314 ms | 97.4 ms | 0.31× |
| one label, 192³ | 1 | 26 | 0.68 ms | 1.05 ms | 1.5× |

How the kernel got there (hull stage, same inputs), for reviewers who want to know which parts matter:

| Version | 192³ blobs | 18 large blobs | 64 balls | one ball |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| one warp per label | 5.62 ms | 92.7 ms | 38.6 ms | 4359 ms |
| a block of 8 warps for labels over 256 candidates, every warp doing every step | 2.34 ms | 16.5 ms | 12.1 ms | 652 ms |
| leader warp, triangle shortcut, integer planes; 16 warps for labels over 1024 candidates | 2.01 ms | 11.2 ms | 10.1 ms | 539 ms |
| + hash table for pending edges, unrolled scans, shuffled reductions (this PR) | 2.08 ms | 9.63 ms | 9.25 ms | 314 ms |

### 3. Add an option to compute the 3D hulls with qhull
