`regionprops_table` and `regionprops_dict` take a new keyword, `convex_hull_3d`: `"gpu"` (the default) or `"qhull"`. With `"qhull"`, every 3D hull is computed with `scipy.spatial.ConvexHull` on the host, as before commit 2, and the device kernel is not launched. This is for images with only a few very large, round labels (see "When the device is slower").

The host path now copies the candidates to the host once and the facet equations back once, instead of once per label. (Before, only the few labels too wide for the kernel went through it.)

End to end, `regionprops_dict(labels, properties=["area_convex"], convex_hull_3d=...)`:

| Input | Labels | `"gpu"` | `"qhull"` | `"qhull"` / `"gpu"` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `binary_blobs` 192³, 0.03 | 1029 | 5.00 ms | 239 ms | 47.9× slower |
| 64 balls in 256³, r ≈ 25 | 64 | 19.3 ms | 366 ms | 18.9× slower |
| `binary_blobs` 256³, 0.2 | 18 | 16.3 ms | 72.2 ms | 4.4× slower |
| one ball in 256³, r ≈ 120 | 1 | 351 ms | 142 ms | **2.5× faster** |

### 4. Spread the 3D Feret diameter of a label over many threads

`feret_diameter_max` in 3D takes the largest distance between all candidates of a label. That all-pairs loop ran on one warp per label, so its time grew with the square of the candidates of the largest label (21,286 candidates: 1.56 s for one ball).

Each label now gets enough threads to cover its candidates (a multiple of 32, at most `_FERET_MAX_THREADS` = 2²⁴ threads in all, so that many small labels stay cheap). Thread t takes every `threads`-th candidate and its distances to all later ones, and the maxima are combined with `atomicMax` on the bits of the squared distance (the bits of a non-negative double order like integers). The results are bit-identical to before.

`regionprops_dict(labels, properties=["feret_diameter_max"])`, wall time:

| Input | Labels | Before | After | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `binary_blobs` 128³, 0.05 | 380 | 28.0 ms | 7.67 ms | 3.7× |
| `binary_blobs` 192³, 0.03 | 1029 | 37.2 ms | 9.28 ms | 4.0× |
| `binary_blobs` 256³, 0.1 | 81 | 735 ms | 28.5 ms | 25.8× |
| `binary_blobs` 256³, 0.2 | 18 | 1,613 ms | 40.5 ms | 39.8× |
| 512 balls in 256³, r ≈ 11 | 512 | 17.1 ms | 16.0 ms | 1.07× |
| 64 balls in 256³, r ≈ 25 | 64 | 69.3 ms | 30.7 ms | 2.3× |
| one ball in 256³, r ≈ 120 | 1 | 4,202 ms | 374 ms | 11.2× |
| one label, 192³ | 1 | 18.7 ms | 4.86 ms | 3.8× |

For the one ball of 21,286 candidates (r = 90 in 192³), the kernel alone goes from about 1.4 s to 12.5 ms; the rest is the construction of the candidates, which `area_convex` and `image_convex` share. The time of the 3D `feret_diameter_max` for one very large label is now that of its candidates and rows, not of the all-pairs loop. New test: `test_feret_diameter_max_batch_3d_thread_cap` (with the cap lowered to one warp per label the results are equal). The cap was also run by hand with 600,000 labels (more than the 524,288 at which it reaches one warp), with results equal to the previous kernel's.

## When the device is slower

A single label's hull takes one block, and its faces are found one after the other. Each face costs one or two passes over all the label's points. So the time for one label grows roughly with faces × points, while qhull grows roughly with the points alone. For one label of growing size (hull stage only):

| Label | Candidates | Faces | Device | qhull | Ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| one ball, r = 20 | 1,814 | 530 | 4.70 ms | 4.34 ms | 0.92× |
| one ball, r = 40 | 5,655 | 1,526 | 17.8 ms | 12.7 ms | 0.72× |
| one ball, r = 60 | 10,955 | 2,861 | 47.4 ms | 24.6 ms | 0.52× |
| one ball, r = 80 | 17,517 | 4,187 | 93.2 ms | 43.3 ms | 0.46× |
| one ball, r = 100 | 25,347 | 6,143 | 178 ms | 67.4 ms | 0.38× |
| one ellipsoid, 30 × 60 × 120 | 6,816 | 2,900 | 34.0 ms | 21.1 ms | 0.62× |
| one ellipsoid, 15 × 40 × 150 | 3,297 | 2,006 | 17.4 ms | 10.3 ms | 0.59× |

For one round label, qhull was faster in every case measured, and also for the largest of the 18 blobs (12,971 candidates, 508 faces: 10.0 ms on the device, 6.4 ms with qhull). A label with very few faces can be faster on the device even alone: the 192³ volume that is one label (2,308 candidates, 26 faces) took 0.68 ms against 1.05 ms (`hull3d_stage.csv`). The device wins by running many labels at once: with n labels of similar size, the device time stays close to one label's, while qhull's grows n times. For 64 balls of r ≈ 25 this is 9.25 ms against 369 ms. Labels that are not round have far fewer faces for their number of points, and are much faster on the device than round ones of the same size (10.0 ms for that blob, 47.4 ms for a ball of 10,955 candidates).

For the one ball of r ≈ 120, the time per face splits into these parts (in clock cycles, from timers in a scratch copy of the kernel):

| Part | Cycles per face |
|---|---:|
| wrap scan | 38,000 |
| coplanar scan (non-triangles) | 24,000 |
| leader's polygon and edges | 7,200 |
| broadcast | 1,400 |

The two scans read all 36,000 points (430 kB, more than the L1 cache) from L2 for every face, on one SM.

**Is a ball the worst case?** Nearly, if a label's size is measured by the volume of its hull. In 191 labels with hulls over 1,000 voxels (balls, random ellipsoids, rough and thinned balls, blobs, boxes and helical tubes), faces ≤ about 3.5·√(hull volume) held for all of them. Balls and ellipsoids reach 2.8–3.0·√(hull volume), rough balls and small blobs up to 3.3. By candidate count, a ball is not the worst case: an ellipsoid flat along z has 0.61 faces per candidate, balls 0.23–0.34. The hull volume is not known in
advance, though. The best estimate available beforehand, from the per-plane hull areas, is within 8 % for round labels but up to 59× too high for large branching blobs. It could order the labels for a race, but not route them by a fixed rule. Details: `regionprops-perf/hull3d_faces_note.md`.

For now, `convex_hull_3d="qhull"` (commit 3) lets users choose the host hulls for such images.

Options, if single large labels matter. None of these is implemented here.

- **Hybrid.** Compute the few largest labels with qhull on the host, while the kernel runs on the others.
  - **Fixed rule.** Choose those labels from their candidate counts. The best choice depends on how long the device would take for each label, and that depends on the face count, which is not known in advance (508 faces for the 12,971-candidate blob, 2,861 for the 10,955-candidate ball).
  - **Racing.** Let a host thread race the kernel (qhull releases the GIL), and have the kernel skip the labels the host has finished.
- **Per-plane queries (Chan [4]).** The candidates of one plane are a convex polygon. The wrap's furthest point in each plane could then be found by binary search, which needs about planes × log(points per plane) tests per face instead of the number of points (about 10× fewer for the large ball).
- **Divide and conquer (Preparata and Hong [5]).** O(n log n) work instead of faces × points. This is the core of CuACD's hull [3], in the integer formulation of Bullet's `btConvexHullComputer` (zlib license). That code would need a license check before anyone reads it.

## How it was measured

- **Hardware and software.** NVIDIA RTX A6000 (driver 595.71.05), Intel Core
  i9-10980XE, CuPy 14.2.0, SciPy 1.17.1, scikit-image 0.26.0.
- **End to end.** `regionprops-perf/convex_ab.py` (not committed): the smallest wall time of at least 3 runs of `regionprops_dict(labels, properties=[prop])`, after a 0.3 s warm-up. The A/B runs used `convex_compare.sh` with `CONVEX_AB_3D_ONLY=1 CONVEX_AB_LARGE_3D=1`, plus the same steps for commit
- **Inputs.**
  - `binary_blobs(..., volume_fraction=0.25, rng=0)`, labeled.
  - Balls on a grid with a spacing of 32 or 64 voxels, with radii 0.8–1.0 times 12 or 28.
  - One ball of radius 0.8–1.0 times 133.
  - A volume that is all one label.
- **Configuration.** The warp/block threshold (1024 candidates) and the block size (16 warps) were chosen on these inputs. Sixteen warps were about 20 % faster than 8 for labels of 10,000 candidates or more, and about 25 % slower for the 512 balls.

## Not addressed yet

- **Single very large labels** (see "When the device is slower"), apart from the `convex_hull_3d="qhull"` option.

## Testing

- `pytest python/cucim/src/cucim/skimage/measure`: 1778 passed, 178 skipped.
  The convex, Feret and row-extent tests alone: 157 passed.
- `test_convex_batch_3d_qhull`: with `convex_hull_3d="qhull"`, the convex images, areas and Feret diameters equal the device's, through both `regionprops_dict` and `regionprops_table`, without launching the device kernel; another value raises `ValueError`.
- **Facets against qhull.** The device facets equal qhull's, merging qhull's coplanar triangles:
  - 228,869 faces over all labels of the 8 benchmark inputs
    (`regionprops-perf/hull3d_check.py`: not committed);
  - 2,686 more labels of random blobs, random label images and boxes (six seeds), each with all labels on warps, all on blocks and on the default split.
- **Against scikit-image.** The convex images, areas and Feret diameters of 929 (convex image and area) and 803 (Feret) 3D regions equal scikit-image's (the regions where its qhull succeeds), as on the convex branch.
